**Create a Linux application by using an orchestration template**

In an orchestration template, you must define the resource objects that are required for running an application and configure mechanisms such as label selectors to manage the resource objects that make up the application. This section describes how to use an orchestration template to create an NGINX application that consists of a Deployment and a Service. The Deployment provisions pods for the application and the Service manages access to the pods at the backend.
1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click Clusters.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the ACK cluster in which your application is deployed, and click the cluster
name or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the Cluster Information page, choose **Workloads > Deployments**.
5. In the upper part of the Deployments page, select a namespace and click **Create from Template**.
6. Configure the parameters and click **Create**.
**Sample Template**: ACK provides YAML templates of various resource types. This simplifies the
deployment of resource objects. You can also create a custom template based on the YAML syntax to define the resources that you want to create.
**Add Deployment**: This feature allows you to define a YAML template.
**Use Existing Template**: You can import an existing template to the configuration page.
**Save As**: You can save the template that you have configured.
The following sample template is based on an orchestration template provided by ACK. You can use this template to create a Deployment to run an NGINX application.

> **Note:** ACK supports Kubernetes YAML orchestration. You can use three hyphens ( `---` ) to separate resource objects. This allows you to define multiple resource objects in one template.
> **Optional:** By default, when you mount a volume to an application, the files in the mount target are overwritten. To avoid overwriting the existing files, you can add the `subPath` parameter.

```
apiVersion: apps/v1 # for versions before 1.8.0 use apps/v1beta1 kind: Deployment metadata:
    name: nginx-deployment
    labels:
      app: nginx
spec:
    replicas: 2
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app: nginx
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          app: nginx
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.7.9 # replace it with your exactly <image_name:tags>
          ports:
          - containerPort: 80
--apiVersion: v1 # for versions before 1.8.0 use apps/v1beta1 kind: Service metadata:
   name: my-service1        #TODO: to specify your service name
   labels:
     app: nginx
spec:
   selector:
     app: nginx             #TODO: change label selector to match your backend pod
   ports:
   - protocol: TCP
     name: http
     port: 30080            #TODO: choose an unique port on each node to avoid port conflict
     targetPort: 80
   type: LoadBalancer        ##In this example, the type is changed from NodePort to LoadBalancer.
```

7. After you click **Create**, a message that indicates the deployment status appears.

**Manage applications by using commands**

This topic describes how to create an application or view containers of an application by using commands.

**Create an application by using commands**

1. Run the following kubectl command to start a pod. An NGINX web server is used in this example.

```bash
 kubectl run -it nginx --image=registry.aliyuncs.com/spacexnice/netdia:latest
```

2. Run the following command to create an Ingress for the pod and specify `--type=LoadBalancer` to use a
load balancer provided by Alibaba Cloud.

```bash
kubectl expose deployment nginx --port=80 --target-port=80 --type=LoadBalancer
```

**View containers by using commands**

In the CLI, run the `kubectl get pods` command to list all running containers in the default namespace.

```
NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE nginx-2721357637-d**** 1/1 Running 1 9h
```

**Create an application by using an image pull Secret**

ACK allows you to use image pull Secrets in the ACK console. You can create an image pull Secret or use an existing image pull Secret. When you create an application from a private image, you must set a Secret for image pulling to ensure the security of the image. In the ACK console, you can specify the authentication information of the private image repository as a Secret of the docker-registry type. This Secret applies to the specified Kubernetes cluster.
1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click Clusters.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the ACK cluster in which your application is deployed, and click the cluster
name or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the Cluster Information page, choose **Workloads > Deployments**.
5. On the **Deployments** page, select the namespace and click **Create from Image** in the upper-right
corner of the page.
6. In the Basic Information step, set the parameters.
7. Configure containers.
The following example describes how to configure an image pull Secret. i. In the **Container** step, enter the address of the private image in the **Image Name** field in the `domainname/namespace/imagename` format.

> **Note:** You do not need to configure a image pulling Secret for a public image registry.

ii. Enter the image version that you want to use in the Image Version field. iii. Click **Set Image Pull Secret**, and create a Secret or select an existing Secret in the dialog box that appears. You can select **New Secret**. If you select New Secret, set the following parameters:

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Name | The key name of the Secret. You can enter a custom name. |
| Repository Domain | The address of the specified Docker repository. If you use an image repository in Container Registry, the address is automatically specified. |
| Username | The username that is used to log on to the Docker repository. If you use an image repository in Container Registry, the username is the username of your Apsara Stack tenant account. |
| Password | The password used to log on to the Docker repository. If you use an image repository in Container Registry, the password is the logon password of the image repository in Container Registry. |
| Email | The email address. This parameter is optional. |

Click **OK**. The Secret appears on the page after it is created. You can also select **Existing Secret**. You can use commands or YAML files to create image pulling Secrets.
8. Configure other parameters based on your requirements. Then, click **Create**.
For more information, see Step 3: Configure advanced settings.
9. In the left-side navigation pane of the Cluster Information page, choose **Workloads > Deployments**.
On the **Deployments** page, check the status of the application. If the application is running as normal, it indicates that the image is successfully pulled by using the Secret that you configured.

#### 7.1.5 Use Apsara Copilot

This topic provides an overview of the core features and usage of Apsara Copilot in Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK). Apsara Copilot helps you to use AI capabilities to enhance efficiency in cluster management, application deployment, and troubleshooting.

> **Important:** The results generated by Apsara Copilot cannot be used as the basis for final technical support conclusions or business decisions. Alibaba Cloud shall not be liable for any direct or indirect losses caused by taking actions based on the output of Apsara Copilot.
> The query results returned by Apsara Copilot are automatically generated by AI models. The results may not be completely accurate and are for reference only. We recommend that you verify the accuracy of the results based on the actual situation.

**Prerequisites**

Apsara Copilot is configured to display in the console by the platform administrator on the **Configurations**
**> Apsara Copilot > Custom Settings** page.

**Use Apsara Copilot to create an ACK dedicated cluster**

When you create an ACK dedicated cluster, Apsara Copilot provides you with optimization and suggestions for cluster configurations.

**Usage method**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane of the ACK console, click **Clusters**. On the Clusters page, click **Create**
**Kubernetes Cluster** in the upper-right corner.
3. On the **ACK Dedicated** tab of the **Create Kubernetes Cluster** page, configure the basic settings and
advanced options of the cluster and then click **Create Cluster**.
4. On the **Confirm** page, click **Cluster Configuration Recommendations** to view the cluster configuration
optimization and suggestions in the **Apsara Copilot** panel.

**Use Apsara Copilot to assist in troubleshooting abnormal pods**

Apsara Copilot supports pod diagnostics: Performs intelligent diagnostics on abnormal pods and analyzes the possible causes. Provides troubleshooting steps and suggestions.

**Usage method**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Workloads > Pods**.
5. On the **Pods** page, find an abnormal pod, click **Smart Diagnosis** to open the **Apsara Copilot** panel.
Apsara Copilot provides intelligent analysis and troubleshooting for the current abnormal status.

**Use Apsara Copilot to assist in creating an application**

Apsara Copilot accelerates application creation with two core AI-powered capabilities: Intelligent template generation: automatically generates standardized YAML configuration examples with a few clicks, eliminating the tedious process of manual authoring. Intelligent YAML analysis: automatically validates configuration files for formatting compliance and syntax correctness, effectively preventing deployment errors.

**Usage method**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Workloads > Deployments**.
5. In the upper part of the **Deployments** page, select a namespace and click **Create from Template**.
6. Click **Smart Template Generator** to generate a YAML template by using Apsara Copilot.

> **Note:** You can click **YAML Intelligent Analysis** to check whether the YAML format and syntax are correct by using Apsara Copilot.

**Select-to-define feature**

The select-to-define feature explains any term, parameter, or option that you select from the interface.

**Prerequisites**

The select-to-define feature is enabled. To enable this feature, click the icon in the upper-right corner of the Apsara Copilot panel and then turn on Enable Word Selection.

**Usage method**

1. Select a term or parameter that you want to know and then click the floating **Consult Apsara Copilot**
icon.
2. View the answer automatically provided by Apsara Copilot.

### 7.2 Authorizations

#### 7.2.1 Grant RBAC permissions to RAM users or RAM roles

**roles**

This topic describes how to grant Resource Access Management (RAM) users or RAM roles role-based access control (RBAC) permissions on a Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster. By default, RBAC is enabled for Kubernetes 1.6 and later. RBAC is important for you to manage clusters. You can use RBAC to specify the types of operations that are allowed for specific users based on their roles in an organization.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Authorizations**.
3. On the **Authorizations** page, configure permissions.
Click the **RAM Users** tab, select the RAM user to which you want to grant permissions, and then click
**Modify Permissions** to grant permissions to the RAM user.
Click the **RAM Roles** tab, select the RAM role to which you want to grant permissions, and then click
**Modify Permissions** to grant permissions to the RAM role.

> **Note:** If you log on to the ACK console as a RAM user, make sure that the RAM user is assigned the predefined RBAC administrator role or the cluster-admin role.

4. In the **Configure Role-Based Access Control** step, click **Add Permissions** to add cluster-scoped or
namespace-scoped permissions and select a predefined or custom RBAC role in the Permission column. You can also click the minus sign (-) to remove permissions. After you add the permissions, click **Next**
**Step**.

> **Note:** For each RAM user, you can assign only one predefined RBAC role but one or more custom RBAC roles to manage the same cluster or namespace.

The following table describes the permissions that the predefined and custom RBAC roles have on clusters and namespaces. Table 1. Roles and permissions

| Role | RBAC permissions on cluster resources |
|---|---|
| Administrator | Read and write permissions on resources in all namespaces. |
| O&M Engineer | Read and write permissions on resources in all namespaces and read-only permissions on nodes, persistent volumes (PVs), namespaces, and service quotas within a cluster. |
| Developer | Read and write permissions on resources in a specified namespace or all namespaces. |
| Restricted User | Read-only permissions on resources in a specified namespace or all namespaces. |
| Custom | The cluster role that you select for a custom role determines what permissions the custom role has. Before you select a cluster role, make sure that you are aware of the permissions that the cluster role has in case the RAM user is granted excessive permissions. |

After the authorization is complete, you can log on to the ACK console as the authorized RAM user and perform the allowed operations to manage ACK.

**Custom RBAC roles**

ACK provides the following predefined RBAC roles: Administrator, O&M Engineer, Developer, and Restricted User. You can use these roles to regulate access to the ACK console in most scenarios. In addition, you can use custom roles to control permissions on clusters. ACK provides a set of custom RBAC roles.

> **Note:** The cluster-admin role is similar to a super administrator. By default, the cluster-admin role has the permissions to manage all resources within a cluster.

You can log on to a master node of a cluster and run the following command to view the custom RBAC roles that are assigned to the current account:

```bash
 # kubectl get clusterrole
# kubectl get clusterrole
NAME AGE admin 13d alibaba-log-controller 13d alicloud-disk-controller-runner 13d cluster-admin 13d cs:admin 13d edit 13d flannel 13d kube-state-metrics 22h node-exporter 22h prometheus-k8s 22h prometheus-operator 22h system:aggregate-to-admin 13d .... system:volume-scheduler 13d view 13d
```

Run the following command to query the details of a role. In this example, the permissions of the clusteradmin role are queried.

```bash
 # kubectl get clusterrole cluster-admin -o yaml
```

> **Important:** After a RAM user is assigned the cluster-admin role, the RAM user has the same permissions as the Alibaba Cloud account to which the RAM user belongs. The RAM user has full control over all resources within the cluster. Proceed with caution.

```bash
# kubectl get clusterrole cluster-admin  -o yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: ClusterRole metadata:
  annotations:
    rbac.authorization.kubernetes.io/autoupdate: "true"
  creationTimestamp: 2018-10-12T08:31:15Z
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/bootstrapping: rbac-defaults
  name: cluster-admin
  resourceVersion: "57"
  selfLink: /apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1/clusterroles/cluster-admin
  uid: 2f29f9c5-cdf9-11e8-84bf-00163e0b2f97
rules:
- apiGroups:
  - '*'
  resources:
  - '*'
  verbs:
  - '*'
- nonResourceURLs:
  - '*'
  verbs:
  - '*'
```

#### 7.2.2 Configure permissions for the RAM role attached to cluster worker nodes

**attached to cluster worker nodes**

This topic describes how to configure permissions in the Container Service console for the Resource Access Management (RAM) role that is attached to worker nodes.

**Step 1: Get the RAM role of the cluster**

1. Log on to the Container Service console. In the left navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the target cluster and click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
3. On the **Cluster Information** page, click the **Cluster Resources** tab to view the **Worker RAM Role**.

**Step 2: Get the AccessKey ID and AccessKey secret of the cluster's**

**organization**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top menu bar, click **Enterprise**.
2. In the navigation pane, click **Resource Management > Organization Management**.
3. On the **Organization Management** page, in the list on the left, select the organization for the cluster,
and then click **Manage AccessKey** on the right.
4. In the **Manage *********** dialog box, obtain the **************** and ********************.

**Step 3: Create a RAM policy**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top menu bar, choose **Products >**
**Developer Tools > Developer Portal**.
2. At the top of the **Developer Portal** page, choose **API Integration** > **Unified Cloud Management**
**Platform** > **API Debugging**.
3. In the left navigation pane, set **Version** to the latest available version. Then, in the text box, search for
and click **CreatePolicy**.
4. On the **CreatePolicy** page, on the **Parameter Name** tab, configure the parameters.
The following table describes some of the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| AccessKeyId | Get this from Step 2. |
| AccessKeySecret |   |
| PolicyName | Enter a name as needed. |
| PolicyDocument | Enter the required permissions in the Action field. The following code provides an example: { "Version": "1", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "ecs:DescribeImages", "ecs:DescribeInstance" ], "Resource": "*" } ] } |

5. After completing the configuration, click **Initiate Call** under the **Parameter Name** tab.
If **200** is displayed on the **Call Result** tab, the API call succeeded and the policy was created.

**Step 4: Attach the policy to the RAM role**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top menu bar, choose **Products >**
**Developer Tools > Developer Portal**.
2. At the top of the **Developer Portal** page, choose **API Integration** > **Unified Cloud Management**
**Platform** > **API Debugging**.
3. In the left navigation pane, set **Version** to the latest available version. Then, search for and click
**AttachPolicyToRole** in the text box.
4. On the **AttachPolicyToRole** page, configure the parameters under the **Parameter Name** tab.
The following table describes some of the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| AccessKeyId | Get this from Step 2. |
| AccessKeySecret |   |
| PolicyType | Set this to Custom . |

| PolicyName | Enter the PolicyName specified in Step 3.5. |
|---|---|
| RoleName | Set this to the worker RAM role of the cluster that you got inS tep 1. |

5. After you complete the configuration, click **Initiate Call** on the **Parameter Name** tab.
If a status code of **200** appears on the **Call Result** tab, the API call is successful. This adds the configured permissions to the worker RAM role of the cluster.

#### 7.2.3 Use RRSA to authorize different pods to access different cloud services

**different cloud services**

You can use the RAM Roles for Service Accounts (RRSA) feature to enforce access control on different pods that are deployed in a Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster. This implements fine-grained API permission control on pods and reduces security risks. This topic describes how to use RRSA in ACK clusters.

**Background information**

Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instance metadata contains information about ECS instances on Apsara Stack. Elastic container instances run on ECS instances. You can log on to a running ECS instance, view its metadata, and then configure or manage the ECS instance. Applications deployed in an ACK cluster can use ECS instance metadata to obtain Security Token Service (STS) tokens that are used to assume different Resource Access Management (RAM) roles. This way, the applications can call the API operations of different cloud services.
1. Access ECS instance metadata shared by a
User Application ECS Instan

|   | 2. Use STS tokens to access cloud resources |
|---|---|

STS Cloud If you want to control the RAM permissions of different applications in a cluster, you can prohibit these applications from using the metadata of ECS instances or elastic container instances to obtain the STS tokens that are used to assume the RAM roles assigned to the instances. Alternatively, you can attach no RAM policies to the RAM roles that are assigned to the ECS instances or elastic container instances. These measures enhance security. However, the applications still need to obtain STS tokens by using a secure method for accessing cloud resources. To resolve these issues, ACK releases the RRSA feature that is developed based on RAM. You can use the RRSA feature to allow different applications in an ACK cluster to assume different RAM roles. Applications can obtain STS tokens, use the tokens to assume specific RAM roles, and then access relevant cloud services. This enforces the principle of least privilege and allows applications to call API operations without the need to use AccessKey pairs, which prevents AccessKey pair leaks.

|   | e a R |   |
|---|---|---|

| 1. Use an OIDC token to assume a RAM role to obtain The OIDC token is bound to the service acc | an STS token ount. |
|---|---|

User Application STS
2. Verify the token ba
3. Use the STS token to access cloud resources
OIDC RAM Cloud The following steps show how an application accesses a cloud resource when RRSA is used to enforce access control:
1. The tenant deploys a pod for which the feature of service account token volume projection is enabled.
2. The ACK cluster creates a service account OpenID Connect (OIDC) token file and mounts the token file to
the pod.
3. The application in the pod uses the OIDC token file to call the AssumeRoleWithOIDC API operation of STS
and obtain the STS token that is used to assume a RAM role.

> **Note:** To enable the application to perform these operations, you must first create an OIDC identity provider and allow the service account used by the pod to assume the specified RAM role.
> The OIDC token in the OIDC token file is a temporary token. We recommend that you configure the application to read the latest token from the OIDC token file. The cluster renews the token in the OIDC token file before the token expires.

4. The application in the pod uses the obtained STS token to assume the specified RAM role and then calls
the API operations of the relevant cloud service. RRSA is available only for ACK clusters that run Kubernetes 1.22 and later.

> RRSA depends on the token volume projection feature. By default, this feature is enabled for clusters that run Kubernetes 1.22 and later. Tokens are generally mounted to pods as statically provisioned volumes. After the token volume projection feature is enabled, the tokens are managed by kubelet in a more flexible manner. This reduces the risk of token leakage due to pod attacks.

**Enable RRSA**

If you have not created a cluster, you can enable RRSA when you create a cluster. If you have created a cluster, you can enable RRSA in the Cluster Information section on the **Basic Information** tab of the cluster details page.

**Enable RRSA when you create a cluster**

Select RRSA OIDC when you create an ACK dedicated cluster.

**Enable RRSA for an existing cluster**

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the Clusters page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name.
3. Click the **Basic Information** tab. In the **Cluster Information** section, click **Enable RRSA** to the right of
**RRSA OIDC**.
4. In the Enable RRSA message, click **Confirm**.
5. In the **Basic Information** section, if the cluster status changes from **Updating** to **Running**, the RRSA
feature is enabled.

**Obtain the URL and ARN of the OIDC provider**

After RRSA is enabled for the cluster, you can view the URL and Apsara Stack Resource Name (ARN) of the OIDC provider in the **Cluster Information** section of the **Basic Information** tab. After RRSA is enabled, ACK performs the following operations in the background: Automatically creates an OIDC issuer that is dedicated to the cluster. The OIDC issuer is managed by ACK. Enable service account token volume projection for the cluster and merges configurations of the OIDC issuer with the value of the existing service-account-issuer parameter of the cluster. Create a RAM role identity provider within your account. The identity provider uses the created OIDC issuer for single sign-on (SSO). The identity provider is named ack-rrsa-<cluster_id>. <cluster_id> indicates the ID of your cluster.

**Example**

This topic describes how to use RRSA in an ACK dedicated cluster. In this example, an OSS bucket is mounted as a statically provisioned volume by using RRSA.

**Sample configurations**

Namespace: ack-csi-fuse ServiceAccount: csi-fuse-ossfs. RAM role: test-role-1022. You can use a custom role.

**Step 1: Install ack-pod-identity-webhook**

ack-pod-identity-webhook injects the following environment variables during pod creation:

```
 ALIBABA_CLOUD_OIDC_PROVIDER_ARN ,  ALIBABA_CLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN_FILE , and  ALIBABA_CLOUD_ROLE_ARN .
```

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column
to go to the cluster details page.
4. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Add-ons**. On the Add-ons page, find the
`ack-pod-identity-webhook` component card and click **Install**. In the message that appears, click OK.

**Step 2: Create a RAM role and grant the required permissions**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top navigation bar, click **Enterprise**
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Permissions > Role Permissions**. On the Role Permissions
page, click **Create Custom Role**.
3. On the **Role Permissions** page, click the **Advanced Settings** tab, and then click **Create RAM Role &**
**Attach Policy**. On the page that appears, enter a role name. In this example, test-role-1022 is used. By
default, Global is selected for the Sharing Scope parameter.
4. Click **Next**. In the Configure Custom Policy step, click **Create Policy**. In the Policy Content section, add
the following code to configure the OSS access policy. Replace `mybucket` with the name of the bucket that you created. In this example, test-bucket is used. `{`

```json
  "Statement": [
```

`{`

```json
      "Action": "oss:*",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Resource": [
        "acs:oss:*:*:mybucket", # Replace mybuket with the actual bucket name.
        "acs:oss:*:*:mybucket/*" # Replace mybuket with the actual bucket name.
```

`]` `}` `],`

```json
  "Version": "1"
```

`}`
5. Find and select the policy that you created in the previous step and click **Next**.
6. In the Configure Trust Policy step, configure the parameters described in the following table, click **Next**,
and then click **Create**.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Trust OIDC Provider | Format: ack-rrsa-<cluster id>. <cluster id> indicates the ID of your cluster. _ _ |
| Condition Keyword | oidc:iss: Use the default value. oidc:aud: By default, sts.aliyuncs.com is selected. oidc:sub: Set the condition operator to StringEquals and enter a value in the system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<serviceAccountName> format. In this example, the value is system:serviceaccount:ack-csi-fuse:csi-fuse-ossfs . |

**Step 3: Use RRSA to mount an OSS bucket as a statically provisioned**

**volume**

1. Create a persistent volume (PV).
i. Use the following code to create a file named test-pv-oss.yaml:

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolume metadata:
  name: test-pv-oss
  labels:
    alicloud-pvname: test-pv-oss
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 5Gi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  csi:
    driver: ossplugin.csi.alibabacloud.com
    volumeHandle: test-pv-oss # The value must be the same as the name of the PV.
    volumeAttributes:
      bucket: "test-bucket"
      url: "http://oss-cn-wulan-env38-d01-a.inter.env38.shuguang.com"
      otherOpts: "-o umask=022 -o max_stat_cache_size=0 -o allow_other -o curldbg"
      authType: "rrsa"
      roleName: "test-role-1022"
```

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| accessModes | The access mode. Valid values: ReadOnlyMany and ReadWriteMany. |
| OSS url | The OSS URL. In Apsara Stack scenarios, OSS does not support access over HTTPS. You must use an HTTP URL. |
| roleName | The name of the RAM role that you created in Step 2: Create a RAM role and grant the required permissions. |
| otherOpts | Enter custom parameters in the -o *** -o *** format. For example, -o curldbg can be used for debugging. |

|   | curldbg |
|---|---|

ii. Run the following command to create the PV:

```bash
kubectl apply -f test-pv-oss.yaml
```

2. Create a persistent volume claim (PVC).
i. Use the following code to create a file named test-pvc-oss.yaml:

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata:
  name: test-pvc-oss
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      alicloud-pvname: test-pv-oss
```

ii. Run the following command to create the PVC:

```bash
kubectl apply -f test-pv-oss.yaml
```

3. Create an application.
i. Use the following code to create a file named oss-static.yaml:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata:
  name: oss-static
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: <YOUR-IMAGE>
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
          - name: pvc-oss
            mountPath: "/data"
          - name: pvc-oss
            mountPath: "/data1"
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - cd /data
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 30
      volumes:
        - name: pvc-oss
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: test-pvc-oss
```

ii. Run the following command to deploy the application:

```bash
kubectl apply -f oss-static.yaml
```

**Step 4: Verify the result**

1. Run the following command to create a file named tmpfile in the `/data` path of a pod:

```bash
kubectl exec oss-static-744dc7c5b-crcxr -- touch /data/tmpfile
```

2. Run the following command to query files in the `/data` path of another pod:

```bash
kubectl exec oss-static-744dc7c5b-lshmf -- ls /data
```

Expected output: The preceding figure shows that the two pods can share the tmpfile file.
3. Log on to the OSS console and check that the tmpfile file exists.

#### 7.2.4 Assume a role to access the ACK console

This topic describes how to assume a role to access the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console and how to grant role-based access control (RBAC) permissions. You can assume roles to access the ACK console to implement security auditing and access control in a finegrained manner. To assume a role to access the ACK console, perform the following steps:
1. Create a custom role. For more information, see **EnterpriseRole management** in **Apsara Uni-**
**manager Management Console User Guide**.
You can also assume a role predefined in the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console to access the ACK console.
2. Grant permissions to the custom role.
For more information about how to grant permissions to a custom role, see **RAM management** > **RAM**
**role authorization** in **Apsara Uni-manager Management Console User Guide** . Follow the principle
of least privilege when you grant permissions to the custom role.
3. Assign the custom role to a user account.
i. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top navigation bar, click **Enterprise**. ii. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Users**. iii. On the Users page, find the user that you want to manage, move the pointer over the icon in the
**Actions** column, and then select **Role authorized**.
iv. In the **Role authorized** dialog box, select the custom role that you created in Step 1 or a predefined role in the Select Role section. For more information, see **EnterpriseUser management** in **Apsara Uni-manager Management**
**Console User Guide**.
4. Assume the role to access the ACK console.
i. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console by using the specified user account. ii. In the top navigation bar, choose **Products** > **Computing** > **Container Service for Kubernetes**. iii. On the **Container Service** page, click **Access with Authorized Role**. For more information about how to access the ACK console with an authorized role and how to use the high security mode, see **Role management**, **Access control management**, and **Configuration**
**center** > **Authentication modes** in the **Enterprise** chapter of **Apsara Uni-manager Management**
**Console User Guide**.

**Grant RBAC permissions**

**Prerequisites**

An administrator that can grant RBAC permissions on ACK must meet the following requirements: The administrator has read and write permissions on applications deployed in ACK clusters. The administrator has permissions to view accounts or roles that belong to an organization. The administrator meets one of the following RBAC permission requirements: The predefined RBAC admin role or the custom cluster-admin role is assigned to the administrator to manage the corresponding cluster or namespace. If the administrator accesses the ACK console with an authorized role, the administrator RBAC admin permissions is granted on ACK by performing the following operations: Log on to the Apsara Unimanager Management Console, click Enterprise in the top navigation bar, and then choose
**Permissions > Role Permissions** in the left-side navigation pane.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top navigation bar, choose **Products** >
**Computing** > **Container Service for Kubernetes**.
2. Click **Access with Authorized Role** or **Access as Administrator** to access the ACK console.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Authorizations**. On the Authorizations page, click the **RAM Roles**
tab. On the **RAM Roles** tab, you can view the role information about the current user account and modify its permissions. The following table describes the operations that you can perform to modify permissions.

| Operation | Description |
|---|---|
| Grant permissions | You can use one of the following methods to grant permissions to a role: Method 1: Find the role that you want to manage and clickM odify Permissions to the right of the role. On the Modify Permissions page, you can view the RBAC permissions of the role, add permissions, or remove permissions. Method 2: Select the role that you want to manage and clickA dd Permissions in the lower part of the page. You can only add permissions to the role on the Add Permissions page. This page does not display the RBAC permissions of the role. |
| Add a permission | On the Modify Permissions or Add Permissions page, click Add Permissions and select a cluster, a namespace, and a predefined RBAC role. Note Method 2 is not applicable to custom authorization. If you want to customize the RBAC permissions that you want to grant, create a Clusterrole instance in your cluster and use Method 1. On the Modify Permissions page, select the Clusterrole role from the Custom drop-down list. |
| Remove a permission | On the Modify Permissions or Add Permissions page, find the permission that you want to remove and click the icon to the left of the permission. |

After you complete authorization, click **Next Step**. If the **Submit Authorization** wizard page displays
**The authorization is complete.**, the authorization is successful.

### 7.3 Clusters

#### 7.3.1 Create an ACK cluster

This topic describes how to create a Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) dedicated cluster and an ACK Edge cluster in the ACK console.

**Create an ACK dedicated cluster**

1. Log in to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane of the ACK console, click **Clusters**. On the Clusters page that appears,
click **Create Kubernetes Cluster** in the upper-right corner of the page.
3. On the **ACK Dedicated** tab of the **Create Kubernetes Cluster** page, configure the basic settings of the
cluster.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Cluster Name | Enter a name for the cluster. The name must be 1 to 63 characters in length, and can contain digits, letters, and hyphens (-). Note The cluster name must be unique among clusters that belong to the same Apsara Stack tenant account. |
| Resource Set | Select a resource set. A resource set is a container used to store resources. Each resource must belong to a resource set. After you select a resource set, virtual private clouds (VPCs) and vSwitches are filtered based on the selected resource set. |
| Region | Select the region where you want to deploy the cluster. |

| IPv4/IPv6 Dual- stack | Specify whether to enable IPv4/IPv6 dual stack. Note You can enable IPv4/IPv6 dual stack only for clusters that run Kubernetes 1.20 or later. Master nodes and worker nodes still use IPv4 addresses to communicate with each other. You must select Terway as the network plug-in. You must use a VPC and Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instances that support IPv4/IPv6 dual stack. |
|---|---|
| VPC | Select the VPC in which you want to deploy the cluster from the drop-down list. If the specified VPC has a NAT gateway, ACK uses this NAT gateway. If the VPC does not have a NAT gateway, the system automatically creates one. If you do not want the system to create a NAT gateway, clear Configure SNAT for VPC. Note If you disallow the system to automatically create a NAT gateway and want the VPC to access the Internet, you must manually associate the VPC with a NAT gateway or create SNAT entries for the VPC. |
| vSwitch | Select the vSwitches that you want to use. You can select up to three vSwitches that are deployed in differentz ones. |
| Kubernetes Version | The Kubernetes version of the cluster. |
| Container Runtime | Select a container runtime based on the Kubernetes version. The following list describes the Kubernetes versions supported by different container runtimes: containerd: requires you to deploy ECS bare metal instances. We recommend that you select the latest version available in the ACK console. Sandboxed-Container: requires you to deploy ECS bare metal instances. We recommend that you select the latest version available in the ACK console. Docker: Use the recommended version in the ACK console. |
| Master Nodes | Specify the number of master nodes that you want to use. You can create three or five master nodes. |
| Instance Type | You can select multiple instance types. You can also select a dedicated host group for the master nodes. For more information, see Instance families and instance types in the ECS documentation. |
| Deployment Set | You must first create a deployment set in the ECS console and select the deployment set for control plane nodes in the ACK console. Important You cannot change the deployment set used by control planes after the control planes are created. |
| Worker Instance | By default, Create Instance is selected. |

| DedicatedHostClus ter | You can select a dedicated host group for worker nodes. |
|---|---|
| Instance Type | Select one or more instance types. For more information, see Instance families and instance types in the ECS documentation. |
| Selected Types | The selected instance types are displayed. |
| Quantity | Specify the number of worker nodes. |
| System Disk | Select the type of system disk. Valid values: Ultra Disk, Premium Performance Disk, SSD Disk, and Standard Performance Disk. Note You can select Encrypt Disk to encrypt disks. Encryption is supported when you select the premium performance disk or standard performance disk type. |
| Mount Data Disk | Select the type of data disk. Valid values: Ultra Disk, Premium Performance Disk, SSD Disk, and Standard Performance Disk. You can select Encrypt Disk to encrypt disks. ACK automatically formats the last data disk if you select two or more data disks, mounts the data disk to /var/lib/container , and mounts /var/lib/kubelet and /var/lib/containerd to /var/lib/container . For other data disks, you can specify a mount directory. For more information, see How do I specify a mount directory for data disks in a node pool? in the Create an ACK cluster topic. Note However, you cannot specify an encryption algorithm for data disks. |

|   | /var/lib/container |   |
|---|---|---|
| /var/lib/containerd |   |   |

| Network Plug-in | Select the network plug-in to use. Valid values: Flannel and Terway. By default, Flannel is selected. If you select Flannel, you must also set the Flannel, Pod Service Block, and Service CIDR parameters. Flannel: If you select Enable Flannel VXLAN mode, you can enable cross-node container network communication through Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN) tunnels. Pod Service Block: Specify the CIDR block of pods. The pod CIDR block cannot overlap with the CIDR block of the VPC that you select or the CIDR blocks of existing ACK clusters in the VPC that you select. The pod CIDR block cannot be modified after it is specified. The Service CIDR block cannot overlap with the pod CIDR block. Service CIDR: Specify the CIDR block of Services. The Service CIDR block cannot overlap with the CIDR block of the VPC that you select or the CIDR blocks of existing ACK clusters in the VPC that you select. The Service CIDR block cannot overlap with the pod CIDR block. The Service CIDR block cannot be modified after it is specified. If you select Terway, the DataPathV2, Support for NetworkPolicy, and Support for ENI Trunking options are available. Service CIDR: Specify the CIDR block of Services. The Service CIDR block cannot overlap with the CIDR block of the VPC that you select or the CIDR blocks of existing ACK clusters in the VPC that you select. The Service CIDR block cannot overlap with the pod CIDR block. The Service CIDR block cannot be modified after it is specified. IPv6 Service CIDR: After IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack is enabled, you need to specify an IPv6 CIDR block for Services. When you set this parameter, take note of the following items: You must specify a unique local address (ULA) space within the address range fc00::/7. The prefix must be 112 bits to 120 bits in length. We recommend that you specify an IPv6 CIDR block that has the same number of IP addresses as the Service CIDR block. For more information, see Network planning in VPC User Guide. Note If you select a shared VPC for the cluster, only the Terway network plug-in is supported. |
|---|---|
| Operating System | Alinux, Alinux 3 Container-Optimized, Alinux 3 LTS 64-bit version that complies with Multi- Level Protection Scheme (MLPS) 2.0, Anolis, Kylin V10 SP3, Kylin V10, Kylin National Defense Version, and UOS are supported. |
| Security Hardening | Disable: disables MLPS Security Hardening for ECS instances. MLPS Security Hardening: enables MLPS Security Hardening for ECS instances. You can enable MLPS Security Hardening only when you select an Alibaba Cloud Linux 2 or Alibaba Cloud Linux 3 image. Alibaba Cloud provides baselines and the baseline check feature to help you check the compliance of Alibaba Cloud Linux 2 images and Alibaba Cloud Linux 3 images with the level 3 standards of MLPS 2.0. For more information, see MLPS Security Hardening. Important MLPS Security Hardening enhances the security of OS images to meet the requirements of GB/T 22239-2019 Information Security Technology - Baseline for Classified Protection of Cybersecurity without compromising the compatibility and performance of the OS images. After you enable MLPS Security Hardening, remote logins through SSH are prohibited for root users. You can use Virtual Network Computing (VNC) to log in to the OS from the ECS console and create regular users that are allowed to log in through SSH. |

| Logon Type | Set Key Key Pair: Select a key pair from the drop-down list. If you do not have key pairs, create one in the ECS console. Password Password: Enter the password that is used to log in to the nodes. Confirm Password: Enter the password again. Note The password must be 8 to 30 characters in length, and must contain at least three of the following character types: uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits, and special characters. The password cannot contain underscores ( ). _ |
|---|---|
| Configure SNAT | Select or clear Configure SNAT for VPC and Expose API Server with EIP. Expose API Server with EIP: The API server provides multiple HTTP-based RESTful APIs that can be used to create, delete, modify, query, and watch resource objects such as pods and Services. If you select the check box, an EIP is created and attached to an internal-facing Server Load Balancer (SLB) instance. Port 6443 used by the API server is exposed on master nodes. You can use a kubeconfig file to connect to the cluster over the Internet and manage the cluster. If you clear the check box, no EIP is created. You can use a kubeconfig file to connect to the cluster only from within the VPC and manage the cluster. |
| SSH Logon | To enable SSH login, you must select Expose API Server with EIP. If you enable SSH login over the Internet, you can access the cluster by using SSH. If you disable SSH login over the Internet, you cannot access the cluster by using SSH or kubectl. If you want to access an ECS instance in the cluster by using SSH, you must bind an elastic IP address (EIP) to the ECS instance and configure security group rules to open SSH port 22. |
| Security Group | The security group of the cluster. You can select Create Basic Security Group, Create Advanced Security Group, or Select Existing Security Group. For more information about security groups, see Create a security group in ECS User Guide. |
| Ingress | Select or clear Install Ingress Controllers. By default, Install Ingress Controllers is selected. By default, SLB Network Type is set to Internal Network. You can also set SLB Network Type to Public Network. Note We recommend that you install an Ingress controller if you want to expose Services. |
| Log Service | Specify whether to enable Simple Log Service (SLS). If you enable SLS, you can select an existing project or create a project. If you select Enable Log Service, the SLS plug-in is automatically installed in the cluster. If you select Create Ingress Dashboard, Ingress access logs are collected and displayed on dashboards. If you select Install node-problem-detector and Create Event Center, Event Center is enabled to provide event storage, event retrieval, and event-driven alerting. By default, Event Center provides a 90-day retention period for events free of charge. |
| Monitoring Agent | Specify whether to enable Managed Service for Prometheus. Select or clearE nable Prometheus Monitoring. Managed Service for Prometheus provides the basic monitoring and alerting features for the cluster. |

| Volume Plug-in | The volume driver of the cluster. By default, CSI is selected. |
|---|---|
| RRSA OIDC | You can enable the RAM Roles for Service Accounts (RRSA) feature for the cluster to enforce access control on different pods that are deployed in an ACK cluster. This implements fine- grained API permission control on pods. |
| AI Suite | Select the AI suite to be deployed with the cluster. The following suites are supported: Deploy Training Components: deploys the ack-arena, kea, cert-manager, and ack-kserve components with the default parameter configurations. Deploy Task Scheduling Components: deploys the kube-queue component to implement task scheduling. Enable Data Acceleration: deploys the fluid component to accelerate access to Object Storage Service (OSS). Enable Image Acceleration: deploys the aliyun-acr-acceleration-suite and ack-dragonfly components to implement image acceleration. |
| Deletion Protection | If you select the check box, the cluster cannot be deleted in the ACK console or by calling API operations. |
| Node Protection | The check box is selected by default to prevent nodes from being deleted in the ACK console or by calling API operations. |
| Labels | Add labels to nodes in the cluster. |

4. Click **Show Advanced Options** to configure the advanced settings for the cluster.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| IP Addresses per Node | Specify the number of IP addresses that can be assigned to a node. |
| Custom Image | You can select a custom image. After you select a custom image, all nodes in the cluster are deployed by using this image. |
| Kube-proxy Mode | iptables and IPVS are supported. iptables: a mature and stable kube-proxy mode. It uses iptables rules to perform Service discovery and load balancing. The performance of this mode is limited by the size of the cluster. This mode is suitable for clusters that run a small number of Services. IPVS: a high-performance kube-proxy mode. It uses Linux IP Virtual Server (IPVS) to perform Service discovery and load balancing. This mode is suitable for clusters that run a large number of Services. We recommend that you use this mode in scenarios where high- performance load balancing is required. |
| Node Port Range | Specify a node port range. |
| Taints | Add taints to all worker nodes in the cluster. |
| Cluster Domain Name | The default domain name is cluster.local. You can enter a custom domain name. |

| Custom Node Name | Specifies whether to enable custom node names. The node name consists of three parts: a prefix, a substring of the node's IP address, and a suffix. The prefix and suffix can be one or more parts separated by periods (.). Each part can contain lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens (-), and must start and end with a lowercase letter or a digit. The IP address substring length specifies the number of digits to take from the end of the node's IP address. The value must be between 5 and 12. For example, if the node IP address is 192.1XX.X.XX , the prefix is aliyun.com , the IP address substring length is 5, and the suffix is test , the resulting node name is aliyun.com00055test . |
|---|---|
| Cluster CA | Specify whether to enable the cluster certification authority (CA) certificate. |
| User Data | Customize the startup behaviors of the ECS instances and import data to the ECS instances. The user data can be used to perform the following operations: Run scripts during instance startup. Pass user data as common data into an ECS instance for future reference. |

5. On the right side of the page, click **Create Cluster**.
6. In the **Confirm** dialog box, read and select the Terms of Service and disclaimer, and then click **OK**.
After the cluster is created, you can view the cluster on the **Clusters** page.

**FAQ**

**How do I specify a mount directory for data disks in a node pool?**

Data disks in node pools support custom mount directories. You can format the data disks in your node pool and mount to a specified directory on your operating system. The following limits apply to the mount directory: Do not mount data disks to the following business-critical directories on the operating system: / /etc /var/run /run /boot Do not mount data disks to the following directories or their subdirectories used by the system and the container runtime: /usr /bin /sbin /lib /lib64 /ostree /sysroot /proc /sys /dev /var/lib/kubelet /var/lib/docker /var/lib/containerd /var/lib/container Multiple data disks cannot be mounted to the same directory. The mount directory must be an absolute path that starts with a forward slash ( `/` ). The mount directory cannot contain carriage returns (the \r escape character in C) or line feeds (the \n escape character in C), and cannot end with a backslash ( \ ).

#### 7.3.2 Create an ACK cluster by using a custom image

**image**

In the cloud-native era, an increasing number of users choose to migrate applications and businesses to the cloud. The requirement on the container platform varies based on different business scenarios. To meet business requirements, many users want to create Kubernetes clusters by using custom images. This topic describes how to create an Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster by using a custom image in the ACK console.

**Prerequisites**

Before you create an ACK cluster by using a custom image, take note of the following limits on the custom images that are supported by ACK: We recommend that you use the latest base images provided by ACK. The base images of ACK can be used to create clusters and have passed the strict tests of the ACK technical team. Custom images that are used to create ACK clusters must meet the following requirements: Apsara Stack cloud-init can be installed. For more information, see the **Import custom images** chapter of
**ECS User Guide**.
If you want to create an ACK dedicated cluster by using a custom image, you must enable the sshd server and use the default port 22. This allows you to transfer files to cluster nodes after the nodes are enabled. For more information, see Connect to a master node of by using SSH. Time synchronization is performed by using a Network Time Protocol (NTP) server provided by Apsara Stack.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. On the Clusters page, click **Create Kubernetes Cluster**
in the upper-right corner.
3. On the **Dedicated Kubernetes** tab of the **Create Cluster** page, click **Show Advanced Options** to show
advanced parameters. Click **Select** to the right side of **Custom Image**. In the **Choose Custom Image** dialog box, click **Use** to the right side of the image that you want to use. For more information about other parameters, see Create an ACK cluster.
4. Click **Create Cluster** in the upper-right corner of the page.
5. In the **Confirm** dialog box, verify that all check items are passed, read and select the terms of service and
disclaimer, and then click **OK** to deploy the cluster. After the cluster is created, you can find the cluster on the **Clusters** page in the ACK console.

#### 7.3.3 View log files of a cluster

You can view the operation log of a cluster in the Container Service console.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. Find the cluster that you want to manage and click **View Logs** in the Actions column.

#### 7.3.4 View cluster information

You can view information about Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) clusters on the cluster information page, including the cluster overview, basic information, connection information, relevant cluster resources, and cluster logs. This topic describes how to view cluster information and introduces the information displayed on each tab.

**Procedure**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the Clusters page, click the name of the cluster that you want to view, or click **Details** in the Actions
column of the cluster. Click a tab to view the corresponding information.

| Tab | Description |
|---|---|
| Overview | You can select a namespace to view the status of applications and components and view resource monitoring data in charts. Application Status: This section displays charts that provide information about the status of Deployments, StatefulSets, and pods in the namespace. The green color indicates that applications are running as expected. The yellow color indicates that errors occurred in applications. Node Status: This section displays a chart that shows the status of the nodes in the cluster. Events: This section displays cluster events, such as warnings and errors. Monitoring: This section displays the charts for CPU utilization and memory usage. CPU utilization is measured in cores and is accurate to three decimal places. The smallest unit is millicores. A millicore is one-thousandth of a core. Memory usage is measured in GiB and is accurate to three decimal places. For more information, see CPU resource units and Memory resource units. |
| Basic Information | Basic Information: displays the ID and region of the cluster, the status of deletion protection, and the status of Secret encryption. For more information about how to configure Secret encryption, see Enable Secret encryption for an ACK cluster. Cluster Information: displays the internal endpoint of the API server, pod CIDR block, Service CIDR block, Resource Access Management (RAM) Roles for Service Accounts (RRSA) OpenID Connect (OIDC), kube-proxy mode, number of node IP addresses, and network plug-in. Master Nodes: displays the master nodes in the current environment. You can clickS cale Nodes on the right to add more master nodes. |
| Connection Information | You can obtain the kubeconfig file that is used to connect a kubectl client to the cluster over the Internet or internal network. |
| Cluster Resources | You can view all Apsara Stack services and resources used by the cluster, including Resource Orchestration Service (ROS), virtual private cloud (VPC), security group, master RAM role, worker RAM role, Simple Log Service (SLS), pod vSwitch, and Server Load Balancer (SLB) instance. Important The resources are managed by ACK. Do not delete or modify the resources in case your cluster and the applications in the cluster cannot work as expected. |
| Cluster Logs | You can view the logs of the ACK cluster. |

#### 7.3.5 Enable Secret encryption for an ACK cluster

This topic describes how to configure Secret encryption for a Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster by using a customer master key (CMK) managed by Key Management Service (KMS).

**Prerequisites**

A Secret is created in KMS. For more information, see **Key Management Service User Guide > Create a**
**CMK**.

**Procedure**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.

> **Important:** This operation will cause the API server to restart. You can enable or disable this feature by using only accounts that are granted the cluster O&M or administrator permissions. We recommend that you perform this operation during off-peak hours.

You can use the Kubernetes command-line tool kubectl to connect to a Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster from your local computer.

**Procedure**

1. Download the latest kubectl client from kubernetes on GitHub.
2. Install and set up the kubectl client.
For more information, see kubectl.
3. Configure the cluster credentials.

| You can use the | scp |   | comm |
|---|---|---|---|
| /etc/kubernetes/kube.conf |   |   |   |
| $HOME/.kube/config |   | directo |   |

You can use the `scp` command to securely copy the master node configuration file from the `/etc/kubernetes/kube.conf` directory of the master virtual machine (VM) and paste it to the $HOME/.kube/config directory of the local computer, where the `kubectl` credentials are expected to be stored.

```
mkdir $HOME/.kube scp root@<master-public-ip>:/etc/kubernetes/kube.conf $HOME/.kube/config
```

You can find the value of `master-public-ip` on the cluster details page. i. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. ii. #### 7.3.7 Connect to a master node by using SSH

You can access a master node in a cluster by using an SSH client.

**Prerequisites**

A Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster is created and SSH logon over the Internet is enabled for the cluster. For more information, see Create an ACK cluster. The SSH client is connected to the network in which the cluster is deployed.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. On the Clusters page, find the cluster that you want to
manage and click its name. You can also click **Details** in the **Actions** column to go to the cluster details page.

If you have an Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instance that is connected to the Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network of the cluster, run the following command to create an SSH connection:

```
ssh root@ssh_ip #ssh_ip specifies the IP address of the master node for SS H connection.
```

You can add or remove master nodes only for clusters that run Kubernetes 1.28 and later.

> **Important:** You can add a maximum of two master nodes at a time. You can add master nodes multiple times.

and click **Submit**. You can also click **Edit Advanced Configuration**, modify the operating system of the master nodes, and then click **Submit**. You can click the name of a master node to go to the Elastic Compute Service (ECS) console of the master node.

**Remove master nodes**

> **Important:** **You can remove a master node only if more than three master nodes are deployed** **within a cluster.**
> After you remove master nodes, take notes of the number of master nodes. If the number of master nodes is an odd number, the high availability of master nodes can be ensured. If the number of master nodes is an even number, we recommend that you add or remove master nodes at the earliest opportunity.

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the Clusters page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to the cluster
details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Node****>****Node**.

column.

#### 7.3.9 Revoke the kubeconfig file of a cluster

In multi-tenant scenarios, Container Service issues kubeconfig files to users that are assigned different roles. The kubeconfig files are used to connect to clusters. If an employee leaves the company or a kubeconfig file is suspected to be leaked, you can revoke the kubeconfig file to ensure cluster security. This topic describes how to revoke a kubeconfig file in the Container Service console.

**Procedure**

> **Important:** After a kubeconfig file is revoked, you cannot use the kubeconfig file to connect to the cluster. Proceed with caution.

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the cluster that you want to manage, or click **Details** in the
**Actions** column of the cluster.
4. On the **Cluster Information** page, click the **Connection Information** tab, and then click **Revoke**
**KubeConfig**.
5. In the message that appears, click **OK**.
The kubeconfig file that is used by the current account to connect to the cluster is revoked. The system then automatically assigns the account a new kubeconfig file.

#### 7.3.10 Update the Kubernetes version of a cluster

Outdated cluster versions may have security and stability issues. To ensure business continuity, Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) uses in-place updates to update ACK clusters. You can update the Kubernetes version of an ACK cluster in the ACK console, or update the control plane and node pools of the cluster separately. This topic describes the usage notes before and after an update and the procedure for updating an ACK cluster.

**Usage notes (important)**

**Kubernetes versions**

You can update an ACK cluster from a major version only to the next major version. For example, to update the Kubernetes version of an ACK cluster from 1.24 to 1.28, you need to first update the cluster to 1.26 and then update it to 1.28. To view the Kubernetes version of an ACK cluster, log in to the ACK console and check the **Version** column of the cluster on the **Clusters** page. Before you update to a Kubernetes version, read the following release notes for the corresponding Kubernetes version to learn the version details and deprecated APIs. This helps you avoid compatibility issues caused by feature updates in new Kubernetes versions. Kubernetes 1.34 release notes Kubernetes 1.32 release notes Kubernetes 1.30 release notes Kubernetes 1.22 release notes Kubernetes 1.20 release notes Kubernetes 1.18 release notes

> **Note:** If the YAML file of your Helm chart uses discontinued resources, modify the file at the earliest opportunity. For more information, see the preceding release notes.

**Features and custom configurations**

If your ACK cluster uses the features listed in the following table, read the considerations and suggested solutions.

| Feature | Consideration | Suggested solution |
|---|---|---|
| Auto scaling of nodes | If auto scaling is enabled, the cluster automatically updates Cluster Autoscaler to the latest version after the cluster is updated. This ensures that the auto scaling feature can work as expected. If auto scaling is enabled, nodes in swift mode may shut down and fail to be updated. | Make sure that Cluster Autoscaler is updated to the latest version. For more information, see Auto scaling of nodes. If nodes in swift mode fail to be updated after the cluster is updated, we recommend that you manually remove the nodes. |
| Resource reservation | After you update the Kubernetes version of an ACK cluster to 1.18, ACK automatically configures resource reservation. If resource reservation is not configured for the cluster and the resource usage of nodes is high, ACK may fail to schedule evicted pods to the nodes after the cluster is updated. | Reserve sufficient resources on the nodes. We recommend that the CPU utilization does not exceed 50% and the memory utilization does not exceed 70%. |

|   | LoadBalancer configurations | ACK clusters require Server Load Balancer (SLB) instances to handle external access. However, if externalTrafficPolicy: Local is specified for an SLB instance, traffic is forwarded only to node- local pods. If your application pods are deployed on other nodes, traffic cannot reach these pods. |   | Check whether externalTrafficPolicy: Local is specified for the SLB instance in case the SLB instance cannot forward traffic to the application pods. |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|   | API Server | When ACK updates a cluster, ACK attempts to update the control plane without interrupting communication with the applications in the cluster. However, communication with the API server may be temporarily interrupted. The interruption affects applications that strongly rely on the API server. For example, if your application needs to watch or list resources, the watch operation is interrupted when the API server restarts. To resolve this issue, you need to configure the application to automatically re-perform the watch operation when an interruption occurs. |   | If your application does not access the API server, the application is not affected by an update. If your application accesses the API server, you must configure a retry mechanism for the application. |
|   | Startup probe | If the pods in a cluster are configured with a startup probe, the pods may temporarily enter the NotReady state after kubelet is restarted. |   | We recommend that you deploy multiple replicated pods and spread the pods across nodes. This ensures that your application has sufficient pods when one of the nodes restarts. |
|   | kubectl | After a cluster is updated, we recommend that you update kubectl on your on-premises machine. Otherwise, the kubectl version may become incompatible with the API server version. As a result, the error message invalid object doesn't have additional properties may appear. |   | Install or update kubectl. For more information, see Install kubectl. |
|   |   |   | invalid object doesn't |   |
|   |   | have additional properties |   |   |

If your cluster uses custom configurations, read the descriptions in the following table.

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| OS image | Custom OS images are not strictly validated by ACK. ACK does not guarantee the success of cluster updates if your cluster uses a custom OS image. |
| Others | If your cluster uses other custom configurations, such as swap partitions or kubelet configurations modified by using the CLI, the cluster may fail to be updated or the custom configurations may be lost during the update. |

**Update procedure, methods, and duration**

**Procedure**

**Preparations and precheck**:
**Usage notes**: Before you update a cluster, read the release notes for the corresponding Kubernetes
version to learn the usage notes for updates. This helps you avoid compatibility issues caused by feature updates. For more information, see the Kubernetes versions section.
**Precheck**: Run a precheck to identify potential update risks. If update risks are identified, follow the
instructions in the ACK console to resolve the issues.
**Cluster update**: After the cluster passes the precheck, you can update the cluster, including the control
plane and node pools. For more information about the update procedure, see Procedures for updating the control plane and node pools. ACK allows you to update a cluster in the following modes: Update concurrently: The control plane and node pools are updated concurrently. Update separately: ACK first updates the control plane and then updates the node pools. Control plane updates involve the key component kube-apiserver. Node pool updates involve the kubelet and the dependent components. To ensure cluster stability and reliability, ACK must ensure that kubeapiserver is up to two versions earlier than the kubelet. To do this, ACK needs to update the control plane separately and then updates the node pools during off-peak hours.
**After cluster update**: Verify the versions of the cluster and kubelet, check whether the node pools run as
normal, and check whether the applications in the cluster run as normal.

**Update mode**

Control plane: Control plane components, such as kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, cloudcontroller-manager, and kube-scheduler, are updated. ACK dedicated clusters use in-place updates to update the control plane components to ensure business continuity and reduce potential risks posed by data migration and configuration modifications. Node pools: During a node pool update, the kubelet, OS image, and container runtime are updated. To replace the OS or update the container runtime from Docker to containerd, ACK replaces the system disks of the nodes during the update. We recommend that you back up the data in the system disks of the nodes before you update the cluster. In other scenarios, ACK uses in-place updates to update node pools. For more information, see Upgrade a node pool

**Update duration**

ACK dedicated clusters update the master nodes one after one. It requires about 8 minutes to update a master node. Nodes in a node pool are updated in batches. It requires about 5 minutes to update a batch.

**Procedure**

**Update the control plane and node pools concurrently**

1. Log in to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to update and choose **More > Upgrade Cluster** in
the **Actions** column.
3. In the **Update Items** section of the **Upgrade Cluster** page, select a Kubernetes version, set **Update**
**Mode** to **Control Planes and All Node Pools** , set **Maximum Number of Nodes to Repair per Batch**
in the **Batch Update Policy** section, and then click **Precheck**. After the precheck is complete, click **View Details** to view the report. If **Result** displays **Normal**, you can continue to update the cluster. If **Result** displays **Abnormal**, click the **Troubleshoot** tab and follow the suggestions to fix the issues.

> **Note:** If your cluster runs Kubernetes 1.20 or later, the precheck checks whether deprecated APIs are used in your cluster. The precheck result is for reference only and does not determine whether the cluster is updatable.

4. After the cluster passes the precheck, click **Start Update**.
During the update, do not add or remove nodes. To add or remove nodes, you need to first cancel the update. You can view the update progress in the **Event Rotation** section at the bottom of the **Upgrade**
**Cluster** page. You can also perform the following operations as needed:
Pause and resume the update: You can click **Pause** to pause the update. To resume the update, click
**Continue**.
After you pause the update, the cluster remains in an intermediate state. Do not perform operations on the cluster when the update is paused and complete the update at the earliest opportunity. The update is terminated after the cluster remains in the Paused state for seven days. ACK automatically deletes the events and logs related to the update. Cancel the update: You can click **Cancel** and click **OK** in the message that appears to cancel the update. After you cancel the update, ACK continues to update the nodes in the current batch and the update cannot be rolled back. The remaining batches are not updated.

> **Note:** If errors occur during the update, ACK pauses the update. The cause of failure is displayed in the lower part of the page. You can follow the suggestions on how to fix the error.
> Do not modify the resources in the kube-upgrade namespace during the update unless an error occurs.

After the update is complete, you can go to the Clusters page and check the Kubernetes version of your cluster to verify that the control plane components are updated. You can also choose **Notes** > **Nodes** in the left-side navigation pane to view the Kubernetes version of the nodes.

**Update only the control plane**

Only ACK clusters whose Kubernetes versions are 1.18 or later allow you to update only the control plane.

**Procedure**

Before you update the node pools, you need to update the control plane first.
1. Log in to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to update and choose **More > Upgrade Cluster** in
the **Actions** column.
3. In the **Update Items** section of the **Upgrade Cluster** page, select a Kubernetes version, set **Update**
**Mode** to **Control Planes Only**, and then click **Precheck**.
After the precheck is complete, click **View Details** to view the report. If **Result** displays **Normal** in the report, the cluster passes the precheck and you can update the cluster. If **Result** displays **Abnormal** in the report, the cluster can still run as expected and the cluster status does not change. Click the **Troubleshoot** tab and follow the suggestions displayed on the page to resolve the issues. For more information, see Cluster check items and suggestions on how to fix cluster issues.

> **Note:** If your cluster runs Kubernetes 1.20 or later, the precheck checks whether deprecated APIs are used in your cluster. The precheck result is for reference only and does not determine whether the cluster is updatable.

4. After the cluster passes the precheck, click **Start Update**.
You can view the update progress on the **Upgrade Cluster** page. After the update is complete, you can go to the Clusters page and check the Kubernetes version of your cluster to verify that the control plane components are updated.

**Next step: Update node pools**

After the control plane is updated, new nodes are added to the cluster based on the updated Kubernetes version. We recommend that you update the existing nodes during off-peak hours at the earliest opportunity and confirm the kubelet version after the update is complete. For more information, see Upgrade a node pool.

**FAQ about cluster updates**

**What do I do if the master node update of an ACK dedicated cluster**

**times out?**

**Cause**

The self-signed server certificate of the admission webhook component does not contain the Subject Alternative Name field. As a result, the master components fail to start up.

**Solution**

Run the following commands to check whether the self-signed server certificate of the admission webhooks contains the Subject Alternative Name field. You need to run the following commands on nodes that have kubectl configured.
1. Run the following command to query the admission webhooks in the cluster:

```bash
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations
```

Expected output:

```
NAME WEBHOOKS AGE ack-node-local-dns-admission-controller 1 27h
```

2. Run the following command to query the Service configured for an admission webhook:

```bash
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations ack-node-local-dns-admission-controller -oyaml | grep ser vice -A 5
    service:
      name: ack-node-local-dns-admission-controller
      namespace: kube-system
      path: /inject
      port: 443
  failurePolicy: Ignore
```

3. Run the following command to query the cluster IP address of the Service:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get service ack-node-local-dns-admission-controller
```

Expected output:

```
NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE ack-node-local-dns-admission-controller ClusterIP 192.168.XX.XX <none> 443/TCP 27h
```

4. Run the following command to use the cluster IP address to access the admission webhook, obtain its
certificate, and check whether the Subject Alternative Name field exists:

```
openssl s_client -connect 192.168.XX.XX:443 -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null|openssl x509 -noout text
```

**How do I handle the PLEG not healthy error?**

The containers or container runtime does not respond. You need to restart the nodes and initiate the update again.

**Procedures for updating the control plane and node pools**

**Update the control plane**

ACK updates the control plane based on the following procedure.
1. When ACK identifies that the etcd and container runtime in your cluster need to be updated, ACK updates
the etcd and container runtime on each master node in sequence.
2. ACK updates only one master node at a time and displays the ID of the master node.
3. Update master components, such as kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, and kube-scheduler.
4. Update the kubelet on master nodes.
5. Update Kubernetes components, such as kube-proxy, after all master nodes are updated.

**Update node pools**

ACK updates the nodes in your cluster in batches. The batch update policy specifies the following rules: ACK updates node pools one after one. The nodes in a node pool are updated in batches. The first batch includes one node. The number of nodes increases based on the powers of two in subsequent batches. The batch update policy still applies after you resume a paused update. You can specify the maximum batch size on the Node Pool Upgrade page. We recommend that you set the maximum batch size to 10. For more information, see Upgrade a node pool.
