#### 7.3.13 Renew the etcd certificates in an ACK dedicated cluster

**dedicated cluster**

This topic describes how to renew the etcd certificates in a Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) dedicated cluster.

**Prerequisites**

An ACK dedicated cluster is created. For more information, see Create an ACK cluster.

**Precautions**

The renewal process takes about 30 minutes. During the renewal process, control plane components, such as the API server, etcd, kube-controllermanager, and kubelet, are restarted on master nodes one by one. Persistent connections to the API server are interrupted. We recommend that you renew etcd certificates during off-peak hours. You are notified by internal message and text message two months before etcd certificates expire, and Renew Etcd Certificate is displayed on the **Clusters** page in the ACK console. If you manually renew the certificates, and **Renew Etcd Certificate** is still displayed in the console, contact technical support to cancel the reminder. If you fail to renew the certificates, contact technical support.

**Scenario 1: Renew etcd certificates that are about to expire**

When the etcd certificates in a cluster are about to expire, you can update the certificates in the ACK console or manually:

**Method 1: Use the ACK console to update the etcd certificates**

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster whose etcd certificates are about to expire and click **Update Etcd**
**Certificate**.
3. In the **Update Certificate** message, click **Update Certificate**. In the **Note** message, click **OK**.
After the certificates are updated, **The certificate has been updated** is displayed in the **Update**
**Certificate** message. On the **Clusters** page, **Update ETCD Certificate** on the right side of the cluster
disappears.

**Method 2: Manually renew etcd certificates**

In the following scenarios, the cluster administrator can log on to a master node and manually renew the etcd certificates. The etcd certificates in an ACK dedicated cluster are about to expire. The etcd certificates cannot be renewed by deploying a new template. The etcd certificates cannot be renewed in the ACK console.
1. Make sure that password-free logon between master nodes is configured for the root user. Use SSH to log
on to a master node from another master node. If the system prompts you to enter a password, perform the following steps to configure password-free logon between master nodes:

```
1. ssh-keygen -t rsa # Generate a key.
2. ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub $(internal-ip) # Use ssh-copy-id to copy the public key to all
other master nodes. Replace $(internal-ip) with the internal IP address of each master node.
```

> **Note:** If you do not configure password-free logon between master nodes, the system prompts you to enter the password of the root user when you run the script.

2. Obtain the domain name of the Cert component.
i. Log on to the Apsara Infrastructure Management Console. In the top navigation bar, choose **Platform**
**Operation > Apsara Infrastructure Management > O&M Tools**.
ii. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **O&M Tools** > **Service Registration Variable Dashboard**. iii. On the **Service Registration Variable Dashboard** page, select **Service Registration** from the dropdown list and search for **acs**. iv. In the **Service Registration** column, click the icon corresponding to **acs-acs_control** to view the details. In the **Registration Variables** dialog box, search for **cert.domain** and obtain the value of
**cert.domain**.
The value of **cert.domain** is the domain name of the Cert component.
3. Run the following script on a master node:

```bash
# Replace xxxxx with the domain name obtained in the previous step.
file_server=xxxxx curl -k -sSL https://$file_server:8080/static/k8s/private/pkg/run/restart-apiserver.sh -o restartapiserver.sh curl -k -sSL https://$file_server:8080/static/k8s/private/pkg/run/rotate-etcd.sh -o rotate-etcd.sh bash rotate-etcd.sh
```

| un the | bash rotate-etcd.sh | command on a m |
|---|---|---|
| etcd CA and certs have succesfully rotated! |   |   |

If etcd CA and certs have succesfully rotated! is returned, the etcd certificates and cluster certificates on all master nodes of the cluster are renewed.

> **Note:** When the system is running the script, the system creates backups for the client certificate and server certificate of the etcd in the following directories:
> /var/lib/etcd/cert_$timestamp
> /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd_$timestamp

**Scenario 2: Renew expired etcd certificates**

In the following scenarios, renew certificates by following the steps in Method 2: Manually renew etcd certificates. The etcd certificates are expired. You need to renew etcd certificates but you cannot access the API server of your cluster. The etcd certificates cannot be renewed by deploying a new template. The etcd certificates cannot be renewed in the ACK console.

#### 7.3.14 Delete a cluster

You can delete clusters that you no longer need in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **cluster list** page, find the cluster to delete and choose **More > Delete** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the **Delete Cluster** dialog box, select the cluster resources to retain, select the **I understand the**
**information above and want to delete the cluster** checkbox, and then click **OK**.

> **Note:** You cannot delete the cluster if the `ACKBlockClusterDeletion` policy is configured for it and its conditions are met.

**Next steps**

If you manually add resources to other resources that were created by Resource Orchestration Service (ROS), ROS cannot delete these manually added resources. For example, if you add a VSwitch to a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) that was created by ROS, ROS cannot delete the VPC. This causes the cluster deletion to fail. ACK provides a force delete feature. If a cluster deletion fails, you can use this feature to forcibly delete the cluster and its associated ROS resource stack. However, the force delete operation does not automatically release manually created resources. You must release them manually. When a cluster deletion fails, an error message appears. For a cluster that failed to delete, choose **More > Delete** in the Actions column. In the dialog box that appears, you can view the resources that could not be deleted. Select the **Force Delete** checkbox and click
**OK** to delete the cluster and its ROS resource stack.

#### 7.3.15 View cluster overview

The Container Service console provides a cluster overview page. This page displays the information such as application status, component status, and resource monitoring status. This allows you to check the health status of your cluster at your convenience.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Overview**. The Overview page appears.
3. Select the target cluster and namespace. You can view the application status, component status, and
resource monitoring charts.
**Application Status**: displays the statuses of the deployments, pods, and replica sets that are running
in the cluster. Green sections indicate a normal state and yellow sections indicate an exception state.
**Node Status**: displays the statuses of the nodes in the cluster.
**Events**: displays events such as warnings and errors. If no events are displayed, the cluster is running in
the normal state.
**Monitoring**: displays CPU and memory monitoring charts. CPU usage is measured in cores or millicores
and accurate to three decimal places. A millicore is one thousandth of a core. Memory usage is measured in GiB and accurate to three decimal places. For more information, see Meaning of CPU and Meaning of memory.

### 7.4 Scheduling configuration

In a Kubernetes cluster, the scheduler component named kube-scheduler assigns pods to the most suitable nodes based on the resource plan to ensure the high availability of applications and improve cluster resource utilization. Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) provides flexible and various scheduling policies for different workloads, including Binpack scheduling, load-aware scheduling, descheduling, and quality of service (QoS)-aware scheduling. The following table describes the scheduling configuration permissions of different roles.

| Role | Permission |
|---|---|
| Cluster administrator | Read/Write |
| Cluster O&M personnel | Read/Write |
| Cluster developer/restricted user | Read-only |

#### 7.4.1 Binpack

Binpack scheduling is an intelligent scheduling mechanism that optimizes the utilization of cluster resources. When Binpack scheduling is enabled, the Kubernetes scheduler preferentially schedules pods to nodes with higher resource usage. This packs active nodes more densely, minimizes idle resource fragmentation, and improves overall resource density. This topic describes how to enable and disable Binpack scheduling.

**Scenarios**

For mixed deployment scenarios with large and small jobs, a differentiated scheduling policy is required: prioritize using small jobs to fill resource fragmentation on nodes, while reserving contiguous blocks of idle resources for large jobs. This effectively prevents scheduling starvation of large jobs caused by resource fragmentation.

**Prerequisites**

A Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster is created and its Kubernetes version is later than 1.32.

**Enable or modify Binpack scheduling**

By default, binpack scheduling is disabled for new clusters. After Binpack scheduling is enabled, pods are preferentially scheduled to nodes with higher resource usage, thereby reducing resource fragmentation and improving overall resource utilization.
1. Log in to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the ACK dedicated cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to
the cluster details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Cluster Configuration > Cluster**
**Scheduler**.
3. On the **Cluster Scheduler** page, click the **Binpack** tab.
4. On the **Binpack** tab, click **Configure**.
5. In the **Cluster Scheduling - Binpack Configuration** panel, configure the following parameters and click
**OK**. |

| Parameter | Description | Sample value |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduling Policy Weight binpackPluginWeight | The weight of the Binpack scheduling policy. The default weight for other scheduling policies is less than 5. A larger weight indicates a higher probability that pods are scheduled to the same node. Default value: 100. This parameter takes effect when you enable the Binpack scheduling policy. | 100 |
| Scheduling Policy Resource Weight | Click Add Custom Resource and specify Resource Type and Weight. Note Custom resources must not conflict with existing resource configurations. Specifically, if CPU resources and their weights are already configured, defining a custom resource of the CPU type is not allowed. | nvidia.com/gpu 50 |

| binpackResourceWeight |   |   |
|---|---|---|
|   | CPU Note A larger weight indicates a higher priority for increasing CPU utilization in the cluster. | 100 |
|   | Memory Note A larger weight indicates a higher priority for increasing memory usage in the cluster. | 70 |

For example, we recommend that you use the following weight ratios for custom GPU resources:
**GPU**: 10
**CPU**: 1
**Memory**: 1
6. After the configuration is submitted, **Cluster Status** changes to **Updating** and a record is added to the
**cluster logs**. This operation is expected to take approximately 3 minutes. Wait until the operation is
complete.

**Disable Binpack scheduling**

> **Note:** After Binpack scheduling is disabled, the default scheduling policy is restored. Specifically, the scheduler prioritizes pod packing during scheduling.

1. On the **Binpack** tab, click **Disable**.
2. In the message that appears, read the tips and click **OK**.

#### 7.4.2 Load-aware scheduling

Load-aware scheduling combines resource profiling with Prometheus metrics to dynamically rank nodes based on their actual load (collected by Koordinator) and automatically prevent scheduling to nodes that exceed predefined thresholds. This policy discards the traditional "request-based scheduling" model and instead makes decisions based on real-time resource utilization. It prioritizes scheduling pods to low-load nodes to achieve more precise load balancing. This topic describes how to enable and disable load-aware scheduling.

**Prerequisites**

A Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster is created and its Kubernetes version is later than 1.32. Prometheus Monitoring 2.0 is installed in the current environment.

**Enable load-aware scheduling**

Once load-aware scheduling is enabled, scheduling can be performed based on collected resource metrics and real-time node utilization. This aligns the scheduling policy more closely with actual node conditions. As a result, pods are preferentially scheduled to nodes with lower loads.
1. Log in to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the ACK dedicated cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to
the cluster details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Cluster Configuration > Cluster**
**Scheduler**.
3. On the **Cluster Scheduler** page, click the **Load-Aware Scheduling** tab.
4. Optional. On the **Load-Aware Scheduling** tab, click **Install** in the component installation step.

> **Note:** If the component is already installed, skip this step.

5. In the **Load-Aware Scheduling Configuration** section, click **Configure**, configure the parameters, and
then click **OK**. |

| Parameter | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Node Scoring (Resource Weight) | CPU: The weight is a positive integer in the range from 1 to 100. A larger weight indicates a higher priority for scoring based on the resource utilization. | 1 |
|   | Memory: The weight is a positive integer in the range from 1 to 100. A larger weight indicates a higher priority for scoring based on the resource utilization. | 1 |
| Node Filtering (Threshold) | Turn on Turn off | Turn on |
|   | CPU: the resource utilization threshold for a node. The value is a positive integer in the range from 1 to 100. Unit: %. A node participates in scheduling only when its resource utilization is below this threshold. If the resource utilization exceeds this threshold, the scheduler will reject scheduling pods to this node. | 80 |
|   | Memory: the resource utilization threshold for a node. The value is a positive integer in the range from 1 to 100. Unit: %. A node participates in scheduling only when its resource utilization is below this threshold. If the resource utilization exceeds this threshold, the scheduler will reject scheduling pods to this node. | 80 |

6. After the configuration is submitted, the **Cluster Status** changes to **Updating**. In this case, you cannot
perform other operations on the cluster.

**Disable load-aware scheduling**

1. On the **Load-Aware Scheduling** tab, click **Disable**.
2. In the message that appears, read the information and click **OK**.

#### 7.4.3 Rescheduling

Rescheduling involves moving improperly scheduled Pods from one node to another to address situations like imbalanced cluster resource usage, high node load, or new scheduling policy requirements. Enabling rescheduling helps optimize cluster resource usage and improve application service quality.

**Background**

In a Kubernetes cluster, high CPU or memory load can create node hotspots, which threaten Pod stability and increase the risk of node failure. To counteract this imbalance, dynamic load balancing strategies use a global view of resource metrics. When a node is overloaded, fails, or has an excessive Pod density, the system automatically migrates Pods from high-load to low-load nodes, ensuring continuous resource balancing and cluster health.

**Prerequisites**

You have created a Kubernetes cluster. The cluster must be version 1.32 or later. You have enabled load-aware scheduling.

**Enable rescheduling**

> **Important:** The hotspot descheduling feature also requires load-aware scheduling. Pods are descheduled based on node utilization.
> Enabling hotspot descheduling triggers the eviction of Pods from hotspot nodes. To prevent these evicted Pods from being rescheduled back to the same node, we recommend setting the hotspot load threshold to the same value as your load balancing node selection threshold. This prevents the scheduler from placing Pods on overloaded nodes.
> The rescheduler continuously monitors utilization and calculates a moving average of the data. Therefore, the rescheduler triggers rescheduling only if a node's utilization consistently exceeds the threshold for a default period of 10 minutes.

1. Log on to the Container Service for Kubernetes console, and in the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Cluster List** page, click the target dedicated cluster. In the left-side navigation pane, choose
**Cluster Configurations > Scheduling Configurations**.
3. On the **Scheduling Configurations** page, click the **Rescheduling** tab.
4. In the **Hotspot Descheduling Configuration** section, click **Enable**.
5. After enabling rescheduling, the system automatically generates and displays a default configuration. Click
**Configure** to modify the settings. The following configuration methods are supported:

**Quick Create**

On the **Hotspot Descheduling** panel, click the **Quick Create** tab, configure the parameters, and then click **OK**.

| Parameter | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| hotspot load threshold | CPU: A positive integer from 1 to 100, representing a percentage (%). Hotspot descheduling is triggered for nodes that exceed this utilization threshold. We recommend setting this value to match the node filtering threshold for load balancing to prevent the scheduler from placing Pods back on hotspot nodes. | 50 |

|   | Memory: A positive integer from 1 to 100, representing a percentage (%). Hotspot descheduling is triggered for nodes that exceed this utilization threshold. We recommend setting this value to match the node filtering threshold for load balancing to prevent the scheduler from placing Pods back on hotspot nodes. | 60 |
|---|---|---|
| idle load threshold | CPU: A positive integer from 1 to 100, representing a percentage (%). A node is eligible for scheduling only if its resource utilization is below this threshold. If the utilization is higher, the scheduler rejects scheduling Pods to the node. | 20 |
|   | Memory: A positive integer from 1 to 100, representing a percentage (%). A node is eligible for scheduling only if its resource utilization is below this threshold. If the utilization is higher, the scheduler rejects scheduling Pods to the node. | 20 |
| Effective scope Note If you configure a node pool, namespace, and Pod selector, only Pods that match all three criteria are eligible for migration. | Node Pool: Specifies the node pools to include in rescheduling. If left unspecified, all nodes are included by default. Supports selecting all or multiple options. | default-nodepool |
|   | Namespace: Restricts rescheduling to Pods within the specified namespaces. If left unspecified, Pods in all namespaces are included by default. Supports selecting all or multiple options. | default |
|   | Pod selector: Further filters Pods based on specific labels. Click Add to specify multiple conditions. | test/foo |
| Rescheduling interval | The interval in seconds at which the rescheduling policy runs. | 60 |
| Scheduling Preview | If selected, the system runs a simulation of the rescheduling policy. It shows a list of Pods it would evict and their potential target nodes, but does not perform the actual eviction. If not selected, rescheduling runs in live mode. The system evicts and reschedules Pods, and you can view related events in the Event Center. | Selected |

**Create with YAML**

On the **Hotspot Descheduling** panel, click the **Create with YAML** tab, configure the parameters, and then click **OK**.
6. After you submit the configuration, the **Cluster Status** changes to **Updating**. During this time, you
cannot perform other operations on the cluster.

**Disable rescheduling**

1. On the **Rescheduling** tab, in the **Hotspot Descheduling Configuration** section, click **Disable**.
2. Read the information in the dialog box carefully, and then click **OK**.

#### 7.4.4 QoS-aware scheduling

This topic describes how to configure QoS-aware scheduling, including CPU Burst, hybrid deployment of latency-sensitive (LS) and BE workloads, dynamic overcommitment, and topology-aware scheduling.

**Background information**

Quality of Service (QoS)-based scheduling and resource management capabilities are designed to improve cluster resource utilization while prioritizing the performance and stability of high-priority applications, such as LS workloads. Key features include CPU Burst, hybrid deployment of LS and BE workloads, dynamic overcommitment, and CPU topology-aware scheduling.

**Prerequisites**

A Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster is created and its Kubernetes version is later than 1.32. Node pools that have sandboxed container enabled do not support QoS-aware scheduling.

**Procedure**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
3. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Node > Node Pools**.
4. On the **Node Pools** page, find the node pool that you want to manage and click **Scheduling** in the
**Actions** column.
5. Optional. On the **QoS-Aware Scheduling Configuration** page, click **Install**.

> **Note:** If the ack-koordinator component is already installed, skip this step.

6. On the **QoS-Aware Scheduling Configuration** page, click **Configure**.
7. Currently, the following two configuration methods are supported:

**Quick Create**

In the **QoS Scheduling** panel, click the **Quick Create** tab, configure the parameters, and then click
**OK**. |

| Parameter |   | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
|   | Enable CPU Burst | Turn on Turn off | Turn on |

| Guide·Kubernetes clust |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU Burst |   |   |   |
|   | CPU Burst Amplification Percentage | After you turn on Enable CPU Burst, the CPU usage of a container can burst above the CPU limit when the CPU demand spikes. This eliminates CPU bottlenecks. This parameter is used to configure the kernel-level CPU Burst feature. This parameter specifies the percentage to which the CPU limit can be increased by CPU Burst. Unit: %. Valid values: 1 to 99999. | 1000 |
| Online-Offline Colocation | Enable Container CPU QoS | If you turn on Enable Container CPU QoS, high- priority LS applications and low-priority BE applications are deployed on the same node in online-offline colocation scenarios, prioritizing CPU resource usage for LS applications. | Turn on |
| Dynamic Resource Overcommitment | Enable Dynamic Resource Overcommitment | If CPU topology-aware scheduling is enabled, it allows application processes to be exclusively bound to specified CPU cores. This reduces the performance uncertainty caused by core switching and cross- NUMA memory access. | Turn on |
|   | CPU Overcommitment Threshold | New pods are allowed to overcommit CPU resources only when the node CPU utilization is less than or equal to this value. Default value: 65 . Unit: %. | 65 |
|   | Memory Overcommitment Threshold | New pods are allowed to overcommit memory resources only when the node memory utilization is less than or equal to this value. Default value: 65 . Unit: %. | 65 |
|   | Memory Overcommitment Basis | The memory reclamation policy is calculated based on the actual usage or request amount. | Actual usage |

| CPU Topology Awareness | The kubelet cpuManagerPolicy for the current node pool is set to static, and topology- aware scheduling is not enabled. To enable topology-aware scheduling, set cpuManagerPolicy to none in the kubelet settings. | - |
|---|---|---|

**YAML Create**

In the **QoS Scheduling** panel, click the **YAML Create** tab, configure the parameters, and then click **OK**.

### 7.5 Nodes

#### 7.5.1 Node pools

##### 7.5.1.1 Create a node pool

You can use a node pool to manage a group of nodes in your cluster. This allows you to apply uniform configurations, such as labels and taints, to all nodes in the pool. This topic describes how to create a node pool.

**Prerequisites**

You have created a Kubernetes cluster, and its version is 1.9 or later.

> **Note:** By default, a cluster supports a maximum of 100 nodes.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the Container Service for Kubernetes console. From the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the target dedicated cluster. In the left-side navigation pane,
choose **Nodes > Node Pools**.
3. On the **Node Pools** page, click **Create Node Pool**.
4. On the **Create Node Pool** page, set the basic parameters. Click **Show Advanced Options** to configure
advanced settings, and then click **Confirm Configuration**. For more information about the parameters, see Create a Kubernetes cluster.

|---|---|
| Node pool name | Enter a name for the node pool. |
| Region | The region where the node pool will be deployed. |
| Container runtime | Only containerd is supported. The available container runtime depends on the cluster version. |
| VPC | Select a VPC. |

| er Guide·Kubernetes clu | sters Container Service for Kubernetes |
|---|---|

| VSwitch | Select one or more VSwitches. You can select VSwitches from different availability zones. |

These operations, such as adding taints, draining nodes, and restarting or repairing nodes, may interrupt services for applications running on the affected nodes. For more information, see Enable node auto- repair. |
| Auto scaling | Select whether to Enable Auto Scaling. |
| Dedicated host cluster | Specifies a dedicated host cluster on which to deploy the nodes. Note This parameter is not available if you enable the security sandbox. |
| Instance type | Select one or more instance types for the nodes in the pool. |
| Selected instance types | Displays the selected instance types. |
| System disk | Supported disk types include Ultra Cloud Disk, ESSD, SSD Cloud Disk, and Basic Cloud Disk. ESSD and Basic Cloud Disk system disks can be encrypted. |
| Mount data disk | Supported disk types include Ultra Cloud Disk, ESSD, SSD Cloud Disk, and Basic Cloud Disk. Data disks can be encrypted. When you add two or more data disks, the last data disk is automatically formatted and mounted to /var/lib/container . The system then mounts the /var/lib/kubelet and /var/lib/containerd directories to /var/lib/container . For other data disks, you can specify custom mount points. For more information, see How do I specify custom mount directories for data disks in a node pool? Note You cannot set an encryption algorithm for data disk encryption. |

| Operating system | A variety of operating systems are supported, including Alibaba Cloud Linux 3, Anolis OS, UnionTech UOS, Kylin OS V10, Alibaba Cloud Linux V3 Linux 64-bit (MLPS 2.0 Level 3), and Alibaba Cloud Linux 4. |

MLPS Compliance Hardening: You can enable MLPS compliance hardening for nodes only when the system image is Alibaba Cloud Linux 2 or Alibaba Cloud Linux 3. For more information, see MLPS compliance hardening for ACK. MLPS compliance hardening prohibits the root user from logging on remotely via SSH. You can use the VNC feature in the ECS console to log on to the system and create a regular user with SSH access. |

This method improves scale-out speed by quickly restarting stopped instances. |

Balanced distribution policy: Distributes ECS instances evenly across the selected availability zones. This policy is effective only in multi-zone scenarios. The prefix and suffix can be one or more parts separated by periods (.). Each part can contain lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens (-), and must start and end with a lowercase letter or a digit. The IP address substring length specifies the number of digits to take from the end of the node's IP address. The value must be between 5 and 12. For example, if the node IP address is 192.1XX.X.XX , the prefix is aliyun.com , the IP address substring length is 5, and the suffix is test , the resulting node name is aliyun.com00055test . |

| User data | Allows you to provide user data to customize instance startup behavior. Common uses include: Run a script when the instance starts. Pass information into the instance, which you can then reference from within the instance. |

6. On the **Node Pools** page, check the **Status** of the node pool.

##### 7.5.1.2 View a node pool

You can view the basic information, node information, and scaling events of a node pool in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.

**Prerequisites**

An ACK cluster is created. For more information, see Create an ACK cluster. A node pool is created in the cluster. For more information, see Create a node pool.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the ACK dedicated cluster that you want to manage. In the left-side navigation
pane of the cluster details page, choose **Nodes > Node Pools**.
3. Click the name of a node pool to view the following information.
View the cluster information, node pool information, and node configuration. If the cluster has auto scaling enabled, you can also view the auto scaling configuration.

> **Note:** You can click a hyperlink in blue on the tab to modify the corresponding item.

View all nodes in the node pool on the Nodes tab. In the node list, select the nodes that you want to manage and click **Remove Node** to remove one or more nodes. Click the **Scaling Activities** tab to view the latest scaling events of the node pool.

##### 7.5.1.3 Edit a node pool

This topic describes how to edit node pool configurations, such as vSwitches, instance types, system disks, and auto scaling settings, in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.

**Prerequisites**

You have created a Kubernetes cluster. For more information, see Create a Kubernetes cluster. You have created a node pool in the Kubernetes cluster. For more information, see Create a node pool.

**Usage notes**

When you edit a node pool, the changes apply only to newly added nodes and do not affect the configurations of existing nodes, except in specific scenarios such as synchronously updating node labels and taints. Node pool operations, such as upgrading a node pool or recovering nodes, modify the configurations of existing nodes. Editing a node pool does not affect the existing nodes or workloads in the pool.

**Limitations**

For **BMCP** node pools, you can only edit **node labels**, **taints**, and **container runtimes**.

**Procedure**

**Clusters**.
2. On the **Cluster List** page, click the name of the target dedicated cluster. In the left-side navigation pane,
choose **Node Management > Node Pools**.
3. On the node pool list page, click the
icon next to the name of the target node pool, modify the node pool name, and then click **OK**.
4. To modify other node pool settings, click **Edit** in the **Actions** column for the target node pool.

A DNS subdomain consists of a series of DNS labels separated by periods (.), cannot exceed 253 characters, and must end with a forward slash (/). Value: A taint value can be empty or up to 63 characters long. NoSchedule: If a node has at least one taint with the NoSchedule Effect, the system does not schedule pods to that node. NoExecute: Any pods that do not tolerate this taint are evicted from the node. Pods that tolerate the taint are not evicted. PreferNoSchedule: The system tries to avoid placing a pod on a node with a taint that the pod does not tolerate, but this is not a strict requirement. Note Modifying taints does not affect existing nodes in a node pool and applies only to new nodes that are added to the node pool. ##### 7.5.1.4 Scale out a node pool

Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) allows you to create node pools and manage nodes in a cluster by node pool. For example, you can centrally manage the labels and taints of the nodes in a node pool. This topic describes how to scale out a node pool in the ACK console.

**Prerequisites**

A node pool is created. For more information, see Create a node pool.

**Procedure**

1. Log in to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the ACK dedicated cluster that you want to manage. In the left-side navigation
pane of the cluster details page, choose **Node > Node Pools**.
3. On the **Node Pools** page, select the node pool that you want to manage and click **Scale Out** in the
**Actions** column.
4. In the dialog box that appears, specify the number of nodes that you want to add to the node pool and
click Submit.
5. **Optional**. In the dialog box that appears, click **Modify Node Pool Settings** to modify the configurations
of the node pool. For more information about the parameters, see Create an ACK cluster. The following list describes some of the parameters: Public IP: If you select Assign a Public IPv4 Address to Each Node, public IPv4 addresses are assigned to the nodes in the node pool. You can connect to the nodes by using the assigned IP addresses. ECS Label: Add labels to the Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instances. Node Label: Add labels to the nodes in the node pool. Taints: Add taints to all worker nodes in the Kubernetes cluster.

> **Note:** If you select **Synchronize Node Labels and Taints**, the added labels and taints are synchronized to both existing and newly added nodes.
> If you select **Set to Unschedulable**, the nodes are unschedulable when they are added to the cluster.

6. Click **Submit**.
On the **Node Pools** page, if the **status** of the node pool is **Scaling**, the scale-out activity is in progress. After the scale-out activity is completed, the node pool changes to the **Active****state**.

**What to do next**

Click **Details** in the Actions column for the node pool. On the **Node** tab, you can check the nodes that are added to the node pool.

##### 7.5.1.5 Delete a node pool

This topic describes how to delete a node pool in a Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster to reduce resource waste.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the ACK dedicated cluster that you want to manage. In the left-side navigation
pane of the cluster details page, choose **Nodes > Node Pools**.
3. On the Node Pools page, find the node pool that you want to delete and click **Delete** in the **Actions**
column.
4. Confirm the information in the message that appears and click **OK**.

##### 7.5.1.6 Schedule an application pod to a specific node pool

Label is an important concept of Kubernetes. Services, Deployments, and pods are associated with each other by **labels**. You can configure pod scheduling policies based on node labels. This allows you to schedule pods to nodes that have specific labels. This topic describes how to schedule an application pod to a specific node pool.

**Procedure**

1. Add a label to the nodes in a node pool.
Container Service allows you to manage a group of cluster nodes by using a node pool. For example, you can centrally manage the labels and taints of the nodes in a node pool. For more information about how to create a node pool, see Create a node pool. i. Log on to the ACK console. ii. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. iii. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column. iv. In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Nodes > Node Pools**. v. In the upper-right corner of the **Node Pools** page, click **Create Node Pool**. vi. In the Create Node Pool dialog box, click **Show Advanced Options** and click on the right of **Node**
**Label** to add labels to nodes.
In this example, the pod: nginx label is added. You can also click **Scale Out** on the right side of a node pool to update or add labels for the nodes. If automatic scaling is enabled for a node pool, click **Modify** on the right side of the node pool to update or add labels for the nodes.
2. Configure a scheduling policy for an application pod.
After the preceding step is completed, the pod: nginx label is added to the nodes in the node pool. You can set the **nodeSelector** or **nodeAffinity** field in pod configurations to ensure that an application pod is scheduled to nodes with matching labels in a node pool. Perform the following steps: Set **nodeSelector**.
**nodeSelector** is a field in the **spec** section of pod configurations. Add the pod: nginx label to
**nodeSelector**. Sample template:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment-basic
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        pod: nginx      # After you add the label in this field, the application pod can run only
on nodes with this label in the node pool.
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.7.9
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

Set **nodeAffinity**. You can also use **nodeAffinity** to schedule an application pod based on your requirements.
**nodeAffinity** supports the following scheduling policies:

```
- requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution
```

If this policy is used, a pod can be scheduled only to a node that meets the match rules. If no node meets the match rules, the system retries until a node that meets the rules is found.
**IgnoreDuringExecution** indicates that if the label of the node where the pod is deployed changes
and no longer meets the match rules, the pod continues to run on the node.

```
- requiredDuringSchedulingRequiredDuringExecution
```

If this policy is used, the pod can be scheduled only to a node that meets the match rules. If no node meets the rules, the system retries until a node that meets the rules is found.
**RequiredDuringExecution** indicates that if the label of the node where the pod is deployed changes
and no longer meets the match rules, the system redeploys the pod to another node that meets the rules.

```
- preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution
```

If this policy is used, the pod is preferably scheduled to a node that meets the match rules. If no node meets the rules, the system ignores the rules.

```
- preferredDuringSchedulingRequiredDuringExecution
```

If this policy is used, the pod is preferably scheduled to a node that meets the match rules. If no node meets the rules, the system ignores the rules. **RequiredDuringExecution** indicates that if the label of a node where the pod is deployed changes and still meets the match rules, the system reschedules the pod to a node that meets the match rules. In the following example, the requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution policy is used to ensure that the application pod always runs on a node in a specific node pool.

```
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata:
  name: nginx-with-affinity
  labels:
    app: nginx-with-affinity
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx-with-affinity
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx-with-affinity
    spec:
      affinity:
        nodeAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
            - matchExpressions:
              - key: pod
                operator: In      # This policy ensures that the application pod can run only on a
node that has the pod: nginx label.
                values:
                - nginx
      containers:
      - name: nginx-with-affinity
        image: nginx:1.7.9
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

**Result**

In the preceding example, all application pods are scheduled to the xxx.xxx.0.74 node. This node has the pod: nignx label.

##### 7.5.1.7 Customize the kubelet parameters of a node pool

If the default kubelet configuration cannot meet your business requirements, you can customize the kubelet parameters for all nodes in a node pool. For example, you can customize the kubelet parameters when you want to modify resource reservations to adjust the resource usage, customize the pod eviction thresholds to resolve the resource shortage issue, and adjust the topology management policy to improve system performance.

**Usage notes**

You must customize the kubelet parameters of nodes in batches. The customized kubelet parameters immediately take effect on existing nodes in the node pool. Nodes that are newly added to the node pool also use the customized kubelet parameters. To apply the customized kubelet parameters, the kubelet process will automatically restart. This may affect the nodes and workloads running in the node pool. We recommend that you perform this operation during off-peak hours. If you do not set the evictionHard, kubeReserved, or systemReserved parameter, the system reserves resources based on the default resource reservation policy. Changing the amount of reserved resources may reduce the amount of allocatable resources of a node. If the resource usage of a node is high, workloads on the node may be evicted. We recommend that you do not use the CLI to customize kubelet parameters that are unavailable in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. Using the CLI to customize kubelet parameters may pose severe stability risks. You are liable for the validity and compatibility of the content in the userdata file. If you use invalid configurations or deprecated configurations, the nodes may become unavailable.

**Customizable kubelet parameters in the ACK console**

| Parameter | Description | Default value | Recommended value |
|---|---|---|---|
| allowedUnsafeS ysctls | A list of allowed unsafe sysctl or sysctl patterns that end with asterisks ( * ). Separate the patterns with commas (,). Important Before you specify this parameter, assess the risks and make sure that your nodes are available after this parameter is configured. | N/A | Unsafe sysctl patterns with the following prefixes are supported: kernel.shm kernel.msg kernel.sem fs.mqueue. net. |
| containerLogMa xFiles | The maximum number of container log files. The value must be greater than or equal to 2, and the container runtime must be containerd. | 10 | [2, 10] |

**Customize kubelet parameters for a node pool in the ACK console**

To apply the customized kubelet parameters, the kubelet process will automatically restart. This may affect your businesses. We recommend that you perform this operation during off-peak hours.
1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to the cluster
details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Nodes > Node Pools**.
3. On the Node Pools page, click the
icon and select **Configure kubelet** in the **Actions** column of the node pool that you want to manage.
4. Read the usage notes on the page, click **Custom Parameters** to select the parameter that you want to
customize, specify **Maximum Number of Nodes to Repair per Batch** , and then click **Submit**. Follow the instructions to complete the operation. After you specify **Maximum Number of Nodes to Repair per Batch** , the kubelet updates the configurations of the nodes in the specified batches. We recommend that you set the number of batches to 10. You can view the update progress in the Event Records section. You can also pause, resume, or cancel the update. You can pause the update and then verify the updated nodes. After you pause the update, the nodes in the current batch will still be updated. The remaining batches of nodes are not updated until you resume the update.

> **Note:** We recommend that you complete the update at the earliest opportunity. If the update remains paused for seven days, the system automatically cancels the update and deletes the related events and logs.

**FAQ**

**Will ACK deprecate customized kubelet parameters?**

Some parameters or feature gates are marked as deprecated or directly removed from new Kubernetes versions. If some custom kubelet parameters are no longer applicable to new Kubernetes versions, ACK will automatically deprecate these parameters during a node configuration update.

**How do I use configuration files to manage the kubelet?**

ACK adjusts the way how the kubelet configuration is managed based on best practices in the Kubernetes community. In Kubernetes versions later than 1.20, the deprecated kubelet startup commands (Command- Line Flags) will be replaced by the configuration file. For more information, Kubelet Configuration (v1beta1). The original configuration and the configuration file are reserved on new nodes (newly added nodes and newly created nodes). Existing nodes are not affected. For more information about how to use the configuration file to manage these nodes, refer to the Customizable kubelet parameters in the ACK console table in this topic to trigger a configuration update to manage the configurations of all nodes in the node pool.

**How do I customize kubelet parameters that are unavailable in the ACK**

**console?**

We recommend that you do not use the CLI to customize kubelet parameters that are unavailable in the ACK console. If you want to use the CLI, assess the risks and run the following command to modify the userdata file of the node pool. After the userdata file is modified, the customized configuration is automatically applied to nodes that are newly added to the node pool.

```bash
echo 'KUBELET_CUSTOMIZED_ARGS=""' > /etc/kubernetes/kubelet-customized-args.conf systemctl daemon-reload systemctl restart kubelet
```

In addition, do not modify the customizable kubelet parameters by modifying the userdata file with the CLI in case configuration conflicts occur. This may result in unexpected consequences during node pool maintenance.

> **Important:** Using the CLI to customize kubelet parameters may pose severe stability risks. You are liable for the validity and compatibility of the content in the userdata file. If you use invalid configurations or deprecated configurations, the nodes may become unavailable.

##### 7.5.1.8 Upgrade a node pool

This topic describes how to upgrade a node pool's kubelet, operating system (OS), or container runtime, in any combination, without affecting data disks.

**Usage notes**

You can only upgrade node pools that contain nodes. During a replacement upgrade, nodes are drained. The drain operation respects Pod Disruption Budgets (PDBs) but has a timeout of 30 minutes. The upgrade proceeds after the timeout, even if pods on the node cannot be rescheduled. For more information about PDBs, see Pod Disruption Budget.

**Upgrade options**

You can upgrade the following three components in any combination.

| Component | Description | Upgrade method | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| kubelet | You can upgrade the kubelet on nodes in the pool to match the version of the cluster's control plane. The available target version is determined by the control plane's current version. | Select only Kubelet Upgrade. This performs an in-place update of the kubelet component. | For more information about upgrading the kubelet version, see Upgrade a cluster. |
| OS Image | OS upgrade scenarios include: Upgrading the OS version Changing the OS type Note The OS types that you can switch to are listed under Upgradable Version in the console. | From the OS Image Upgrade drop-down list, select the target OS image. This performs a replacement upgrade by resetting the nodes in the node pool. You can select the Create Snapshots for Nodes Before Upgrading option to create a snapshot for each node. | Upgrading the OS version or changing the OS type replaces the system disk of each node in batches. Do not store important data on the system disk, or ensure it is backed up. Data disks are not affected during the upgrade. |
| container runtime | You can upgrade the container runtime on the nodes in the pool when a new version is available. | You can select the Create Snapshots for Nodes Before Upgrading option to create a snapshot for each node. | A container runtime upgrade replaces the system disk of a node. Do not store important data on the system disk, or ensure it is backed up. Data disks are not affected. During the runtime upgrade, pod probes and lifecycle hooks may fail, which can cause pods to restart. |

> **Note:** During a replacement upgrade, the system applies the node pool's configuration to the new node components to ensure consistency.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. In the left-side navigation pane, choose
**Clusters**.
2. On the **Cluster List** page, click the name of the target cluster. In the left-side navigation pane, choose
**Node Management > Node Pools**.
3. On the **Node Pools** page, find the target node pool and click **Upgrade** in the Actions column.
4. On the **Upgrade Node Pool** page, select the components to upgrade and click **Start Upgrade**. Use the
**Batch Upgrade Policy** to set the maximum number of nodes that can be upgraded concurrently in a
batch.

**More operations**

During an upgrade, you can perform the following operations in the **Event Rotation** area: Pause or Continue: To pause or resume the upgrade at any stage, click **Pause** or **Continue**. A paused upgrade is an intermediate state. We recommend that you do not perform other operations on the cluster and resume the upgrade as soon as possible. If an upgrade remains in a paused state for more than seven days, the system automatically terminates the process and clears all related events and logs. After you click **Pause**, completed kubelet and container runtime upgrades cannot be rolled back. However, you can roll back the OS to its original version, provided that the original image is still supported by the node pool. Cancel: To cancel the upgrade at any stage, click **Cancel**. After you click **Cancel**, completed kubelet and container runtime upgrades cannot be rolled back. However, you can roll back the OS to its original version, provided that the original image is still supported by the node pool.

**In-place and replacement upgrades**

**In-place update and replacement upgrade workflow**

The upgrade proceeds in batches. The batch size starts at 1 and doubles (1, 2, 4, ...) until it reaches the maximum parallelism you set. All subsequent batches use this maximum value. For example, if you set the maximum parallelism to 4, the batch sizes would be 1, 2, 4, 4, 4, and so on.

**Replacement upgrade logic for a single node**

1. Drain the node (and mark it as unschedulable).
2. Shut down the ECS instance (which stops the node).
3. Replace the system disk. The system disk ID changes, but the cloud disk type, instance IP address, and
elastic network interface MAC address remain the same.
4. Reinitialize the node.
5. Restart the node. Once the node is in a Ready state, it becomes schedulable.

**FAQ**

**How do I restore data from a snapshot?**

When you upgrade a node pool, you can choose to create a snapshot for each node. These snapshots are retained for 30 days by default, but you can delete them earlier. In extreme cases, such as data loss after an upgrade, you can restore data as follows: For an in-place update, such as a kubelet version upgrade, you can restore data by rolling back the system disk to its pre-upgrade snapshot. For more information, see the "Roll back a disk" section in the **ECS User**
**Guide**.
For a replacement upgrade, such as an OS or container runtime upgrade, you can restore data by creating a new cloud disk from the snapshot.

**How long does each upgrade batch take?**

In-place update: Less than 5 minutes. Replacement upgrade: Typically less than 8 minutes if no snapshot is created. If you choose to create a snapshot, the upgrade begins after the snapshot is complete. The total time depends on how long it takes to create the snapshot. The upgrade process allows a maximum of 40 minutes for snapshot creation. If the snapshot is not completed within this time, the node upgrade fails with a timeout error. The node itself is not modified in this case. If you do not store business data on the system disk, skip snapshot creation to speed up the upgrade.

**Are my workloads affected during the upgrade?**

In-place update: Pods are not restarted, so your workloads are not affected. Replacement upgrade: During a replacement upgrade, nodes are drained. If your pods implement graceful shutdown logic (Graceful shutdown and zero downtime deployments in Kubernetes) and you deploy multiple replicas across multiple nodes, your workloads can run without disruption. To prevent multiple replicas of the same application from being upgraded in the same batch, set the parallelism to a value smaller than the number of pod replicas.

**Can I roll back a node pool upgrade?**

Currently, kubelet and container runtime upgrades cannot be rolled back. However, you can roll back an OS upgrade by replacing the image with the original version, provided that the original image is still supported for the node pool.

**Is node data lost during an upgrade?**

A container runtime upgrade replaces the system disk of a node. Do not store important data on the system disk, or ensure it is backed up. Data disks are not affected during the upgrade.

**Does the node IP address change after the system disk is replaced?**

When the system disk is replaced, its ID changes. However, the cloud disk type, instance IP address, and elastic network interface MAC address remain the same.

**How to clean up the Docker directory after switching to containerd?**

The Docker directory may contain your own files in addition to those managed by the Kubernetes cluster such as containers, images, and logs. If you no longer need these files, manually delete the Docker directory from the data disk after you switch the container runtime.

##### 7.5.1.9 Best practices for associating deployment sets with node pools

**with node pools**

Deployment sets are policies used to control the distribution of Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instances. You can use a deployment set to distribute your ECS instances to different physical servers to achieve high availability. This topic describes how to associate a deployment set with a node pool and the use scenarios of deployment sets.

**Prerequisites**

A deployment set is created. For more information, see **Deployment sets** > **Create a deployment set** in **ECS User Guide**. The ECS quota of the deployment set is sufficient and sufficient ECS instances of the specified instance type are available. By default, each deployment set can contain up to 20 ECS instances in each zone. You can associate only one deployment set with each node pool. You cannot add ECS instances on dedicated hosts to deployment sets. You cannot manually add nodes to or remove nodes from deployment sets. You can change the number of nodes in a deployment set by scaling the node pool that is associated with the deployment set. For more information, see Scale out a node pool. After the deployment set feature is enabled, you can create at most 20 ECS instances in each zone. The maximum number of ECS instances that you can create in an Apsara Stack region is calculated as **20 ×**
**Number of zones**. The number of zones depends on the vSwitches that are specified for the associated
node pool.

**Usage notes**

In most cases, an application is deployed across multiple ECS instances on the same physical server in a zone to ensure high availability. When the physical server is down, all replicated pods of the application are affected. To resolve this issue, you can use deployment sets provided by ECS. After you associate a deployment set with a node pool, ECS instances created by the node pool will be deployed on different physical servers. Node affinity enables applications to be aware of the underlying node topology and ensures that application pods are evenly distributed across nodes. This improves the disaster recovery capability and high availability of applications. For more information about deployment sets, see **Deployment sets** in **ECS User Guide**. For more information about ECS instance families supported by deployment sets, see **API reference** > **Deployment**
**sets** > **DescribeDeploymentSetSupportedInstanceTypeFamily** in **ECS Developer Guide**.

**Associate a deployment set with a node pool in the ACK console**

> **Important:** After you associate a deployment set with a node pool, the maximum number of nodes supported by the node pool is limited. Proceed with caution.
> By default, the maximum number of nodes supported by a deployment set is calculated as **20 ×** **Number of zones**. Make sure that the deployment set has a sufficient node quota to avoid node scaling failures.

1. Log on to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to the cluster
details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Nodes > Node Pools**.
3. In the upper-right corner of the **Node Pools** page, click **Create Node Pool**.
4. In the **Create Node Pool** dialog box, click **Show Advanced Options**, specify **Configure Set**, configure
the parameters, and then click **Confirm Order**. For more information about the parameters, see Create a node pool.

**Scenario 1: All pods of an application are deployed in the same node**

**pool, anti-affinity is configured for the pods, and each node hosts only**

**one pod**

1. Create a node pool and specify a deployment set.
i. Create a node pool that contains three nodes and specify the ID of the deployment set that you want to associate with the node pool. For more information, see the Associate a deployment set with a node pool in the ACK console section of this topic. ii. On the **Node Pools** page, click the name of the node pool that you want to manage. On the **Nodes** tab of the node pool details page, view the node information. If three nodes are displayed, the node pool is created. iii. Log on to the ECS console. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Deployment Sets and Elasticity >**
**Deployment Sets** to view the deployment set.
If the three nodes in the node pool belong to the deployment set, the node pool is associated with the deployment set. For more information, see **Deployment sets** in **ECS User Guide**.
2. Deploy the application.
i. Create a file named nginx.yaml and copy the following content to the file: Configure anti-affinity for the three pods of the application so that the pods are scheduled to different nodes in the node pool.

```
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata:
  name: nginx
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      name: nginx
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:  # Configure the scheduling policy.
          - labelSelector:
              matchExpressions:
              - key: app
                operator: In
                values:
                - nginx
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      nodeSelector:
          alibabacloud.com/nodepool-id: <nodepool-id>  # Specify the ID of the node pool.
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: 1
          requests:
            cpu: 1
```

ii. Run the following command to deploy the application:

```bash
kubectl apply -f nginx.yaml
```

3. View the pod scheduling information.
i. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. ii. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to the cluster details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Workloads > Deployments**. iii. On the **Deployments** page, click the name of the Deployment that you want to manage. On the **Pods** tab of the Deployment details page, view the pod information. If the three pods are scheduled to different nodes in the node pool, the pod scheduling policy works as expected.

**Scenario 2: All pods of an application are deployed in the same node pool**

**and the pods are evenly distributed across zones and nodes**

1. Create a node pool and specify a deployment set.
i. Create a node pool that consists of four nodes, specify the ID of the deployment set to be associated with the node pool, and specify vSwitches in different zones. For more information, see the Associate a deployment set with a node pool in the ACK console section of this topic. ii. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Nodes > Nodes** to view the node information. If the nodes in the node pool are deployed in four different zones, the node pool is created. ECS instances are deployed in four different zones and are added to the same deployment set based on the balanced distribution policy of auto scaling. iii. Log on to the ECS console. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Deployment Sets and Elasticity >**
**Deployment Sets** to view the deployment set.
If the four nodes in the node pool belong to the deployment set, the node pool is associated with the deployment set. For more information, see **Deployment sets** in **ECS User Guide**.
2. Deploy the application.
i. Create a file named nginx.yaml and copy the following content to the file: Add pod topology spread constraints to evenly distribute the pods of the application across zones and nodes.

```
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata:
  name: nginx
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      name: nginx
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
              matchLabels:
                app: nginx
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
              matchLabels:
                app: nginx
      nodeSelector:
          alibabacloud.com/nodepool-id: <nodepool-id>  # Specify the ID of the node pool.
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: 1
          requests:
            cpu: 1
```

ii. Run the following command to deploy the application:

```bash
kubectl apply -f nginx.yaml
```

3. View the pod scheduling information.
i. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. ii. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to the cluster details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Workloads > Deployments**. iii. On the **Deployments** page, click the name of the Deployment that you want to manage. On the **Pods** tab of the Deployment details page, view the pod information. If the four pods are evenly distributed across zones and nodes, the pod scheduling policy works as expected.

##### 7.5.1.10 Enable node auto repair

You can enable the node auto repair feature for a node pool. Then, Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) automatically monitors the status of nodes and automatically executes auto repair tasks when nodes do not work as expected. This simplifies node O&M. Due to the complexity of faults, the auto repair task cannot fix all issues. Therefore, you must manually fix specific complex issues.

**Procedure**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
3. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Node > Node Pools**.
4. Configure the node auto repair feature for a new node pool or an existing node pool.
**For a new node pool** : In the upper-right corner of the **Node Pools** page, click **Create Node Pool**.
**For an existing node pool**: On the **Node Pools** page, find the node pool for which you want to enable
the node auto repair feature and click **Edit** in the Actions column.
5. In the **Create Node Pool** or node pool editing dialog box, select **Enable Node Auto Repair**, configure
the required parameters, and then click **Confirm** or **Submit**.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Restart Node | Specifies whether to allow ACK to restart nodes. If an exception occurs in the system or a Kubernetes component, ACK automatically executes actions to fix the exception, such as restarting the component. You can set the Restart Node parameter to Allow. If the exception persists after repair, ACK automatically marks a faulty node as unschedulable, drains the faulty node, and restarts the node. You can also set the Restart Node parameter to Not Allow |

| Maintenance Window | The time window during which auto repair can be performed. If you set this parameter to Close, the system automatically performs the auto repair operation when a node fault is detected. If you set this parameter to Open, the system automatically performs the auto repair operation based on the set maintenance window. You can click Set Maintenance Window to set a maintenance window. Weekly: If you set the Cycle parameter to Weekly, select the days of a week and configure the Started At, Duration, and Time Zone parameters. Custom: If you set the Cycle parameter to Custom, use a regular expression to define a custom maintenance cycle, and configure the Started Time, Duration, and Time Zone parameters. Note Fields in a regular expression: FREQ : the frequency at which auto repair is performed. Valid values: WEEKLY and MONTHLY. BYDAY : the days of a week. Valid values: MO, TU, WE, TH, FR, SA, and SU. INTERVAL : the interval between two consecutive cycles. The value must be greater than 0. Example: Definition: Every other Thursday. Custom regular expression: FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=TH;INTERVAL=2 . |
|---|---|

|   |   |   | FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=TH;INTERVAL=2 |
|---|---|---|---|

**Note**

For more information about other parameters required to create a node pool, see Create a node pool and Edit a node pool.

**Exception-triggered auto repair**

**Auto repair process**

ACK determines whether to run auto repair tasks based on the status ( `condition` ) of nodes. To check the status of a node, run the `kubectl describe node` command and check the value of the `condition` field in the command output. If ACK detects a system or Kubernetes component exception and the duration of the exception exceeds the threshold, ACK automatically runs an auto repair task. The following section describes a complete process for node auto repair.
1. ACK attempts to repair the faulty system or Kubernetes component. For example, ACK may restart the
kubelet or the container runtime.
2. If you allow ACK to restart nodes and the exception persists, ACK continues to perform the following
operations: i. ACK automatically marks the faulty node as unschedulable. ii. ACK drains the faulty node to be restarted. The draining operation times out after 30 minutes. During the draining process, ACK drains a node and evicts pods from the node to other available nodes based on the Pod Disruption Budgets (PDBs) that are configured for the pods. To ensure high service availability, we recommend that you deploy your workloads with multiple replicas across different nodes to distribute workloads. You can also configure PDBs for key services to control the number of pods that are interrupted at the same time. If the draining process fails, ACK proceeds with the subsequent operations. iii. ACK restarts the node. iv. When the status of the node becomes normal, ACK marks the node as schedulable. If a node is unschedulable before the node is repaired, ACK will not automatically mark the node as schedulable after the repair.

**Conditions that trigger node auto repair**

| Node condition | Description | Risk level | Threshold | Repair action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KubeletNotReady( KubeletHung) | The node is in the NotReady state because the kubelet unexpectedly stopped. | High | 180 seconds | 1. Restart kubelet. 2. Restart the Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instance if the Restart Node parameter is set to Allow. |
| KubeletNotReady( PLEG) | The node is in the NotReady state because the Pod Lifecycle Event Generator (PLEG) module failed to pass health checks. | Mediu m | 180 seconds | 1. Restart containerd or Docker. 2. Restart kubelet. 3. Restart the ECS instance if the Restart Node parameter is set to Allow. |
| RuntimeOffline | containerd is stopped and the node is unavailable. | High | 90 seconds | 1. Restart containerd. 2. Restart the ECS instance if the Restart Node parameter is set to Allow. |
| NTPProblem | The time synchronization service (ntpd or chronyd) is abnormal. | High | 10 seconds | Restart ntpd or chronyd. |
| SystemdOffline | Systemd is abnormal and cannot start or destroy containers. | High | 90 seconds | Restart the ECS instance if the Restart Node parameter is set to Allow. |

| ReadonlyFilesyste m | The node file system is read- only. | High | 90 seconds | Restart the ECS instance if the Restart Node parameter is set to Allow. |
|---|---|---|---|---|

**Node status during auto repair**

The node is in the Repairing state while the auto repair task is running. If the node exception is fixed after the auto repair task is complete, the state of the node changes to Normal. If the node exception persists after the repair task is complete, the state of the node changes to Recover Failed. If a node fails to be repaired, the auto repair task is no longer triggered for the node. In this case, auto repair can be triggered for the node only after the node recovers from the exception.

#### 7.5.2 Nodes

##### 7.5.2.1 Add existing nodes

You can add existing Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instances as worker nodes to a Kubernetes cluster in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. This topic describes how to add nodes automatically and manually.

**Prerequisites**

A Kubernetes cluster is created. For more information, see Create a Kubernetes cluster. The ECS instances that you want to add are in the security group that is automatically created for the Kubernetes cluster. For more information, see Add an ECS instance to a security group in the Security groups chapter of the **ECS User Guide**. Make sure that your cluster has a sufficient node quota. The Elastic Compute Service instances that you want to add must be in the same region and Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) as the cluster. You can add only ECS instances that belong to the same account as the cluster.

**Limits on adding instances**

**Limit on the number of security groups**

When you add an existing instance to a node pool, the instance is also added to the security group of the node pool. An instance that is already in the security group is not added again. An ECS instance can belong to a limited number of security groups. Make sure that the total number of security groups for the instance does not exceed the limit after the instance is added to the node pool. For more information about ECS limits, see Limits in the **Product Introduction** of ECS.

**Limits on security group rules**

A security group is a virtual firewall that controls the inbound and outbound traffic of the ECS instances in the security group to improve security. Security groups are classified as basic security groups, advanced security groups, and managed security groups. Managed security groups are created by Alibaba Cloud services. The rules of a managed security group can be modified only by the Alibaba Cloud service that created it. Do not select a managed security group when you create a node pool. Otherwise, the node pool cannot be created. The following table describes the differences between basic and advanced security groups.

| Feature | Basic security group | Advanced security group |
|---|---|---|
| Access control policy if no rules are added | Inbound: Denies all access requests. Outbound: Allows all access requests. | Inbound: Denies all access requests. Outbound: Denies all access requests. |

| Maximum number of private IP addresses | 2,000 | 65536 |
|---|---|---|
| Network connectivity between instances in the same security group | By default, instances can communicate with each other over the internal network. | By default, instances are isolated from each other. You must manually add security group rules to allow communication. |
| Authorization to other security groups | Support | Not supported |

When you create a node pool, default rules are added to the security group of the node pool to allow communication within the cluster. For more information about how to configure cluster access rules for a security group, see Add a security group rule in the Security groups chapter of the **ECS User Guide**. When you add an instance to a security group, make sure that the existing rules of the security group do not conflict with the following rules. Otherwise, pods cannot communicate with each other. The pod CIDR block The secondary IPv4 CIDR block of the VPC

**Automatically add nodes**

The automatic method lists the available ECS instances in your account. You can then use the web interface to install, deploy, and automatically add the instances to the cluster.
1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. On the cluster management page, choose **Node Management > Node Pools**.
5. On the **Node Pools** page, find the target node pool and click **Add Existing Nodes** in the **Actions**
column.
6. On the **Select Existing ECS Instance** page, select to automatically add existing ECS instances.
Set **Add Method** to **Auto Add**. In the list of existing ECS instances, select the instances that you want to add.
7. Click **Next** and configure the **Instance Information**.

| Configuration Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Cluster ID/Name | Information about the cluster to which you want to add nodes. This item is automatically configured. |
| Mount Data Disk | Specifies whether to store container and image data on a data disk. If a data disk is mounted on the ECS instance and the file system of the last data disk is not initialized, the system automatically formats the data disk to ext4. The disk is then used to store the content in /var/lib/docker and /var/lib/kubelet. Note The original data on the data disk will be lost. Back up your data. If no data disk is mounted on the ECS instance, a new data disk is not mounted. |
| Logon Method | By default, Set Password is selected. |
| Password | Enter the Password for the instance. |

| ntainer Service for Kube | rnetes User Guide·Kubernetes clusters |
|---|---|

| Confirm Password | Enter the password again to confirm. |
|---|---|
| Retain Instance Name | When you add nodes, Retain Instance Name is enabled by default. If you do not want to retain the instance names, you can disable Retain Instance Name. The nodes are then renamed based on the custom node naming rules. |
| Instance Information | The instance IDs and names of the ECS instances to be added. |

8. Click **Next**. In the **Add Existing Instances To Cluster** dialog box, click **OK**.

**Manually add nodes**

> **Important:** ECS nodes that are manually added to an ACK cluster are not released when the cluster is deleted.

To manually add a node, you must obtain an installation command and log on to the corresponding ECS instance to run the installation script. You can add only one ECS instance at a time.
1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. On the cluster management page, choose **Node Management > Node Pools**.
5. On the **Node Pools** page, find the target node pool and click **Add Existing Nodes** in the **Actions**
column.
6. On the **Select Existing ECS Instance** page, select to manually add an existing ECS instance.
Set **Add Method** to **Manual Add**. In the list of existing ECS instances, select the ECS instance that you want to add.
7. Click **Next** and configure the **Instance Information**.

| Configuration Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Cluster ID/Name | Information about the cluster to which you want to add nodes. This item is automatically configured. |
| Mount Data Disk | Specifies whether to store container and image data on a data disk. If a data disk is mounted on the ECS instance and the file system of the last data disk is not initialized, the system automatically formats the data disk to ext4. The disk is then used to store the content in /var/lib/docker and /var/lib/kubelet. Note The original data on the data disk will be lost. Back up your data. If no data disk is mounted on the ECS instance, a new data disk is not mounted. |
| Retain Instance Name | When you add nodes, Retain Instance Name is enabled by default. If you do not want to retain the instance names, you can disable Retain Instance Name. The nodes are then renamed based on the custom node naming rules. |
| Instance Information | The instance ID and name of the ECS instance to be added. |

8. Click **Next** to go to the **Add Complete** page. On the **Add Complete** page, copy the command and click
**Complete**.

0. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Instances & Images > Instances**. Select the region where
the cluster is located, and then select the ECS instance that you want to add.
1. Click **Connect** next to the ECS instance to connect to it using Virtual Network Computing (VNC). For more
information, see **Elastic Compute Service User Guide > Quick Start > Connect to an instance >**
**Connect to an instance using VNC**.
2. On the remote connection interface of the ECS instance, follow the on-screen instructions. Paste the
command that you copied in Step 8 and click **Execute** to run the script. Wait for the script to finish running. After the script runs successfully, the ECS instance is added.

**Execution Result**

1. In the navigation pane on the left of the cluster management page, choose **Node Management > Node**
**Pools**.
2. On the **Node Pools** page, find the target node pool and click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
3. On the node pool details page, click the **Node Management** tab.
You can view information about the added node on this tab.
