In the **Access Settings** section, you can view the created service and Ingress. You can click **Update** and **Delete** to reconfigure them. In the **Scaling Configuration** section, configure whether to enable **Metrics-based Scaling** to meet the application's needs under different loads. ACK supports metrics-based scaling for pods. This feature automatically adjusts the number of pods based on container CPU and memory usage.

> **Note:** To enable auto scaling, you must set resource requests for the container. Otherwise, auto scaling does not take effect.

| Configuration Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Metric | CPU and memory are supported. The metric type must be the same as the requested resource type. |
| Trigger Condition | The resource usage percentage. If the usage exceeds this value, the container starts to scale out. |
| Maximum Number of Replicas | The maximum number of containers to which the application can be scaled out. |
| Minimum Number of Replicas | The minimum number of containers to which the application can be scaled in. |

In the **Scheduling Settings** section, set **Update Method**, **Node Affinity**, **Pod Affinity**, **Pod Anti-**
**affinity**, and **Toleration**. For more information, see Affinity and anti-affinity.

> **Note:** Affinity-based scheduling depends on node labels and pod labels. You can use built-in labels for scheduling, or configure relevant labels for nodes and pods in advance.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Update Method | Select Rolling Update or OnDelete. For more information, see Deployments. The Maximum Number of Unavailable Pods and Excess Pods parameters are available if you select Rolling Update. |
| Node Affinity | Set the Node Affinity parameter by selecting worker node labels as selectors. Node affinity supports required and preferred rules, and various operators such as In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist, Gt, and Lt. Required: Specify the rules that must be matched for pod scheduling. In the YAML file, these rules are defined by the requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution affinity. These rules have the same effect as the NodeSelector parameter. In this example, pods can be scheduled only to nodes with the specified labels. You can create multiple required rules. However, only one of them must be met. Optional: Specify the rules that are optional to be matched for pod scheduling. In the YAML file, these rules are defined by the preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution affinity. If you specify an optional rule, the scheduler attempts to schedule a pod to a node that matches the optional rule. You can also set weights for optional rules. If multiple nodes match the rule, the node with the highest weight is preferred. You can create multiple optional rules. However, all of them must be met before the pod can be scheduled. |

| Pod Affinity | Pod affinity rules specify how pods are deployed relative to other pods in the same topological domain. For example, you can use pod affinity to deploy services that communicate with each other to the same topological domain, such as a host. This reduces the network latency between these services. Pod affinity enables you to specify the node to which pods can be scheduled based on the labels of the pods. Pod affinity supports required and preferred rules, and the following operators: In, NotIn, Exists, and DoesNotExist . Required: Specify the rules that must be matched for pod scheduling. In the YAML file, these rules are defined by the requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution affinity. A node must match the required rules before pods can be scheduled to the node. Namespace: Specify the namespace to apply the required rule. Pod affinity rules are defined based on the labels that are added to pods and therefore must be scoped to a namespace. Topological Domain: Set the topologyKey. This specifies the key for the node label that the system uses to denote the topological domain. For example, if you set the parameter to kubernetes.io/hostname , topologies are determined by nodes. If you set the parameter to beta.kubernetes.io/os , topologies are determined by the operating systems of nodes. Selector: Click the plus icon to the right of Selector. You can specify multiple selectors of the rule. You can set the Label Name, Operator, and Label Value parameters for each selector. In this example, the required rule specifies that the application to be created is scheduled to a host that runs applications with the app:nginx label. View Applications: Click View Applications and set the namespace and application in the dialog box that appears. You can view the pod labels of the selected application and add these labels as selectors. Optional: Specify the rules that are optional to be matched for pod scheduling. In the YAML file, these rules are defined by the preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution affinity. If you specify an optional rule, the scheduler attempts to schedule the pod to a node that matches the optional rule. You can set weights for optional rules. The other parameters are the same as those of required rules. Note Weight: Set the weight of a preferred rule to a value from 1 to 100. The scheduler calculates the weight of each node that meets the preferred rule based on an algorithm, and then schedules the pod to the node with the highest weight. |
|---|---|
| Pod Anti-affinity | Pod anti-affinity rules specify that pods are not scheduled to topological domains where pods with matching labels are deployed. Pod anti-affinity rules apply to the following scenarios: Schedule the pods of an application to different topological domains, such as multiple hosts. This allows you to enhance the stability of your service. Grant a pod exclusive access to a node. This enables resource isolation and ensures that no other pods can share the resources of the specified node. Schedule pods of an application to different hosts if the pods may interfere with each other. Note The parameters of pod anti-affinity rules are the same as those of pod affinity rules. Create rules based on scenarios. |
| Toleration | Configure toleration rules to allow pods to be scheduled to nodes with matching taints. |

In the **Labels And Annotations** section, click **Add** to set labels and annotations for the pod.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Pod Labels | Add a label to the pod. The label is used to identify the application. |
| Pod Annotations | Add an annotation to the pod configurations. |

To the right of the Nginx application, click **Details** in the **Actions** column, and then select the **Pods** tab. You will notice that when you scale out, the pods are created in ascending order. Conversely, when you scale in, pods are terminated in descending order. This demonstrates the ordinal stability of pods in a StatefulSet. ii. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Storage > PersistentVolumeClaims**. You can see that new cloud storage volumes are created for the new pods when you scale out the application. The created PVs and PVCs are not deleted after you scale in the application.

**What to do next**

Connect to a master node and run the following commands to verify the data persistence feature.
1. Run the following command to create a temporary file on the disk.

```bash
kubectl exec nginx-1 ls /tmp # List the files in the /tmp directory. The lost+found file is listed. kubectl exec nginx-1 touch /tmp/statefulset # Create a temporary file named statefulset. kubectl exec nginx-1 ls /tmp
```

Expected output:

```
lost+found statefulset
```

2. Run the following command to delete the pod and verify data persistence.

```bash
kubectl delete pod nginx-1
```

Expected output:

```
pod"nginx-1" deleted
```

3. Wait for a period of time. After the pod automatically restarts, verify data persistence. This demonstrates
the high availability of the StatefulSet application.

```bash
kubectl exec nginx-1 ls /tmp # The lost+found directory indicates data persistence.
```

Expected output:

```
statefulset
```

##### 7.10.1.3 Create a DaemonSet

A DaemonSet ensures that each node runs a copy of a pod. You can use a DaemonSet to run a log collection daemon, a monitoring daemon, or a system management application on each node. This topic describes how to create a DaemonSet for a Container Service cluster.

**Create a DaemonSet in the Container Service console**

**Create a DaemonSet from an image**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name or click **Details** in the
**Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Workloads > DaemonSets**.
5. On the **DaemonSets** page, click **Create from Image** in the upper-right corner.
6. Set parameters for the DaemonSet.
i. On the **Basic Information** wizard page, configure the basic settings. For more information, see Create a stateless workload (Deployment). ii. On the **Container** wizard page, configure one or more containers. For more information, see Create a stateless workload (Deployment). iii. On the **Advanced** wizard page, configure the advanced settings. A DaemonSet can schedule a pod to a node that is in the Unschedulable state. To run a pod on only a specific node, set node affinity, pod affinity, or toleration rules. For more information about the configuration parameters, see Create a stateless workload (Deployment).
7. Click **Create**.
After the DaemonSet is created, you can view the DaemonSet on the DaemonSets page.

**Create a DaemonSet from a YAML template**

1. In the upper-right corner of the **DaemonSets** page, click **Create from YAML**.
2. On the **Create** page, configure the DaemonSet in the **Template** section.
3. Click **Create** below the **Template** section.
After the DaemonSet is created, you can view the DaemonSet on the DaemonSets page.

**Create a DaemonSet by using kubectl**

Before you use kubectl to create a DaemonSet, you must download kubectl and connect to your cluster by using kubectl. For more information, see Connect to an ACK cluster by using kubectl. A DaemonSet can schedule a pod to a node that is in the Unschedulable state. To run a pod on only a specific node, set the following parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| nodeSelector | A pod is scheduled only to the node with the specified labels. |
| nodeAffinity | Node affinity. Pods are scheduled to nodes based on node labels. Node affinity allows you to set other matching rules. |
| podAffinity | Pod affinity. Pods are scheduled to nodes based on pod labels. A pod is scheduled only to the node that runs a pod that matches the affinity rules. |

To demonstrate how to create a DaemonSet by using kubectl, a DaemonSet named fluentd-elasticsearch is created in this example.
1. Create a daemonset.yaml file and copy the following content into the file:

```bash
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: DaemonSet metadata:
  name: fluentd-elasticsearch
  namespace: kube-system
  labels:
    k8s-app: fluentd-logging
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      name: fluentd-elasticsearch
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: fluentd-elasticsearch
    spec:
      tolerations:
      # this toleration is to have the daemonset runnable on master nodes
      # remove it if your masters can't run pods
      - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/master
        effect: NoSchedule
      containers:
      - name: fluentd-elasticsearch
        image: quay.io/fluentd_elasticsearch/fluentd:v2.5.2
        resources:
          limits:
            memory: 200Mi
          requests:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 200Mi
        volumeMounts:
        - name: varlog
          mountPath: /var/log
        - name: varlibdockercontainers
          mountPath: /var/lib/docker/containers
          readOnly: true
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      volumes:
      - name: varlog
        hostPath:
          path: /var/log
      - name: varlibdockercontainers
        hostPath:
          path: /var/lib/docker/containers
```

2. Run the following command to create the DaemonSet:

```bash
kubectl create -f daemonset.yaml
```

If `daemonset.apps/fluentd-elasticsearch created` is returned, the DaemonSet is created.

**More operations**

After you create a DaemonSet, you can perform the following operations: On the DaemonSets page, find the DaemonSet that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column. On the details page, you can view basic information about the DaemonSet. The information includes pods, access method, events, and logs. On the DaemonSets page, find the DaemonSet that you want to manage and choose **More > View in**
**YAML** in the **Actions** column to view the YAML file of the DaemonSet.
On the DaemonSets page, find the DaemonSet that you want to manage and choose **More > Delete** in the **Actions** column to delete the DaemonSet.

##### 7.10.1.4 Create a Job

You can create Jobs in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. This topic describes how to create a busybox Job and demonstrates the features of a Job.

**Prerequisites**

A Kubernetes cluster has been created. For more information, see Create a Kubernetes cluster.

**Background information**

A Job is used for the batch processing of short-lived, one-off tasks. A Job ensures that one or more pods for a task run to successful completion. Kubernetes supports the following types of Jobs: Non-parallel Job: Starts one pod and ensures that the pod completes successfully.

| t: You can set |   | .spec.completions |
|---|---|---|
| .spec.completions |   |   |
| et | .spec.parallelism |   |

successful completions matches `.spec.completions` . `.spec.completions` unspecified. The Job is considered complete when at least one pod has completed successfully and all other pods have terminated. Parallel Job with a fixed completion count: Set both `.spec.completions` and `.spec.parallelism` . Multiple pods run in parallel to process a work queue. Jobs can be categorized into the following patterns based on the settings of `.spec.completions` and

```
 .spec.parallelism :
```

> **Note:** The Job created in this example is a parallel Job with a fixed completion count.

| Job type | Example | Behavior | completions | Parallelism |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One-off Job | Database migration. | Starts one pod and runs it to successful completion. | 1 | 1 |
| Job with a fixed completion count | Pods that process a work queue. | Starts pods one by one until the number of successful pods reaches the value of `completions`. | 2+ | 1 |
| Parallel Job with a fixed completion count | Multiple pods process a work queue in parallel. | Starts multiple pods in parallel until the number of successful pods reaches the value of `completions`. | 2+ | 2+ |
| Parallel Job | Multiple pods process a work queue in parallel. | Starts one or more pods. The Job is successful when at least one pod completes successfully. | 1 | 2+ |

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the target cluster and click its name, or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Workloads > Jobs**.
5. On the **Jobs** page, click **Create From Image**.
6. On the **Application Basic Information** page, configure the basic information for the application. For
more information about the parameters, see Create a Deployment. Then, click **Next**.
7. On the **Container Configuration** page, configure the container. For more information about the
parameters, see Create a Deployment. Then, click **Next**.
8. On the **Advanced Configuration** page, configure the Job, labels, and annotations.
In the **Job Settings** section, set the parameters for the Job.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Succeeded Pods | The number of pods that must run to successful completion for the Job. This corresponds to the `completions` field. The default value is 1. |
| Parallelism | The number of pods that can run in parallel at any time. This corresponds to the `parallelism` field. The default value is 1. |
| Timeout | The time limit for the Job to run. If the Job does not complete within this time, the system attempts to terminate it. This corresponds to the `activeDeadlineSeconds` field. |
| Retry Count | The number of retries for a failed Job. This corresponds to the `backoffLimit` field. The default value is 6. A failed Job is retried with an exponential back-off delay. The maximum delay is 6 minutes. |
| Restart Policy | The only supported options are Never and OnFailure. |

In the **Labels and Annotations** section, click **Add** to add labels and annotations for the pods.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Pod Labels | Add a label to the pod. The label is used to identify the application. |
| Pod Annotations | Add an annotation to the pod configurations. |

9. Click **Create**.
On the cluster details page, choose **Workloads > Jobs**. On the **Jobs** page, you can see the created Job. In the **Status** column for the Job, view the creation status of the pods. In this example, two pods are created in parallel, as defined in the Job.

> **Note:** After the Job is complete, you can view its completion time on the **Jobs** page. If the Job has not completed, the completion time is not displayed.

**Related operations**

You can manage a Job from its details page. To navigate to the page, click **Clusters** in the navigation pane on the left. On the Clusters page, find the target cluster and click its name or click **Details** in the **Actions** column. Then, choose **Workloads > Jobs**. On the Jobs page, find the target Job and click its name or click
**Details** in the **Actions** column. On the Job details page, you can **Scale**, **View YAML**, or **Refresh** the
application. Scale: On the Job details page, click **Scale** to change the number of pods. View YAML: On the Job details page, click **View YAML**. You can then **Update**, **Download**, or **Save As**
**Template** the YAML file.
Refresh: On the Job details page, click **Refresh** to refresh the Job.

##### 7.10.1.5 Create a CronJob

CronJobs are used to create periodic and recurring tasks. For example, you can create CronJobs to perform backup operations or send emails. Jobs are used to process short-lived, one-off tasks. A CronJob creates one or more Jobs based on a specific schedule. This topic describes how to create a CronJob.

**Create a CronJob in the ACK console**

**Create a CronJob from an image**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left navigation pane, click **Cluster**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the cluster or click **Details** in the **Actions** column of the cluster.
4. In the navigation pane on the left of the details page, choose **Workloads > CronJobs**.
5. On the **CronJobs** page, click **Create from Image** in the upper-right corner.

**Note**

You can also click **Create from Template** to create a CronJob. For more information, see Create a Linux application from an orchestration template.
6. Set parameters for the CronJob.
i. In the **Basic Information** step, configure the basic settings. For more information, see Create a Deployment. ii. In the **Container** step, configure one or more containers. For more information, see Create a Deployment. iii. In the **Advanced** step, configure the advanced settings.

| Classification | Parameter | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduled task | Schedule | Set a schedule on a daily, weekly, or monthly basis, or use a cron expression. A cron expression is a string of six or seven fields separated by five or six spaces. Each field represents a part of the schedule. Cron has the following two syntax formats: Seconds Minutes Hours DayofMonth Month DayofWeek Year Seconds Minutes Hours DayofMonth Month DayofWeek For more information, see Cron Expressions. |
|   | Concurrency policy | You can set one of the following three concurrency policies: Allow: Allows jobs to run concurrently. Concurrent jobs compete for cluster resources. Forbid: Prohibits jobs from running concurrently. If a previous job is not yet complete, the next job is skipped. Replace: If a previous job is not yet complete when it is time to create a new job, the new job replaces the previous one. |
|   | Job history | The number of successful or failed jobs for which you want to retain records. If you set the parameters to 0, the system does not retain the records of jobs. |
| Job settings | Succeeded Pod Count | For more information about the parameters for job settings, seeJ ob configuration. |
|   | Parallelism |   |
|   | Timeout |   |
|   | Retry count |   |
|   | Restart policy |   |
| Labels and annotations | Pod labels | Add labels to the pod in key-value pairs. Note The key of a label must be 1 to 253 characters in length and can contain only letters, digits, hyphens (-), underscores ( ), _ and periods (.). |
|   | Pod annotations | Add annotations to the pod in key-value pairs. Note The name of an annotation must be 1 to 253 characters in length and can contain only letters, digits, hyphens (-), underscores ( ), and periods (.). _ |

7. Click **Create**.
After the CronJob is created, you can view the CronJob on the CronJobs page.

**Create a CronJob from a YAML template**

1. On the **CronJobs** page, select a namespace from the **Namespace** drop-down list and click **Create from**
**Template** in the upper-right corner.
2. On the **Create** page, select a template and configure the template in the **Template** section.
3. Click **Create**.

**Create a CronJob using kubectl**

Before you use kubectl to create a CronJob, you must download kubectl and connect to your cluster using kubectl. For more information, see Connect to an ACK cluster using kubectl. The following table describes the main parameters of a CronJob.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| .spec.schedule | The running period of the task. The format is the same as aC ron schedule. |
| .spec.jobTemplate | The task to run. The format is the same asJ ob patterns. |
| .spec.startingDeadlineSeconds | The deadline for starting the task. |
| .spec.concurrencyPolicy | The concurrency policy of the task. Valid values are Allow, Forbid, and Replace. Allow: Allows jobs to run concurrently. Concurrent jobs compete for cluster resources. Forbid: Prohibits jobs from running concurrently. If a previous job is not yet complete, the next job is skipped. Replace: If a previous job is not yet complete when it is time to create a new job, the new job replaces the previous one. |

A CronJob named hello is created in this example to demonstrate how to create a CronJob using kubectl.
1. Create a file named cronjob.yaml and copy the following content to the file:

```
apiVersion: batch/v1beta1 kind: CronJob metadata:
  name: hello
spec:
  schedule: "*/1 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: hello
            image: busybox
            args:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - date; echo Hello from the Kubernetes cluster
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

2. Run the following command to create a CronJob:

```bash
kubectl create -f cronjob.yaml
```

If `cronjob.batch/hello created` is returned, the CronJob is created.

**Related operations**

After a CronJob is created, you can perform the following operations:

> **Note:** On the **CronJobs** page, you can select multiple CronJobs and delete them in a batch.

In the **Actions** column of the CronJob, click **Details** to view its basic information, such as the job list, events, and logs. In the **Actions** column of the CronJob, choose **More > View in YAML**, **More > Stop**, or **More > Delete** to view the YAML file, stop the task, or delete the task.

##### 7.10.1.7 Manage pods

Pods are the smallest deployable units in Kubernetes. A pod runs an instance of an independent application in Kubernetes. Each pod contains one or more containers that are tightly coupled. You can modify, view, access, delete, and export pods and manually scale the number of pods for an application in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.

**View detailed pod information**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Workloads > Pods**.
5. Click **View Details** to the right of the pod that you want to view.

> **Note:** To modify the configuration of the pod, click **Edit** in the upper-right corner of the page and modify the pod YAML file.

You can view details of pods by using one of the following methods: Method 1: In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Workloads > Deployments**. Find the application that you want to manage and click its name. On the **Pods** tab, click the name of the pod to view details. Method 2: In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Network > Services**. Click the name of the Service that you want to manage. On the details page, find and click the name of the application that you want to manage. On the **Pods** tab, click the name of the pod to view details.

> **Note:** On the Pods page, you can modify and delete pods. For pods that are created by using a Deployment, we recommend that you use the Deployment to manage the pods.

**View pod logs**

You can view the logs of a pod on the Deployments page or the Pods page. Navigate to the Pods tab, find the pod that you want to manage, and then click **Logs** on the right side of the pod.

**Modify the configuration of a pod**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Workloads > Pods**.
5. On the **Pods** page, select a pod and click **Edit** on the right side.
6. In the **Edit YAML** dialog box, modify the pod configuration and click **Update**.

**Manually scale pods**

After an application is created, you can scale the pods that are provisioned for the application.
1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Workloads > Deployments**.
5. In the upper part of the **Deployments** page, select a **namespace**. Find the application that you want to
manage and click **Scale** in the **Actions** column.
6. In the Scale dialog box, set Desired Number of Pods to 4 and click **OK**.

> **Note:** By default, Deployments are updated based on the rollingUpdate policy. This ensures that a minimum number of pods are available during the update. You can change this number in the YAML file.

**Use a terminal to access a pod**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Workloads > Pods**.
5. In the upper part of the **Pods** page, select a **namespace**. Find the pod that you want to manage and click
**Terminal** on the right side. Then, click the pod name.
Then, you can run commands to manage the pod by using the terminal.

**Delete a pod**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Workloads > Pods**.
5. In the upper part of the **Pods** page, select a **namespace**. Find the pod that you want to delete and click
**Delete** on the right side. Then, click **Confirm** in the message that appears.

> **Note:** On the **Pods** page, you can select multiple pods and delete them at a time.

**Export pods**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the desired cluster and click the name of the cluster in the Cluster Name/ID
column or click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Workloads > Pods**.
5. In the upper part of the **Pods** page, select a **namespace** and click **Export** in the upper-right corner.
6. In the message that appears, you can view the download path and the file name. The pod records are
exported to an EXCEL file.

> **Note:** After the download is complete, you can view the pod records on the on-premises machine.

##### 7.10.1.8 Manage custom resources

Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) clusters allow you to extend the Kubernetes API by adding custom resources. You can use custom resource definitions (CRDs) to define custom resources. You can view the API groups in an ACK cluster and the types of resources in each API group. You can also manage these resources. This topic describes how to create, view, modify, and delete custom resources.

**Prerequisites**

An ACK dedicated cluster or ACK edge cluster is created.

**Create custom resources**

When you create a CRD, the Kubernetes API server specifies a RESTful resource path for each resource version that you specified. You can set the **spec.scope** parameter in a CRD to specify whether the CRD takes on effect on a namespace or a cluster. For more information about CRDs, see Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions.
1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters** and click the name of the
cluster that you want to manage.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Workloads > Custom Resources**.
3. On the **Custom Resources** page, click **Create from YAML**.
4. On the **Create** page, set **Sample Template** to **Custom**. Enter YAML content into the **Template** editor
and click **Create**. For more information, see Create CRDs.

**View custom resources**

1. On the **Custom Resources** page, click the **CRDs** tab and click the **name** of the CRD that you want to
view.
2. On the **Resource Objects** tab, view the API groups and custom resources.

| Operation | Description |
|---|---|
| View API groups and resource types. | The left-side pane displays all API groups supported by the cluster. You can click the name of an API group to view all resource types that are included in the group. You can also enter a keyword into the search box to search for specific resource types. |
| View resource objects | Select a resource type from an API group to view the resource objects of the specified resource type. |

**Modify custom resources**

| Object | Procedure |
|---|---|
| CRD | 1. On the Custom Resources page, click the CRDs tab. Then, click Edit YAML in the Actions column of the CRD that you want to modify. 2. In the View in YAML panel, modify the parameters and click OK. |
| Resource object | 1. On the Custom Resources page, click the Resource Objects tab. 2. On the Resource Objects tab, click the name of an API group in the left-side pane and click the resource object that you want to modify. 3. On the Resource Objects tab, click Edit YAML in the Actions of the resource object. 4. In the View in YAML panel, modify the parameters and click OK. |

**Delete custom resources**

| Object | Procedure |
|---|---|
| CRD | 1. On the Custom Resources page, click the CRDs tab. Then, click Delete in the Actions column of the CRD that you want to delete. 2. In the Confirm message, click OK. |
| Resource object | 1. On the Custom Resources page, click the Resource Objects tab. 2. On the Resource Objects tab, click the name of an API group in the left-side pane and click the resource object that you want to delete. 3. On the Resource Objects tab, click Delete in the Actions of the resource object. 4. In the Confirm message, click OK. |

#### 7.10.2 Create a Service

You can create a Service for your application in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console to provide access to the application. In Kubernetes, a Service is an abstraction that defines a logical set of pods and a policy that is used to access the pods. This pattern is known as a microservice. A label selector determines whether the set of pods can be accessed by the Service. Each pod in an ACK cluster has its own IP address. However, pods are frequently created and deleted. Therefore, if you directly expose pods to external access, high availability is not ensured. Services decouple the frontend from the backend. The frontend clients do not need to be aware of which backend pods are used. This provides a loosely-coupled microservice architecture. For more information, see Service.

**Prerequisites**

An ACK cluster is created. For more information, see Create an ACK cluster.

**Step 1: Create a Deployment**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column
to go to the cluster details page.
4. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Workloads > Deployments**.
5. On the **Deployments** page, select a namespace and click **Create from Template** in the upper-right
corner.
6. Select a sample template or customize a template, and click **Create**.
In this example, the template of an NGINX Deployment is used.

```
apiVersion: apps/v1 # for versions before 1.8.0 use apps/v1beta1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: n ginx-deployment-basic labels: app: nginx spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: nginx template: metadata: labels: app: nginx spec: # nodeSelector: # env: test-team containers: - name: n ginx image: nginx:1.7.9 # replace it with your exactly <image_name:tags> ports: - containerPort: 80
```

Query the status of the Deployment.

**Step 2: Create a Service**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column
to go to the cluster details page.
4. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Network > Services**.
5. On the Services page, select a namespace and click **Create** in the upper-right corner.

> **Note:** You can also click **Create Resources in YAML** in the upper-right corner to create a resource by using an existing YAML template and deploy the resource to the application. You can also set the resource as a template. This way, you can create service resources based on the template.

6. In the Create Service dialog box, configure the parameters.
**Name**: the name of the Service. In this example, nginx-svc is used.
**Type**: the type of the Service. This parameter specifies how the Service is accessed. Valid values:
Cluster IP: a ClusterIP Service. This type of Service exposes pods by using an internal IP address of the cluster. If you select this option, pods can be accessed from only within the cluster. This is the default value. Node Port: a NodePort Service. This type of Service exposes pods by using the IP address and a static port of each node. A NodePort Service can be used to route requests to a ClusterIP Service, which is automatically created by the system. You can access a NodePort Service from outside the cluster by sending requests to `<NodeIP>:<NodePort>` . Server Load Balancer: a LoadBalancer Service. This type of Service exposes pods by using Server Load Balancer (SLB) instances, which support Internet access or internal access. SLB instances can be used to route requests to NodePort and ClusterIP Services.
**Backend**: the backend object that you want to associate with the Service. In this example, select nginx-
deployment-basic that you created in the preceding step. If you do not associate the Service with a backend object, no Endpoints object is created. You can also manually associate the Service with an Endpoints object. For more information, see Services without selectors.
**Port Mapping**: the Service port and container port. The container port must be the same as the one
that is exposed in the backend pod.
**Annotations**: the annotations that you want to add to the Service. For example, you can add the
LoadBalancer annotation `service.beta.kubernetes.io` with a value of `20` . This indicates that the maximum bandwidth of the Service is 20 Mbit/s. This way, the amount of traffic that flows to the Service is limited. For more information about the parameters, see Use SLB to access Services.
**Labels**: the labels that you want to add to the Service.
7. Click **Create**. After the nginx-svc Service is created, it appears on the Services page.
On the **Services** page, you can view basic information about the Service. You can also access its external endpoint by using a browser.

**What to do next**

After a Service is created, you can perform the following operations on the Service by clicking buttons in the
**Actions** column:
Click **Details** to view the basic information and application information about the Service. Click **Update** to update the configurations of the Service. Click **View in YAML** to modify the Service configurations in a YAML file. Click **Delete** to delete the Service if it is no longer needed.

> **Note:** On the **Services** page, you can also select multiple Services and delete the selected Services at a time.

#### 7.10.3 View a Service

You can view details about a Service in the Container Service console.

**Background information**

Each pod in Kubernetes clusters has its own IP address. However, pods are frequently created and deleted. Therefore, it is not practical to directly expose pods to external access. Services decouple the frontend from the backend, which provides a loosely-coupled microservice architecture.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Network > Services**.
5. On the **Services** page, select the namespace, find the Service that you want to view, and then click
**Details** in the Actions column.
On the details page, you can view detailed information about the Service.

You can update a Service in the Container Service console. This topic describes how to update a Service.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Network > Services**.
5. On the **Services** page, select the namespace, find the Service that you want to update, and then click
**Update** in the Actions column.
6. In the **Update Service** dialog box, modify the configurations and click **Update**.
In the Service list, find the Service that you updated and click **Details** in the Actions column to view configuration changes. In this example, the labels of the Service are modified.

#### 7.10.5 Delete a Service

This topic describes how to delete a Service.

**Prerequisites**

An ACK cluster is created. For more information, see Create an ACK cluster. A Service is created. For more information, see Create a Service.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column
to go to the cluster details page.
4. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Network > Services**.
5. On the Services page, select a namespace, find the Service that you want to delete, and then click **Delete**

#### 7.10.6 Use a trigger to redeploy an application

You can create a trigger and use it to redeploy an application. This topic describes how to use a trigger.

**Prerequisites**

A Kubernetes cluster is created. For more information, see Create a Kubernetes cluster. An application is created. Then, a trigger is created for the application and the application is used to test the trigger. In this example, an NGINX application is created.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Manage** in the **Actions** column
of the cluster.
4. In the left-side navigation pane, click Deployments. On the **Deployments** page, find the NGINX
application and click **Details** in the Actions column.
5. On the details page of the application, click the **Triggers** tab. Then, click **Create Trigger**.
6. In the dialog box that appears, set Action to **Redeploy** and click **Confirm**.

> **Note:** You can create triggers only to redeploy applications.

After the trigger is created, the webhook URL of the trigger appears in the Trigger Link Address column on the **nginx - deployment** page.
7. Copy the webhook URL, enter it into the address bar of your browser, and press Enter. A message that
indicates specific information such as the request ID appears.
8. Go to the **nginx - deployment** page. A new pod appears on the **Pods** tab.
After the new pod is deployed, the original pod is automatically deleted.

**What to do next**

You can run triggers by sending GET or POST requests from an external system. For example, you can use the **curl** command-line tool to run triggers. To run the redeploy trigger, run the following command:

```bash
 curl https://cs.console.aliyun.com/hook/trigger?token=xxxxxxx
```

#### 7.10.7 Use kritis-validation-hook to automatically verify the signatures of Container Registry Standard Edition images

**verify the signatures of Container Registry Standard**

**Edition images**

This topic describes how to use kritis-validation-hook to automatically verify the signatures of container images. This ensures that only images signed by trusted authorities are deployed and reduces the risk of malicious code execution.

**Prerequisites**

Your container image is signed. For more information, see the **Sign container images** topic in **Container**
**Registry Standard Edition** of **Container Registry User Guide**.

**Procedure**

1. Install the image signature verification component.
i. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. ii. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. iii. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name. Alternatively, click
**Details** in the **Actions** column.
iv. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Add-ons**. v. In the **Security** section of the **Add-ons** page, find kritis-validation-hook and click **Install**. vi. In the **Install kritis-validation-hook** message, click **OK**. Install the component and grant it the required permissions.
2. Configure a signature verification policy.
i. Configure the following signature parameters in the command-line interface (CLI) of your on-premises machine to configure a signature verification policy:

```
export namespace=The actual namespace export noteName=The value of noteName export publicKeyData=The value of publicKeyData
```

namespace: the namespace of Container Registry that is used to sign the image. noteName: the noteName setting used to sign the image. publicKeyData: the Base64-encoded GNU Privacy Guard (GPG) public key. ii. Connect to your ACK cluster by using kubectl. iii. Run the following commands to set AttestationAuthority.

> **Note:** In the following example, the default namespace is used.

```bash
cat <<EOF > aa.yaml apiVersion: kritis.grafeas.io/v1beta1 kind: AttestationAuthority metadata:
  name: ${noteName}
spec:
  noteReference: namespaces/${namespace}
  publicKeyData: ${publicKeyData}
EOF kubectl -n default apply -f aa.yaml
```

iv. Run the following commands to set GenericAttestationPolicy.

> **Note:** In the following example, the default namespace is used.

```bash
cat <<EOF > gap.yaml apiVersion: kritis.grafeas.io/v1beta1 kind: GenericAttestationPolicy metadata:
  name: my-gap
spec:
  attestationAuthorityNames:
  - ${noteName}
EOF kubectl -n default apply -f gap.yaml
```

3. Verify the signature verification feature.
In this example, the **registry.acs.example.com/kritis-**

**test/signed@sha256:2f122941b5850006dbb7adda78d2ea5b382841ca6569fd174bd24c14bfff**

image is signed. The **registry.acs.example/kritis-test/not-** sign@sha256:efc961b2b3499c25753d3c9f29977f494f49125cf1191071057aa68bffa7**** image is not signed. If the feature functions as expected, the signature verification policy enables the signed image and disables the unsigned image for the default namespace. If you use an unsigned image when you create an application, the application fails to be deployed, and the following error message is

```
returned: admission webhook "kritis-validation-hook-deployments.grafeas.io" denied the request . Run
```

the following commands to verify the signature verification feature:

```bash
#A Deployment is created by using the signed image.
kubectl -n default run test-signed --image=registry.acs.example.com/kritistest/signed@sha256:2f122941b5850006dbb7adda78d2ea5b382841ca6569fd174bd24c14bff**** deployment.apps/test-signed created
#A Deployment fails to be created by using the unsigned image.
kubectl -n default run test-not-signed --image=registry.acs.example/kritis-test/notsign@sha256:efc961b2b3499c25753d3c9f29977f494f49125cf1191071057aa68bffa7**** Error from server: admission webhook "kritis-validation-hook-deployments.grafeas.io" denied the req uest: image registry.acs.example/kritis-test/notsign@sha256:efc961b2b3499c25753d3c9f29977f494f49125cf1191071057aa68bffa7**** is not attested
```

> **Important:** When you create a resource after signature verification is enabled, you must specify the image by using the digest of the image, such as @sha256:<hash>.

#### 7.10.8 Use kritis-validation-hook to automatically verify the signatures of Container Registry Advanced Edition images

**verify the signatures of Container Registry Advanced**

**Edition images**

This topic describes how to use Container Registry, Key Management Service (KMS), Security Center, and kritis-validation-hook to automatically verify the signatures of container images. This allows you to deploy only container images that have been signed by trusted authorities and reduce the risk of malicious code execution in your environment.

**Step 1: Install kritis-validation-hook**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name. Alternatively, click
**Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Add-ons**.
5. In the **Security** section of the **Add-ons** page, find kritis-validation-hook and click **Install**.
6. In the **Install kritis-validation-hook** message, click **OK**. Install the component and grant it the required
permissions.

**Step 2: Create a key that is used to sign images in the KMS console**

1. Sign in to the Apsara Uni-manager Operation Console.
2. In the top navigation bar, choose **Products > Security > Key Management Service**.
3. On the **Customer Master Keys** page, click **Create Key**.
4. On the **Create Key** page, select an **organization**. The system automatically populates the **resource set**
and **region** fields.
5. In the **Basic configurations** section, configure the following parameters.

> **Note:** The image signing feature is implemented based on asymmetric key algorithms. When you create the KMS key, select an EC or RSA key type and set the Key Purpose parameter to SIGN/VERIFY. Configure other parameters based on your business requirements.

| Paramete r | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Key Type | Symmetric key types: Aliyun AES 256 _ _ Asymmetric key types: RSA 2048 _ EC P256 _ EC P256K _ | Asymmetric customer master keys (CMKs): RSA 2048 _ EC P256 _ EC P256K _ |
| Key Purpose | ENCRYPT/DECRYPT: Encrypt and decrypt data. SIGN/VERIFY: Generate and verify a digital signature. | SIGN/VERIFY |

6. Click **Submit**.

**Step 3: Create a witness that uses the key in the Security Center console**

1. Sign in to the Apsara Uni-manager Operation Console.
2. In the top navigation bar, choose **Security > Server Security > Container Security Service (CSS)**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Runtime Detection > Container Signature**. On the Container
Signature page, create a witness and associate it with the KMS key for container image signing.

**Step 4: Enable image signing in Container Registry**

1. Log in to the Container Registry console.
2. In the top navigation bar, select a region.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Instances**.
4. On the **Instances** page, click the Enterprise Edition instance that you want to manage.
5. On the management page of the Container Registry Enterprise Edition instance, choose **Security and**
**Trust > Image Signature** in the left-side navigation pane. Click **Add a signature rule**.
6. In the **Key Configuration** step, select the witness that you created in the Security Center console and
associate the witness with the KMS key. Then, click **Next**.
7. In the **Signature Configurations** step, configure the parameters and click **Create Signing Rule**.

> **Note:** A signature rule applies only to new images that are pushed to the specified namespace. Existing images are not signed based on the signature rule.

**Algorithms**: You can select **RSA_PSS_SHA_256** or **RSA_PKCS1_SHA_256**.
**Scope**: Select the namespace that you want to automatically sign.
**Signature Type**:
Default: Image digests and tags are signed. The default mode is applicable to the signature verification of images in the current instance. Simple: Only image digests are signed. Image tags are not signed. The simple mode is suitable for cross-instance image replication scenarios. The signatures of corresponding images are verified when image tags change. Trigger Type: the mode in which image signing is triggered. The default value is Automatic Trigger, which indicates that image signing is automatically triggered whenever an image is pushed to Container Registry.

**Step 5: Enable signature verification in Security Center**

To enable signature verification for a namespace, add and enable a security policy for the cluster in the Security Center console.
1. Sign in to the Apsara Uni-manager Operation Console.
2. In the top navigation bar, choose **Security > Server Security > Container Security Service (CSS)**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Runtime Detection > Container Signature**.
4. On the **Security Policy** tab, click **Add Policy**. After you configure the parameters, click **OK**.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Policy Name | Enter a name for the security policy. When you configure a security policy, you must select a witness to enable the container feature for the required cluster. We recommend that you enter an informative name. |
| Application Cluster | Select the cluster group for which you want to enable the container signature feature. Then, select the required Cluster Namespace. |
| Witness | Select the witness that you created from the witness list. |
| Policy Enabled | Turn on the switch. The policy is automatically enabled after it is created. Note The switch is turned off by default. In this case, the policy does not take effect after it is created. |
| Remarks | Enter a description for the security policy. |

**Step 6: Check whether signature verification is enabled**

> **Note:** The image is immutable if signature verification is disabled. You must specify the image by using the digest of the image. For more information, see Configure a repository to be immutable.

Run the following commands to check whether signature verification is enabled. After signature verification is enabled for the default namespace, unsigned images cannot be deployed in the namespace. To specify an image by tag, run the following commands:

```bash
kubectl -n default create deployment not-sign --image=alpine:3.11 -- sleep 10 Error from server: admission webhook "kritis-validation-hook-deployments.grafeas.io" denied the req uest: image alpine:3.11 is not attested
```

To specify an image by digest, run the following commands:

```bash
kubectl -n default create deployment not-sign -image=alpine@sha256:ddba4d27a7ffc3f86dd6c2f92041af252a1f23a8e742c90e6e1297bfa1bc0c45 -- sleep 10 Error from server: admission webhook "kritis-validation-hook-deployments.grafeas.io" denied the req uest: image alpine@sha256:ddba4d27a7ffc3f86dd6c2f92041af252a1f23a8e742c90e6e1297bfa1bc0c45 is not a ttested
```

Push an image to a namespace for which image signature signing is enabled. Then, verify that the image can be deployed after the image is signed.

```bash
docker push kritis-demo***.cn-hongkong.cr.aliyuncs.com/kritis-demo***/alpine:3.11 The push refers to repository [kritis-demo***.cn-hongkong.cr.aliyuncs.com/kritis-demo***/alpine] 5216338b40a7: Pushed 3.11: digest: sha256:ddba4d27a7ffc3f86dd6c2f92041af252a1f23a8e742c90e6e1297bfa1bc0c45 size: 528
```

To accept requests to deploy signed images, run the following commands:

```bash
kubectl -n default create deployment is-signed --image=kritis-demo***.cnhongkong.cr.aliyuncs.com/kritisdemo***/alpine@sha256:ddba4d27a7ffc3f86dd6c2f92041af252a1f23a8e742c90e6e1297bfa1bc0c45 -- sleep 10 deployment.apps/is-signed created
```

#### 7.10.9 Schedule pods to specific nodes

You can add labels to nodes and schedule pods to the nodes with specified labels. This topic describes how to schedule a pod to a node with specified labels. You can add labels to nodes and then configure `nodeSelector` to schedule pods to nodes with specified labels. For more information about how nodeSelector works, see nodeselector. To meet business requirements, you may want to deploy a controller service on a master node, or deploy services on nodes that use standard SSDs. You can use the following method to schedule pods to nodes with specified labels.

**Prerequisites**

A Kubernetes cluster is created. For more information, see Create a Kubernetes cluster.

**Step 1: Add a label to a node**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Nodes > Nodes**.
5. On the **Nodes** page, click **Manage Labels and Taints** in the upper-right corner.
6. Select one or more nodes and then click **Add Label**. In this example, a worker node is selected.
7. In the dialog box that appears, enter the name and value of the label and click **OK**.
On the Labels tab, you can find the `group:worker` label next to the selected node. You can also run the following command to add a label to a node: `kubectl label nodes <node-name> <label-`

```
key>=<label-value> .
```

**Step 2: Schedule a pod to the node**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Workloads > Deployments**.

 apiVersion: v1

#### 7.10.10 Simplify application deployment by using Helm

**Helm**

This topic describes the basic concepts of Helm and shows how to use it to deploy sample applications, such as WordPress and Spark, on an Alibaba Cloud Kubernetes cluster.

**Prerequisites**

You have created a Kubernetes cluster in Container Service. For more information, see Create a Kubernetes cluster. When you create a Kubernetes cluster, Container Service automatically deploys Tiller in the cluster, installs the Helm command-line interface (CLI) on all master nodes, and configures a chart repository that points to Alibaba Cloud. You have checked the Kubernetes version of your cluster. Only Kubernetes clusters of version 1.8.4 or later are supported. If your cluster runs Kubernetes 1.8.1, use the **Upgrade Cluster** operation in the cluster list to upgrade it. If you need to synchronize Helm charts from Container Registry Enterprise Edition (ACR EE), first create a chart repository and upload the chart files. For more information, see **Create a Chart Repository** and
**Manage Chart Repositories** in the **Container Registry User Guide**.

**Background information**

Helm provides a unified software packaging method that supports version control and simplifies the distribution and deployment of Kubernetes applications. Alibaba Cloud Container Service integrates Helm into its App Catalog feature and provides extended capabilities. Container Service supports the official repository, allowing you to quickly deploy applications. You can deploy applications by using the command line or the Container Service console.

**Key concepts of Helm**

Helm is an open source tool created by Deis that helps simplify the deployment and management of Kubernetes applications. Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. It makes it easy to discover, share, and use applications built for Kubernetes. It includes the following key concepts: chart: A Helm package that contains all the necessary resources for running an application, such as images, dependencies, and resource definitions. It may also include service definitions for the Kubernetes cluster. A chart is similar to a formula in Homebrew, a dpkg package in APT, or an rpm package in Yum. release: An instance of a chart running on a Kubernetes cluster. A chart can be installed multiple times on the same cluster. Each installation creates a unique, named release. For example, if you want to run two databases by using a MySQL chart, you can install the chart twice. Each installation generates its own release with its own release name. repository: A location for storing and sharing charts.

**Helm components**

Helm uses a client/server architecture and consists of the following components: The Helm CLI is the client-side component. You can run it on a master node of the Kubernetes cluster or on your local machine. Tiller is the server-side component. It runs on the Kubernetes cluster and manages the lifecycle of Kubernetes applications. A repository is a chart repository. The Helm client accesses the index files and compressed packages of charts in the repository over the HTTP protocol.

**Deploy an application by using the console**

1. Log on to the Container Service console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Cluster List** page, click the name of the target cluster. In the left-side navigation pane, choose
**Applications > Helm**.
3. On the **Helm** page, click **Create**. Configure the basic information, then find and select the desired chart in
the chart section.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Application Name | A custom name for the application. |
| namespace | Select the namespace where the application will be deployed. |

| Source | The source of the Helm chart package. App Marketplace: A public chart repository provided by Alibaba Cloud. chart: You can search for a chart by use case, supported architecture, or name, and then click the chart card. Container Registry Enterprise Edition (ACR EE): Pull a private chart from an instance of Alibaba Cloud Container Registry Enterprise Edition. Note You can use the console to deploy charts from chart repositories in Container Registry Enterprise Edition, but you must use a client to deploy charts from OCI repositories. Instance: Select a region, instance, and repository, and then click the chart card. |
|---|---|

4. Click **Next**. Select the latest chart version, confirm the parameters, and then click **OK**.

**Use a third-party chart repository**

You can add any network-accessible third-party chart repository in addition to the pre-configured Alibaba Cloud repository. Use the following command format to add a third-party chart repository:

```
helm repo add <REPO_NAME> <REPO_URL> # Add a chart repository. Replace <REPO_NAME> with the name of the chart repository and <REPO_URL> with the URL of the repository. helm repo update
```

For more information about Helm commands, see the Helm documentation.

**References**

Helm has a large and growing community. Many software providers, such as Bitnami, offer high-quality charts. You can discover more charts at `https://kubeapps.com/` .

### 7.11 Agent Sandbox

#### 7.11.1 ACK Agent Sandbox

ACK Agent Sandbox is a sandboxed compute service for production-grade AI agents. It integrates fully with the Kubernetes ecosystem to provide a secure and isolated runtime environment that supports large-scale elastic scheduling and state persistence.

**Product positioning**

Built on proprietary sandboxing technology, ACK Agent Sandbox provides a kernel-level isolated runtime environment and offers state management capabilities such as hibernation and wake-up and checkpoint cloning. The service supports large-scale elastic scaling, creating tens of thousands of Sandboxes per minute. It is fully compatible with the Kubernetes ecosystem and seamlessly integrates with mainstream AI agent frameworks and tools such as the E2B SDK and AgentScope.

**Key features**

**Strong security isolation**

Built on a proprietary sandboxed runtime environment, ACK Agent Sandbox provides an independent and secure execution space for each Sandbox. It provides end-to-end isolation across compute, network, and storage resources. The service also supports Sandbox-level logging and monitoring to simplify auditing and troubleshooting. Network isolation supports multi-layer policies:
**Layer 4**: The `TrafficPolicy` CRD enables access control at the CIDR, Service, and FQDN levels. It also
supports priority-based rules and cluster-wide global policies.
**Layer 7**: The `SecurityProfile` CRD provides fine-grained control over egress traffic based on attributes
such as domain, path, method, and headers. It also supports HTTPS TLS termination and audit webhooks.

**Large-scale, low-latency elasticity**

**Image cache acceleration**: Makes images ready in seconds and reduces pull times by over 90% in
typical use cases.
**Warm pool**: A `warm pool` optimized with `SandboxSet` allows you to create new Sandboxes in
hundreds of milliseconds. In high-concurrency scenarios, the creation rate can reach tens of thousands of Sandboxes per minute.
**Pre-scheduling optimization**: Optimizes scheduling based on workload characteristics, improving
creation efficiency in high-concurrency scenarios and accelerating `AgentRL` training iterations.

**State persistence**

**Hibernation and wake-up**: Lets you hibernate running Sandboxes on demand, fully preserving their in-
memory state for quick wake-ups. Both automatic (timeout-based) and manual hibernation modes are supported. In typical scenarios, restoring a Sandbox from its memory state takes 1 to 10 seconds. You are not billed for CPU and memory resources while a Sandbox is hibernated.
**Checkpoint cloning**: Supports creating checkpoint snapshots of a Sandbox's file system state. You can
then create new Sandboxes by cloning these snapshots. This feature makes the `AI agent` state storable and portable, accelerating parallel exploration and branch-and-explore workflows.

**Flexible access methods**

**Sandbox CR (Declarative)**: Use Kubernetes custom resources (CRs), such as `SandboxSet` and
`SandboxClaim` , to declaratively manage Sandbox templates, runtime parameters, and lifecycles. This method is ideal for platform engineering scenarios.

**Kubernetes native ecosystem**

Fully compatible with the Kubernetes feature set:
**Storage**: Supports mounting `shared storage` , such as `OSS` and `NAS` , by using the Container Storage
Interface (CSI). The system automatically injects storage drivers as a `sidecar` .

| k: Use the |   | TrafficPolicy |
|---|---|---|
| TrafficPolicy |   |   |
| over | Pod |   |

**Network**: Use the `TrafficPolicy` CRD to control network access for agent-based applications in the
cluster. `TrafficPolicy` supports multi-level, priority-based network policies and provides fine-grained control over `Pod` ingress traffic and egress traffic by using various matching criteria, including CIDR, Service, and FQDN.

**Use cases**

**AgentRL training**

Ideal for `reinforcement learning` training, trajectory sampling, environment interaction, and multi-path exploration. It supports large-scale concurrent Sandbox creation, rapid termination, and checkpoint state reuse to improve training throughput and resource utilization.

**AgentServing online services**

Designed for online `AI agent` services, such as in-depth research, tool invocation, multi-turn conversations, and intelligent coding assistants. It provides a strongly isolated execution environment, hundreds-of-milliseconds Sandbox startups from a `warm pool` , and `hibernation and wake-up` capabilities. This combination balances a responsive experience with low running costs.

**Personal assistants and digital employees**

Enables rapid development and deployment of personal assistant and `digital employee` applications. It supports various tool environments for tasks such as code execution, browser automation, and desktop automation, facilitating a smooth transition from prototype to production.

**Limitations**

Your `ACK cluster` must be version 1.32 or later. The `ack-agent-sandbox-controller` and `ack-sandbox-` `manager` components must be installed. When you create a Sandbox from a `snapshot` , ensure that the image used to create the `snapshot` is the same as the image specified in the Sandbox YAML configuration. The number of concurrent Sandboxes in a single cluster is limited by the size of your node resource pool. Plan your `warm pool` capacity based on your expected peak workload.

#### 7.11.2 Quick start

##### 7.11.2.1 Create an Agent Sandbox

This topic describes how to create an Agent Sandbox in an ACK cluster. Learn how to create a pre-warmed pool, claim an Agent Sandbox, and delete a sandbox.

**Prerequisites**

Create a Kubernetes cluster and enable **Enable Sandboxed-Container** and **Install ack-kruise-agent-**
**sandbox component**.
If you already have a cluster, you must also create a node pool and enable **Enable Sandboxed-**
**Container** and **Install ack-kruise-agent-sandbox component**.

**Procedure**

**Step 1: Create a pre-warmed pool with SandboxSet**

> **Note:** A pre-warmed pool is a set of pre-created sandbox replicas managed by a SandboxSet custom resource (CR). Applications can claim ready-to-use sandboxes directly from this pool, significantly improving delivery efficiency.

1. Log on to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, click **Details** in the **Actions** column of the target cluster.
4. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Workloads > Custom Resources**.
5. On the **Custom Resources** page, click in the upper-right corner.
6. Use the following YAML manifest to create a SandboxSet resource. When created, the ack-sandbox-
manager automatically detects this resource and initializes a sandbox template configuration named code-interpreter.

```
apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: SandboxSet metadata:
  name: code-interpreter
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        sandbox-name: "code-interpreter"
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: runsc
      containers:
      - image: registry-cn-test-vpc.ack.aliyuncs.com/acs/code-interpreter:v1.6 # Replace with the c
orrect image URL for your cluster's region.
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        name: sandbox
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 1Gi
          requests:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 1Gi
            ephemeral-storage: 30Gi
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
```

7. In the navigation pane on the left, click , select the corresponding namespace, and then view the created
`code-interpreter` sandbox.

> **Note:** You can run the `kubectl get sbs` command to view SandboxSet resources. The `AVAILABLE` column indicates the number of ready sandboxes.

When a sandbox is claimed, the SandboxSet automatically creates a new one to maintain the number of replicas in the pre-warmed pool.

**Step 2: Claim an Agent Sandbox**

After you claim a sandbox from the pre-warmed pool, the SandboxSet automatically creates a new instance to replenish the pool.
1. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Workloads > Custom Resources**.
2. On the **Custom Resources** page, click in the upper-right corner.
3. To claim a sandbox, create a SandboxClaim resource with the following YAML manifest.

```
apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: SandboxClaim metadata:
  name: code-interpreter              # The name of the SandboxSet.
  namespace: default                  # The namespace of the SandboxSet.
spec:
  templateName: code-interpreter      # Specify the name of the SandboxSet.
  replicas: 1                         # The number of sandboxes to claim from the SandboxSet.
  claimTimeout: 5m                    # The timeout period for the SandboxClaim.
  ttlAfterCompleted: 15m              # The Time-to-Live (TTL) period after the claim is completed.
The SandboxClaim resource is deleted after this period, but the claimed sandbox is not.
```

4. In the navigation pane on the left, click , select the `default` namespace, and then view the newly
claimed sandbox. The sandbox is named in the format `code-interpreter-xxxxx` .

> **Note:** You can run the `kubectl get sbx -l agents.kruise.io/claim-name=code-interpreter` command to check the status of the claimed sandbox.

**Delete an Agent Sandbox**

To delete a sandbox instance, run the following command.

```bash
# Before you run the command, replace <NAMESPACE> with the namespace of the resource and <RESOURCE_NA
ME> with the name of the custom resource. kubectl -n <NAMESPACE> delete sandbox <RESOURCE_NAME>
```

#### 7.11.3 Lifecycle management

##### 7.11.3.1 Hibernate and wake up an Agent Sandbox

When running large-scale AI agent tasks, you can reduce costs of idle compute resources by using kubectl to modify the `spec` field of the Agent Sandbox Custom Resource (CR). This lets you hibernate sandbox instances on demand and wake them up without context loss, improving cluster resource utilization.

**Applicability**

Use this feature only with sandbox instances created by the `ack-kruise-agent-sandbox` component. For more information, see Create an Agent Sandbox.

> **Note:** You can run the `kubectl get sandbox <RESOURCE_NAME> -o yaml` command to check the
> `metadata.creationTimestamp` field. If the instance does not meet any of the preceding conditions, recreate the Sandbox.

**Hibernate an Agent Sandbox**

Hibernating a sandbox instance releases its idle resources to reduce operational costs. Modify the Sandbox instance configuration to set `spec.paused` to `true` .

```bash
# Before you run this command, replace <RESOURCE_NAME> with the name of your resource and <NAMESPACE>
with the namespace of the resource. kubectl patch sandbox <RESOURCE_NAME> -n <NAMESPACE> --type='merge' -p '{"spec":{"paused":true}}'
```

> **Note:** By default, hibernated Sandbox CRs are not automatically deleted. To schedule an automatic deletion, set the `shutdownTime` field in the Agent Sandbox resource to the desired time.

After you hibernate the sandbox instance, go to the cluster details page, select **Workloads > Custom**
**Resources**, and filter the list to view its hibernation status.

**Wake up an Agent Sandbox**

In the Sandbox instance configuration, set `spec.paused` to `false` .

```bash
# Before you run this command, replace <RESOURCE_NAME> with the name of your resource and <NAMESPACE>
with the namespace of the resource. kubectl patch sandbox <RESOURCE_NAME> -n <NAMESPACE> --type='merge' -p '{"spec":{"paused":false}}'
```

After you wake up the sandbox instance, go to the cluster details page, select **Workloads > Pods**, and filter the list to view its running status.

> **Note:** Check the standard output of the container logs to verify that the application continues to run correctly after its memory state is restored.

**Check the Agent Sandbox status**

A Pod in hibernation does not consume any cluster CPU resources.

```bash
kubectl -n <NAMESPACE> top pod
```

**Delete a hibernated Agent Sandbox**

To permanently remove a hibernated instance, run the following command to delete the Agent Sandbox.

```bash
# Before you run this command, replace <NAMESPACE> with the namespace of the resource and <RESOURCE_N
AME> with the actual CR name. kubectl -n <NAMESPACE> delete sandbox <RESOURCE_NAME>
```

**Limitations**

**Request interruption and long-lived connection loss** : Hibernating an instance immediately freezes its
CPU. Any in-flight requests time out and fail. After the instance wakes up, it does not automatically restore long-lived connections such as WebSocket, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and gRPC. Clients must reconnect manually. Trigger hibernation only after confirming that there are no active requests or long-lived connections.

**References**

##### 7.11.3.2 Clone an Agent Sandbox with Checkpoint

When developing complex AI agents, you may need to save the running state of a sandbox environment to quickly reuse it. You can create a snapshot of a running container using the E2B SDK or a Checkpoint Custom Resource (CR). This method ensures file system consistency and reduces environment initialization costs.

**Prerequisites**

The `ack-kruise-agent-sandbox` and `ack-fluid` components are installed in your cluster.

**Limitations**

You can create a Checkpoint only when the target Pod is in the `Running` and `Ready` state. Only one Checkpoint operation can be in progress for a single Pod at a time. You can create a new Checkpoint after the previous one reaches a terminal state ( `Succeeded` or `Failed` ). After a Checkpoint task enters the Running state, you cannot interrupt the task by deleting the Checkpoint resource.

**Before you begin**

The Checkpoint feature uses Fluid as the data plane for acceleration and stores Checkpoint files in OSS. You must meet the following requirements:

| d the Dataset is in the Bound |   |
|---|---|
| containerd-shim-runsc-v1 | su |

1. Ensure that Fluid is deployed in the cluster and the Dataset is in the `Bound` state.
feature.
3. Create an OSS access key Secret in the `sandbox-system` namespace:

```bash
kubectl -n sandbox-system create secret generic oss \
  --from-literal=accessKeyId=<YOUR_AK> \
  --from-literal=accessKeySecret=<YOUR_SK>
```

**Procedure**

**Step 1: Create a Sandbox**

```bash
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: Sandbox metadata:
  name: demo-checkpoint
  namespace: sandbox-system
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: runsc
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: nginx:1.17
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo CHECKPOINT_STATE_TEST > /tmp/testfile; i=0; while true; do echo
$i > /tmp/counter; i=$((i+1)); sleep 1; done"] EOF kubectl -n sandbox-system get sandbox demo-checkpoint -w
```

**Step 2: Create a Checkpoint**

```bash
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: Checkpoint metadata:
  name: demo-cp
  namespace: sandbox-system
spec:
  sandboxName: demo-checkpoint
  keepRunning: true
  repository:
    type: "oss"
    repository: "checkpoint-test-1"
    distributed: true
    ossAuth:
      endpoint: "<OSS-ENDPOINT>"
      accessKeySecret:
        name: "oss"
EOF kubectl -n sandbox-system get checkpoint demo-cp -w
```

Expected: The STATUS transitions through `Preparing` → `InProgress` → `Succeeded` . The checkpoint file is persisted to OSS. The source sandbox continues to run ( `keepRunning: true` ).

```
NAME STATUS AGE demo-cp Succeeded 50s
```

**Step 3: Restore a Sandbox from a Checkpoint**

> **Important:** When restoring, the container spec (including `command` and `image` ) must be identical to the spec used when the Checkpoint was created. `runsc` performs a strict validation.

```bash
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: Sandbox metadata:
  name: demo-restored
  namespace: sandbox-system
spec:
  restoreFrom:
    checkpointName: demo-cp
  template:
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: runsc
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: nginx:1.17
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo CHECKPOINT_STATE_TEST > /tmp/testfile; i=0; while true; do echo
$i > /tmp/counter; i=$((i+1)); sleep 1; done"] EOF kubectl -n sandbox-system get sandbox demo-restored -w
```

Expected result: The restored Sandbox enters the `Running` state, and its process resumes execution from the memory state captured by the Checkpoint.

```
NAME STATUS AGE demo-restored Running 1s
```

**Step 4: Verify the state restoration**

```bash
kubectl -n sandbox-system exec demo-restored -c app -- sh -c ' echo "testfile: $(cat /tmp/testfile)" echo "counter: $(cat /tmp/counter)"'
```

Expected result: The content of `/tmp/testfile` is preserved, and the counter continues to increment from its value when the Checkpoint was taken, instead of resetting to 0.

```
testfile: CHECKPOINT_STATE_TEST counter: 221
```
