##### 7.12.3.12 API Gateway Ingress Controller

###### 7.12.3.12.1 Overview

API Gateway Ingress Controller is an enterprise-grade service built on the open source Higress gateway. It is compatible with NGINX Ingress and is designed for API management and microservices scenarios.

**Introduction to Ingress**

In a Kubernetes cluster, an Ingress serves as an access point that exposes services in the cluster and provides Layer 7 load balancing. It distributes most of the traffic that is destined for the services in the cluster. An Ingress is a Kubernetes resource that manages external access to the services in a Kubernetes cluster. By configuring Ingress resources, you can define various forwarding rules to route traffic to backend pods of different services within the cluster. Ingress resources allow you to configure only the rules for routing HTTP traffic. Advanced features such as load balancing algorithms and session affinity cannot be configured. The advanced features require support from NGINX Ingress gateways or APIG Ingress gateways.

**Usage notes of API Gateway Ingress Controller**

The API Gateway Ingress Controller component is developed based on Cloud-native Gateway and provides a more powerful method to manage Ingress traffic. This component is compatible with NGINX Ingress gateways and more than 50 annotations defined in NGINX Ingress gateways. It is suitable for more than 90% of scenarios of NGINX Ingress gateways. This component supports canary releases of multiple service versions at the same time and provides flexible service governance capabilities and comprehensive security protection. It can meet requirements for traffic governance in scenarios in which a large number of cloudnative distributed applications are used. While maintaining compatibility with annotations defined in NGINX Ingress gateways, API Gateway Ingress Controller introduces additional annotations to enhance traffic governance and security protection capabilities. After you deploy API Gateway Ingress Controller in your cluster, it listens to ApigConfig resources and dynamically manages the lifecycles, global parameter settings, and listening items of Ingress resources for cloud-native gateways. Cloud-native gateways are used to listen to Ingress resources in a Kubernetes cluster and convert the listened Ingress resources into the required traffic governance configurations. This way, cluster services are externally exposed.

**Working principles of API Gateway Ingress Controller**

API Gateway Ingress Controller: API Gateway Ingress Controller is not a network data plane, but is a control plane that manages cloudnative gateways and their configurations. API Gateway Ingress Controller does not process any service requests. It works as a traffic bypass to manage cloud-native gateways that process service traffic. You need to manage the API Gateway Ingress Controller component in your cluster, use the ApigConfig CRDs provided by this component to manage cloud-native gateways based on annotations, and configure Ingress resource listening items for the gateways. Cloud-native gateway: Cloud-native gateways are created by the API Gateway Ingress Controller component based on ApigConfig CRDs that you configured. A cloud-native gateway consists of a control plane and a data plane. Control plane: listens to resources such as Ingresses, Ingress classes, and services in an associated ACK cluster. The resource configurations are internally parsed and then sent to the data plane of the gateway in real time. Data plane: implements traffic governance. The data plane processes external requests based on the governance rules that are sent from the control plane, and routes the requests to the destination backend services.

**How it works**

API Gateway Ingress Controller listens to the ApigConfig resources created in your ACK cluster and dynamically maintains the lifecycle of the cloud-native gateway that corresponds to the resources and the association between the gateway and your cluster in real time. The control plane of the cloud-native gateway obtains the changes of Ingress resources by using the API server of the associated ACK cluster and dynamically updates the routing rules of the cloud-native gateway. After the cloud-native gateway receives a request, the gateway matches the request with an Ingress routing rule and routes the request to the pod that corresponds to the backend service based on the matched routing rule. The following content describes the relationships among services, Ingresses, Ingress classes, ApigConfig, and APIG Controller in a Kubernetes cluster. Service: an abstraction of an application that is deployed in a group of replicated pods. Ingress: a set of reverse proxy rules. An Ingress specifies the services to which HTTP or HTTPS requests are routed. For example, an Ingress routes requests to different services based on the hostnames and URLs in the requests. Ingress class: a description of the Ingress processor. An Ingress class is used to declare the implementation of an Ingress processor in a Kubernetes cluster. The Ingress resources that are associated with the Ingress class are parsed by the Ingress processor. You must associate an ApigConfig (cloud-native gateway) with the **Parameter** field of the Ingress class to implement the traffic management rule that is specified in the parsed Ingress resource description. ApigConfig: a CRD that is provided by the API Gateway Ingress Controller. An ApigConfig CRD provides basic information about a cloud-native gateway. APIG Controller: a control plane that manages cloud-native gateways and their configurations. The APIG Controller is not a network data plane. API Gateway Ingress Controller is used to listen to ApigConfig resources in a cluster and coordinate cloud-native gateways to implement the traffic management rule that is specified in the parsed Ingress resource description. The following figure shows how API Gateway Ingress Controller works.

| Deployment One-to-on Mo Traffi Cloud-native Gateway | ACK Cluster API Gateway Ingress and Management Controller IngressClass ApigConfig Specify an Ingress Controller e Mappings Ingress Service Specify a Traffic nitoring Processing Rule Pod c Forwarding |

##### 7.12.3.13 Higress Ingress Controller

This topic describes the features and usage notes of the Higress Ingress Controller component.

**Component introduction**

Higress is a cloud-native API gateway built on Istio and Envoy at its core. It allows you to write WebAssembly (Wasm) plug-ins in languages such as Go, Rust, and JavaScript. It provides dozens of ready-to-use generalpurpose plug-ins and an out-of-the-box console. Higress was born within Alibaba Cloud to address the issues of Tengine reloads causing disruptions to persistent connections, as well as insufficient load balancing capabilities for gRPC and Dubbo. Alibaba Cloud has built Cloud-native API Gateway based on Higress, providing a large number of enterprise customers with gateway services that guarantee 99.99% high availability. Based on AI gateway capabilities, Higress powers AI services such as Qwen app, Model Studio API, and Platform for AI (PAI). This project is open source. For more information, see Higress.

**Procedure**

**Install the Higress Ingress Controller component**

**Install the component in an existing cluster**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the cluster that you want to manage. In the left-side navigation
pane, click **Add-ons**.
4. On the **Add-ons** page, find the Higress Ingress Controller component and click **Install**.
5. In the **Install Higress Ingress Controller** dialog box, you can choose whether to select **Create public**
**network service** based on your business requirements, select **Load Balancer Specification**, and then
click **OK**.

> **Note:** If you select **Create public network service**, an additional public network service higress-gateway- internet will be established, and a private network service higress-gateway-intranet will be established by default.

**Install the component when you create a cluster**

When you create a cluster, select Higress Ingress Controller for Ingress in the Component Configurations step. For more information about how to create a cluster, see Create a Kubernetes cluster.

**Create a sample application**

1. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name. In the left-side pane,
choose **Workloads > Deployments**.
2. On the **Deployments** page, click **Create from Template**. For example, use the following YAML code to
create an NGINX service:

```xml
apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata:
  name: nginx-html
data:
  index.html: |
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html>
    <head><title>Hello World</title></head>
    <body>
    <h1>Hello World from Nginx!</h1>
    </body>
    </html>
--apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata:
  name: backend
  labels:
    app: backend
    service: backend
spec:
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
  selector:
    app: backend
--apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata:
  name: backend
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
      version: v1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: backend
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
        - image: <Your-Registry>/nginx:1.17
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          name: backend
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: html
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
      volumes:
        - name: html
          configMap:
            name: nginx-html
```

> **Note:** Replace <Your-Registry> with the address of your image repository and upload the image file of the corresponding version.

**Create a route**

1. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Network > Ingresses**. On the Ingresses page, click **Create**.
2. In the **Create** dialog box, set **Ingress Type** to **Higress Ingress**, **Path** to `/` , and Name to `backend` .
Then, click **Create**.

**Verify the results**

1. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Network > Services**. On the Services page, select `kube-`
`system` from the Namespace drop-down list, and obtain the external endpoints of the higress-controller, higress-gateway, higress-gateway-intranet, higress-gateway-internet, and higress-plugin-server services.
2. Run the following commands in sequence to initiate requests to the external endpoints of the preceding
services:

```bash
curl -H "Host: hello.example.com" http://<External endpoint>
```

##### 7.12.3.14 Poseidon

Poseidon is an ACK-developed container NetworkPolicy plugin that supports standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy features. This topic describes the Poseidon component and its usage. As an ACK-developed plugin, Poseidon supports standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy specifications.

**Usage**

**Install Poseidon**

**In an existing cluster**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the target cluster and then click **Add-ons** in the left-side
navigation pane.
4. On the **Add-ons** page, find the Poseidon component and click **Install**.
5. In the **Install** dialog box, configure the following parameters and then click **OK**.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| cos.k8s.addon.config.poseidon.description.networ kPolicy | Specifies whether to enable basic network policy support. |
| cos.k8s.addon.config.poseidon.description.acknet workPolicy | Specifies whether to enable support for enhanced ACK network policies. |
| cos.k8s.addon.config.poseidon.description.trafficP olicy | Specifies whether to enable support for traffic policies. |
| kubeClientQPS | The maximum number of queries per second (QPS) that the Poseidon client can send to the Kubernetes API server. |
| kubeClientBurst | The number of requests allowed to burst above the QPS limit. |
| fqdnDNSServers | The IP addresses of DNS servers that Poseidon uses to resolve FQDNs. Note Click Add to add more DNS servers. Click Delete to remove the current entry. |
| fqdnDNSProtocol | Specifies the protocol that Poseidon uses to communicate with the DNS servers. udp tcp |
| fqdnDNSTimeout | The timeout for a single DNS query. |

**During cluster creation**

When you create a cluster, selecting **Enable sandbox** also selects **Install sandbox-runv-agent** and automatically installs the Poseidon component. For detailed instructions on how to create a cluster, see Create a Kubernetes cluster.

**Limitations**

The network policy feature is supported only in ACK Serverless clusters, on ECI in ACK clusters, and on ACS CPU instances. This feature supports only IPv4 addresses. The traffic policy feature is supported only on ACS instances in ACK clusters and in ACS clusters. This feature supports only IPv4 addresses. The ACK GlobalNetworkPolicy feature is supported only on ECS instances in ACK clusters. The cluster network plugin must be Terway, and the network policy feature must be enabled.

**Configuration**

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| NetworkPolicy | boolean | false | Enables network policies. |
| ACKNetworkPolicy | boolean | false | Enables ACK network policies. |
| TrafficPolicy | boolean | true | Enables the traffic policy feature. |
| kubeClientQPS | integer | 500 | The number of queries per second (QPS) for the kube client. Valid values: 1 to 99999. |
| kubeClientBurst | integer | 600 | The burst for the kube client. Valid values: 1 to 99999. |
| fqdnDNSServers | array<string> | Not set by default | A list of FQDN DNS servers. Each entry must be in the ip or ip:port format. |
| fqdnDNSProtocol | string | "udp" | The FQDN DNS protocol supports the following enumerated values: "" , tcp , and udp . An empty value defaults to udp . |
| fqdnDNSTimeout | integer | 5 | The timeout for a single DNS query, in seconds. Valid values: 1 to 9. |

| "" | tcp |
|---|---|
| udp |   |

resource "alicloud_cs_kubernetes_addon" "poseidon" {
    cluster_id = alicloud_cs_managed_kubernetes.default.id
    name       = "poseidon"
    version    = "v0.7.6"
    config = jsonencode({
      NetworkPolicy    = true
      ACKNetworkPolicy = true
      TrafficPolicy    = true
      kubeClientQPS    = 500
      kubeClientBurst  = 600
      fqdnDNSServers   = ["100.100.2.136", "100.100.2.138"]

##### 7.12.3.16 AHPA

Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) supports the Advanced Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (AHPA) to manage auto scaling for your applications. For applications with cyclical workloads, AHPA uses elasticity prediction to perform resource warm-up, which helps prevent elastic scaling lag. You can install the AHPA component to use its predictive capabilities. This topic describes the components and usage of AHPA. AHPA mitigates elastic scaling lag by predicting the required number of pods based on historical application metrics. AHPA combines proactive and passive prediction to adjust the number of pods in real time. It also includes a fallback protection strategy, which allows you to set minimum and maximum pod counts for specific time ranges as a scaling guardrail.

**How it works**

Auto scaling helps you save costs, improve service stability, and reduce operational overhead. The AHPA architecture follows these principles: Stability: Scales your application while maintaining service stability. Reduced operational overhead: The AHPA Autoscaler offers a simpler configuration than a standard HPA. The following figure shows the architecture of AHPA. resource metrics custom metrics external metrics MQ CPU/Memory QPS/RT Length Smarter algorithms scaling metrics Scaling methods Knative/HPA/ Deployment pod pod pod pod pod pod Rich metrics: AHPA supports various metrics, including resource metrics such as CPU and memory, custom metrics such as QPS and RT, and external metrics. Stability guarantee: The AHPA scaling logic combines proactive resource warm-up and passive scaling with fallback protection to ensure resource stability. Proactive prediction: Uses machine learning algorithms from DAMO Academy to predict the required number of pods for the next 24 hours based on historical metrics. This approach is ideal for applications with cyclical workloads. Passive prediction: Calculates the required number of pods based on real-time application metrics. This helps your application handle sudden traffic spikes. Fallback protection: Allows you to configure the minimum and maximum number of pods for different time ranges. Multiple scaling methods: AHPA can manage auto scaling for various resources, including Knative services, HPA objects, and Deployments. Knative: Addresses cold start issues for serverless applications by scaling based on concurrency, QPS, and RT. HPA: Simplifies HPA policy configuration, making auto scaling easier to adopt, and resolves cold start issues common in standard HPA. Deployment: Directly scales the pods within a Deployment.

##### 7.12.3.17 AI profiling

AI Profiling is an advanced analysis tool for performance observability, diagnostics, and optimization across the full lifecycle of AI applications. It provides an end-to-end solution for developers and operations teams by tracing cross-layer call traces in the software stack of AI models during training and inference, including the Python stack, Torch layer, video memory, CUDA runtime, and GPU kernel functions. AI Profiling combines this trace data with fine-grained, operator-level performance metrics, such as FLOPs, time spent on computation, communication, and video memory, idle time, and overall resource consumption.

**Key benefits**

**Non-intrusive**: AI Profiling is non-intrusive, requiring no changes to your containers.
**Comprehensive data collection**: Collect metrics on demand, including the Python call stack, CPU
information, GPU operators, Torch details, video memory usage, and FLOPs. You can also collect monitoring metrics for RDMA, GPU, and CPU as needed.
**Centralized analysis**: Analyzes collected data automatically on a central server to provide a multi-
dimensional view of your job's performance.
**Stability**: Proven stable in large-scale clusters with thousands of GPUs, AI Profiling has zero impact on AI
jobs.
**Flexible collection modes**: Supports data collection based on time intervals or by iteration. It also offers
advanced configurations, such as defining custom iteration entry points and skipping the first N iterations.
**Low overhead**: You can configure the level of detail for data collection based on your needs. The system
overhead during collection ranges from 5% to 40%.
**Multi-process support**: Supports simultaneous data collection from multiple processes.

**Use cases**

Use AI Profiling to diagnose common performance issues and find recommended solutions. Diagnose failures that occur after you deploy your AI application. Investigate why your AI application is running slower than expected. Identify performance bottlenecks on your server, such as an operator that is taking too long to execute.

### 7.13 SLB and Ingress

#### 7.13.1 Overview

Container Service allows you to flexibly manage load balancing and customize load balancing policies for Kubernetes clusters. Kubernetes clusters provide you with a variety of methods to access containerized applications. They also allow you to use SLB or Ingress to access internal services and implement load balancing.

#### 7.13.2 Use SLB to access Services

You can access a Service by using Server Load Balancer (SLB).

**Procedure**

1. Create an NGINX application by using a CLI.

```
root@master # kubectl run nginx --image=registry.aliyuncs.com/acs/netdia:latest
       root@master # kubectl get po
       NAME                                   READY     STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
       nginx-2721357637-dvwq3                 1/1       Running   1          6s
```

2. Create a Service for the NGINX application and specify `type=LoadBalancer` to expose the Service to the
Internet through an SLB instance.

```
root@master # kubectl expose deployment nginx --port=80 --target-port=80 --type=LoadBalancer
       root@master # kubectl get svc
       NAME                  CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP      PORT(S)                        AGE
       nginx                 172.19.XX.XX    101.37.XX.XX     80:31891/TCP                   4s
```

3. Enter `http://101.37.XX.XX` in the address bar of your browser and press Enter to access the nginx
Service.

**SLB parameters**

SLB provides a variety of parameters that you can use to configure features and services such as health check, billing method, and SLB instance type. For more information, see SLB annotations.

**Annotations**

You can add annotations to use the load balancing features provided by SLB.

**Use an existing internal-facing SLB instance**

Add two annotations. You must replace your-loadbalancer-id with the ID of your SLB instance.

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata:
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud-loadbalancer-address-type: intranet
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud-loadbalancer-id: your-loadbalancer-id
  labels:
    run: nginx
  name: nginx
  namespace: default
spec:
  ports:
  - name: web
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 80
  selector:
    run: nginx
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: LoadBalancer
```

Save the preceding code as an slb.svc file and run the `kubectl apply -f slb.svc` command.

**Create an HTTPS-based LoadBalancer Service**

You must first create a certificate in the SLB console. Then, you can use the certificate ID (cert-id) and the following template to create a LoadBalancer Service and an HTTPS-based SLB instance.

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata:
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud-loadbalancer-cert-id: your-cert-id
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud-loadbalancer-protocol-port: "https:443"
  labels:
    run: nginx
  name: nginx
  namespace: default
spec:
  ports:
  - name: web
    port: 443
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 443
  selector:
    run: nginx
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: LoadBalancer
```

> **Note:** Annotations are case-sensitive.

Table 1. SLB annotations

| Annotation | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud- loadbalancer-protocol-port | The listening port. Separate multiple ports with commas (,). Example: https:443,http:80. | N/A |
| service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud- loadbalancer-address-type | The type of the SLB instance. Valid values: internet and intranet. | internet |
| service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud- loadbalancer-slb-network-type | The network type of the SLB instance. Valid values: classic and vpc. | classic |
| service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud- loadbalancer-charge-type | The billing method of the SLB instance. Valid values: paybytraffic and paybybandwidth. | paybybandwidth |
| service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud- loadbalancer-id | The ID of an existing SLB instance. You can set the loadbalancer-id parameter to specify an existing SLB instance. In this case, the existing listeners are overwritten by the SLB instance. The SLB instance is not deleted when the Service is deleted. | N/A |
| service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud- loadbalancer-backend-label | The labels that are used to select the nodes to be added as the backend servers of the SLB instance. | N/A |
| service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud- loadbalancer-region | The region where the SLB instance is deployed. | N/A |
| service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud- loadbalancer-bandwidth | The bandwidth of the SLB instance. | 50 |
| service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud- loadbalancer-cert-id | The certificate ID. You must first upload the certificate. | "" |
| service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud- loadbalancer-health-check-flag | Valid values: on and off. | Default value: off. If TCP is used, do not modify this parameter. The health check feature is automatically enabled for TCP listeners and cannot be disabled. |

#### 7.13.3 Configure Ingress monitoring

You can enable the virtual host traffic status (VTS) dashboard to view Ingress monitoring data.

**Enable the VTS dashboard by using the CLI**

| Add the following configuration item to the Ingress ConfigMap: | enable-vts-status: "true" | . |
|---|---|---|
| root@master # kubectl edit configmap nginx-configuration -n kube-system configmap "nginx-configuration" edited |   |   |

The following template shows the modified Ingress ConfigMap:

```json
apiVersion: v1 data:
  enable-vts-status: "true"# Enables the VTS dashboard.
  proxy-body-size: 20m
kind: ConfigMap metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: |
      {"apiVersion":"v1","data":{"proxy-body-size":"20m"},"kind":"ConfigMap","metadata":
{"annotations":{},"labels":{"app":"ingress-nginx"},"name":"nginx-configuration","namespace":"kube-s ystem"}}
  creationTimestamp: 2018-03-20T07:10:18Z
  labels:
    app: ingress-nginx
  name: nginx-configuration
  namespace: kube-system
  selfLink: /api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/configmaps/nginx-configuration
```

2. Verify that the VTS dashboard is enabled for the NGINX Ingress controller.

```
root@master # kubectl get pods --selector=app=ingress-nginx -n kube-system NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE nginx-ingress-controller-79877595c8-78gq8 1/1 Running 0 1h root@master # kubectl exec -it nginx-ingress-controller-79877595c8-78gq8 -n kube-system -- cat /etc/nginx/nginx.conf | grep vhost_traffic_status_display
         vhost_traffic_status_display;
         vhost_traffic_status_display_format html;
```

3. Access the VTS dashboard from an on-premises machine.

> **Note:** By default, the VTS port is not exposed due to security concerns. In the following example, port forwarding is used to access the VTS dashboard.

```
root@master # kubectl port-forward nginx-ingress-controller-79877595c8-78gq8 -n kube-system 18080 Forwarding from 127.0.0.1:18080 -> 18080 Handling connection for 18080
```

4. Visit `http://localhost:18080/nginx_status` to access the VTS dashboard.

#### 7.13.4 Ingresses

Kubernetes clusters support Ingress rules. You can define Ingress rules to meet your needs for load balancing. In Kubernetes clusters, an Ingress is a set of routing rules that authorize external access to Services in clusters. You can use an Ingress to enable Layer 7 load balancing. You can configure an Ingress with URLs, Server Load Balancing (SLB) instances, SSL connections, and name-based virtual hosts to expose Services to external access.

**Prerequisites**

To test a complex routing scenario, an NGINX application is used in this example. A Deployment and multiple Services are created for the NGINX application. Replace Service names with the actual names.

```bash
kubectl run nginx --image=registry.cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/acs/netdia:latest kubectl expose deploy nginx --name=http-svc --port=80 --target-port=80 kubectl expose deploy nginx --name=http-svc1 --port=80 --target-port=80 kubectl expose deploy nginx --name=http-svc2 --port=80 --target-port80 kubectl expose deploy nginx --name=http-svc3 --port=80 --target-port=80
```

**Create a simple Ingress**

Run the following commands to create a simple Ingress that redirects traffic to the /svc path to an http-svc Service. `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /` redirects traffic destined for the /svc path to the / path that can be recognized by the backend Service.

```
cat <<EOF | kubectl create -f apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 kind: Ingress metadata:
  name: simple
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  rules:
  - http:
      paths:
      - path: /svc
        backend:
          serviceName: http-svc
          servicePort: 80
EOF
```

```bash
kubectl get ing NAME HOSTS ADDRESS PORTS AGE simple * 101.37.19*.*** 80 11s
```

You can visit `http://101.37.19*.***/svc` to access the Service of the NGINX application.

**Create a simple fanout Ingress that uses multiple domain names**

You can create a simple fanout Ingress to route traffic to multiple Services with different domain names. The following example shows the configuration of a simple fanout Ingress:

```bash
cat <<EOF | kubectl create -f apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 kind: Ingress metadata:
  name: simple-fanout
spec:
  rules:
  - host: foo.bar.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /foo
        backend:
          serviceName: http-svc1
          servicePort: 80
      - path: /bar
        backend:
          serviceName: http-svc2
          servicePort: 80
  - host: foo.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /film
        backend:
          serviceName: http-svc3
          servicePort: 80
EOF kubectl get ing NAME HOSTS ADDRESS PORTS AGE simple-fanout * 101.37.19*.*** 80 11s
```

After the preceding configuration is implemented, you can visit `http://foo.bar.com/foo` to access `http-`

| visit | http://foo.bar.com/bar |   |
|---|---|---|
| http-svc3 |   | . |

`svc1` , visit `http://foo.bar.com/bar` to access `http-svc2` , and visit `http://foo.example.com/film` to

> **Note:** In a production environment, you must point the domain name to the returned address

```
 101.37.XXX.XXX .
```

> In a test environment, you must add the following mapping rules to the `hosts` file.

```
101.37.19*.*** foo.bar.com 101.37.19*.*** foo.example.com
```

**Create a simple Ingress that uses the default domain name**

If you have no domain names, you can create a simple ingress that uses the default domain name provided by Container Service. Then, you can use the default domain name to access Services. The default domain name is in the following format: `*.[cluster-id].[region-id].alicontainer.com` . You can find the default domain name in the basic information of the Kubernetes cluster in the Container Service console. The following example shows the configuration of a simple Ingress that allows external access to Services through the default domain name:

```bash
cat <<EOF | kubectl create -f apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 kind: Ingress metadata:
  name: shared-dns
spec:
  rules:
  - host: foo.[cluster-id].[region-id].alicontainer.com  ## Replace with the default domain name of y
our cluster.
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        backend:
          serviceName: http-svc1
          servicePort: 80
  - host: bar.[cluster-id].[region-id].alicontainer.com  ## Replace with the default domain name of y
our cluster.
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        backend:
          serviceName: http-svc2
          servicePort: 80
EOF kubectl get ing NAME HOSTS ADDRESS PORTS AGE shared-dns foo.[cluster-id].[region-id].alicontainer.com,bar.[cluster-id].[regionid].alicontainer.com 47.95.16*.*** 80 40m
```

| can visit | http://foo.[cluster-id].[region-id].alicontainer.com/ |   |
|---|---|---|
| http://bar.[cluster-id].[region-id].alicontainer.com |   | to access |

| s Service | http-svc1 |   |
|---|---|---|
| http-svc2 |   | . |

**Create an Ingress to secure data transmission**

Container Service allows you to use multiple types of certificates to reinforce the security of your applications.
1. Prepare a certificate.
If you do not have a certificate, perform the following steps to generate a test certificate:

> **Note:** The domain name must be the same as the one specified in your Ingress configurations.

```
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -subj "/CN=foo.bar .com/O=foo.bar.com"
```

After you run the preceding command, a certificate file tls.crt and a private key file tls.key are generated. Use the certificate and private key to create a Kubernetes Secret named foo.bar. The Secret is referenced when you create the Ingress.

```bash
kubectl create secret tls foo.bar --key tls.key --cert tls.crt
```

2. Create an Ingress to secure data transmission.

```bash
cat <<EOF | kubectl create -f apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 kind: Ingress metadata:
  name: tls-fanout
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - foo.bar.com
    secretName: foo.bar
  rules:
  - host: foo.bar.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /foo
        backend:
          serviceName: http-svc1
          servicePort: 80
      - path: /bar
        backend:
          serviceName: http-svc2
          servicePort: 80
EOF kubectl get ing NAME HOSTS ADDRESS PORTS AGE tls-fanout * 101.37.19*.*** 80 11s
```

3. You must configure the `hosts` file or set a domain name to access the tls Ingress, as described in the
**Create a simple fanout Ingress that uses multiple domain names** section.

| visit | http://foo.bar.com/foo |   |
|---|---|---|
| http-svc2 |   | . |

You can visit `http://foo.bar.com/foo` to access `http-svc1` and visit `http://foo.bar.com/bar` to You can also access the HTTPS Service by using HTTP. By default, an HTTPS Ingress redirects HTTP traffic to HTTPS. Therefore, access to `http://foo.bar.com/foo` is redirected to `https://foo.bar.com/foo` .

**Create an Ingress**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Network > Ingresses**.
5. On the **Ingresses** page, select a namespace and click **Create Resources in YAML**.
6. On the **Create** page, select **Custom** from the **Sample Template** drop-down list, copy the following
content into the template, and then click **Create**.

```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 kind: Ingress metadata:
  name: simple
spec:
  rules:
  - http:
      paths:
      - path: /svc
        backend:
          serviceName: http-svc
          servicePort: 80
```

An Ingress that routes Layer 7 traffic to the `http-svc` Service is created.

#### 7.13.5 Configure an NGINX Ingress to use a public IPv6 address

**IPv6 address**

Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) supports IPv4/IPv6 dual stack. You can associate a LoadBalancer Service that uses a public IPv6 address with the NGINX Ingress controller to support IPv6. This topic describes how to configure an NGINX Ingress to use a public IPv6 address.

**Prerequisites**

An ACK dedicated cluster that has **IPv4/IPv6 dual stack** enabled is created. For more information, see Create a Kubernetes cluster.

> **Note:** Only ACK dedicated clusters support IPv4/IPv6 dual stack. ACK edge clusters do not support IPv4/IPv6 dual stack.

The NGINX Ingress controller is installed. For more information, see Create a Kubernetes cluster and Manage components.

**Features**

After you create a cluster that has IPv4/IPv6 dual stack enabled, the system assigns an IPv4 cluster address and an IPv6 cluster address to the LoadBalancer Service that is associated with the NGINX Ingress controller. You can connect to these IP addresses from within the cluster. By default, the LoadBalancer Service is named nginx-ingress-lb and belongs to the kube-system namespace. You can access the cluster by using the cluster IP addresses or domain name of the nginx-ingress-lb Service in the kube-system namespace. The nginx-ingress-lb Service is associated with an IPv4 Server Load Balancer (SLB) instance. Each Service can be associated only with one SLB instance. To use a public IPv6 address to access the cluster, you must create an IPv6 SLB instance and another Service, and then associate the Service with the IPv6 SLB instance.

**Procedure**

1. Use the following YAML template to create an IPv6 LoadBalancer Service.
We recommend that you create the Service in the kube-system namespace and use `nginx-ingress-lb-` `v6` as the Service name.

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata:
 name: nginx-ingress-lb-v6
 namespace: kube-system
 labels:
   app: nginx-ingress-lb
 annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/alibaba-cloud-loadbalancer-spec: slb.s2.small  # Specifies the
specification of the SLB instance.
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/alicloud-loadbalancer-address-type: internet   # Specifies that an
Internet-facing SLB instance is created.
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/alibaba-cloud-loadbalancer-ip-version: ipv6    # Specifies that the
SLB instance uses an IPv6 address.
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/alibaba-cloud-loadbalancer-backend-ip-version: ipv6  # Specifies
that IPv6 is used to connect backend servers to the SLB instance. spec:
 type: LoadBalancer
 externalTrafficPolicy: Local
 ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack
 ports:
 - port: 80
   name: http
   targetPort: 80
 - port: 443
   name: https
   targetPort: 443
 selector:
   app: ingress-nginx
```

> **Note:** You cannot create internal-facing IPv6 SLB instances.
> For more information about the specifications of SLB instances, see the **Preparations** topic in the **Getting Started** chapter of the **SLB User Guide**.

2. Run the following command to create a Service named `nginx-ingress-lb-v6` and use the Service to
expose your application.

```bash
kubectl apply -f nginx-ingress-lb-v6.yaml
```

**Verify the result**

Use one of the following methods to check whether the IPv6 SLB instance is created.

**Method 1: Check the external endpoint of the nginx-ingress-lb-v6 Service**

**in the ACK console**

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the cluster where the Service is deployed. In the left-side
navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Network > Services**.
3. On the **Services** page, find the nginx-ingress-lb-v6 Service and check whether an external endpoint is
displayed in the **External Endpoint** column. If an external endpoint is displayed, the IPv6 SLB instance is created.

**Method 2: Check the external endpoint of the nginx-ingress-lb-v6 Service**

**by using kubectl**

Run the following command to query the nginx-ingress-lb-v6 Service:

```bash
kubectl get svc -n kube-system nginx-ingress-lb-v6
```

Expected output:

```
NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE nginx-ingress-lb-v6 LoadBalancer 192.168.252.52 2408:XXXX:1f8::205 80:30587/TCP,443:30217/TCP 13m
```

The value in the `EXTERNAL-IP` column is the external endpoint of the Service. If a value is displayed in the `EXTERNAL-IP` column, the IPv6 SLB instance is created.

#### 7.13.6 Compatibility of NGINX Ingress annotations in Higress

**in Higress**

This document analyzes the compatibility of all Nginx Ingress Controller official annotations in Higress. Based on the complete annotation list on the Nginx Ingress Controller official annotation page, a total of 130 annotations are displayed by function.
**Release notes:** This document is based on the list of notes for the latest version (v1.15.1) of the Nginx
Ingress Controller. Some annotations are introduced or changed in different versions. Version information has been marked in related entries.
**Annotation Source Description:** The official Nginx Ingress Controller Annotations page contains two
annotations:
**Top index table (117)**: The annotations listed in the summary table at the top of the page, which
serves as a quick index to the core annotations.
**Text Supplementary Notes (13)**: Notes (such as auth-signin and limit-rpm) that are only described in
the functional chapters of the page body but are not listed in the top index table. These annotations are implemented in the code and are valid annotations that are fully supported by the latest version, but are not included in the top index table in document orchestration. In this document, the label `The` 13 annotations are only described in the text chapters and are not listed in the top 117 annotation index table; the remaining 117 annotations are in the top index table.
**Cross-validation:** This document has been cross-validated with annotations supported by APIG Ingress.
For annotations marked as "compatible" in APIG documents but judged different in this document, the reason for the difference is explained in the remarks.

**Statistical summary**

| Compatibility Classification | Quantity | Proportion | Main description |
|---|---|---|---|
| ␀Fully compatible | 39 | 30.0% | Higress is supported natively. It directly uses the original annotation or higress.io/* prefix. |
| equivalent replacement | 37 | 28.5% | /higress-config global configuration /EnvoyFilter through the WASM plug-in. |
| ␀Incompatible | 35 | 26.9% | Differences in the Envoy architecture result in missing features. You must evaluate alternatives. |

| ⚠️ Partially compatible | 7 | 5.4% | Semantics are not completely consistent. Some values /scenarios are available but there are gaps. |
|---|---|---|---|
| No migration required | 12 | 9.2% | The Envoy architecture is naturally overwritten or has outdated features, which are directly ignored during migration. |
| Total | 130 | 100% | Contains all the annotations listed Nginx Ingress Controller the official annotations page. |

**Differences between**annotations supported by an APIG Ingress**:**
The APIG document claims "51 supported annotations", and its statistical caliber contains "partially compatible" annotations (such as server-alias, auth-tls-secret, etc.), and includes denylist-source-range (gateway version 1.2.31 required), auth-secret/auth-secret-type, etc. as "compatible". This document uses a more stringent classification standard: only when Higress natively supports it and the semantics are completely consistent, it is marked as␀Fully compatible; tags replaced by plugins /configurations are; markers with functional subset gaps are⚠️. For specific differences, see "in each note entry.⚡APIG document differences "Remarks.

**Compatibility Identification Description**

␀**Fully compatible** :Higress supports native applications and can be used directly.
**Equivalent Replacement**: You can use plug-ins or other configuration methods to implement the same
features. ␀**Incompatible**: The service cannot be supported due to different architectures. ⚠️ **Partially compatible**: The semantics are not completely consistent. Some values or scenarios are available but there are gaps.
**No Migration Required**: The Envoy architecture is overwritten by the Envoy architecture or has outdated
features. The Envoy architecture is ignored during migration.

**Annotation Compatibility by Function**

**Routing and Rewriting (8)**

| Serial Number | Annotat ion Name | Compat ibility | Functio n descript ion |   | Priority | Equivalent method or description |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nginx.ing ress.kub ernetes.i o/rewrite -target | ␀ | Rewrite the request path to rewrite the matchin g URL path to the specified target path. |   | Importan t and common | API Gateway core functions, front-end separation, microservice routing required. Use the original annotation directly, or use the higress.io/rewrite- target . |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |   |   | higress.io/rewrite- |   |
|   |   |   |   | URL ath to | ly used | target |   |   |

| 2 | nginx.ing ress.kub ernetes.i o/use- regex | ␀ | Enable path regular expressi on matchin g and use rewrite- target to impleme nt complex path rewriting . |   | Importan t and common ly used | rewrite-Required configuration items of target for flexible path matching. Use the original annotation directly, or use the higress.io/use-regex . ⚠️ Difference in route priority: In NGINX, the priority is exact > regex > prefix . In Higress, the priority is exact > prefix > regex . The priority is descending order by path length. This means that the regex path takes precedence over the prefix path in Nginx. However, the prefix path has a higher priority after migration to Higress, which may cause traffic to be routed to different backends. During migration, you must check whether the priorities of the regex path and the prefix path conflict in the same host. |   |   |

Verified in rewrite.go, or use higress.io/upstream-vhost . |   |   |

This is common ly used in SPA applicati ons. |   | Not importan t but | The default route configuration of the frontend application. Use the original annotation directly (verified in redirect.go), or use the higress.io/app- root . |   |   |

This affects all routes. | Importa nt but not common ly used | This annotation in the NGINX Ingress controls whether global external authentication is enabled for an Ingress. The global authentication service is defined by the global-auth-url configuration items in the ConfigMap. Each authentication plug-in in Higress, such as key-auth, basic-auth, jwt-auth, and ext-auth, supports global auth configuration fields to control whether _ the plug-in takes effect globally. In addition, you can use a allow list to fine-grained control at the domain name or route level. | 2 | nginx.in gress.ku bernete s.io/satis fy | ␀ | The multi- authenti cation mode meets the conditio ns (all/any) . | Not importa nt and not common ly used | The combination logic used to control multiple authentication modules (such as IP whitelist + Basic Auth) in NGINX: "all" requires all to pass, and "any" only needs one to pass. Higress is not supported: The authentication model of Envoy is different from that of NGINX. Each authentication filter (such as ext-auth, basic-auth, and IP address control) is executed independently and has the "must pass" semantics. The "any" mode is not supported by the native system. To implement the "any" logic, you must develop a custom WASM plug-in to encapsulate multiple authentication methods. |

| 1 |   | nginx.in gress.ku bernete s.io/bac kend- protocol | ⚠️ | Specify the backen d protocol type (HTTP/H TTPS/G RPC/GR PCS). | Importa nt and commo nly used | Higress supports five protocols: HTTP, HTTP2, HTTPS, GRPC, and GRPCS. However, it does not support the AJP and FCGI protocols of NGINX Ingress. Partially compatible: HTTP, HTTPS, and gRPC are fully available in most scenarios. | 2 |   | nginx.in gress.ku bernete s.io/pro xy- body- size |   | Limit the size of the request body to prevent resourc e abuse by uploadi ng large files. | Importa nt and commo nly used | It can be safely ignored during migration. The core function of this annotation in Nginx is to protect the gateway itself-Nginx architecture is "receive the request body first and then forward". Oversized requests will directly occupy worker memory /disk, so they need to be rejected actively. However, Envoy uses a streaming forwarding architecture. Data is forwarded block by block after it arrives. The upper limit of the memory usage of a single connection is only per connection buffer limit bytes KB (32KB by _ _ _ _ default), which does not cause memory overflow no matter how large the request body is. Therefore, this limit is no longer necessary from the perspective of "protection gateway". If you want to adjust the connection buffer globally, you can use the higress-config downstream.connectionBufferLimits configuration. For a small number of business scenarios where large requests need to be intercepted at the gateway layer (you do not want traffic to reach the backend), you can use WasmPlugin to check the Content-Length in the OnHttpRequestHeaders phase or accumulate the body size in the OnHttpRequestBody phase, and return the request body limit of 413 to achieve routing granularity. |   |

Envoy processes all requests in memory and uses per connection buffer limit bytes to control the _ _ _ _ upper limit of connection-level buffering. Global configuration is supported only through the higress-config downstream.connectionBufferLimits (default 32768) and cannot be configured at the Ingress level. The semantics are not equal. | 14 | nginx.in gress.ku bernete s.io/pro xy- bufferin g |   | Enables /disable s backen d respons e bufferin g. | Not importa nt and not commo nly used | The NGINX proxy-buffering controls the upstream response buffering behavior of the reverse proxy. When NGINX is enabled, the reverse proxy caches the upstream response to the memory or disk before sending it to the client. This way, the upstream connection can be quickly released. When NGINX is disabled, the reverse proxy immediately forwards the received data (streaming), which is suitable for SSE /long polling scenarios. The Envoy architecture does not have Nginx, a proxy-buffering equivalent mechanism-Envoy is naturally streaming forwarding. After data arrives from the upstream, it is gradually forwarded to the downstream through the filter chain, and will not "save enough and send it again". The buffer filter of Envoy is only used for buffering in the request direction. The per connection buffer limit bytes is L4 layer flow _ _ _ _ control (1MB by default), which has completely different semantics. Therefore, scenarios such as SSE and long polling are naturally available on Envoy. You can directly delete this annotation during migration. |

The processing mechanism of the Envoy response header is different. The default configuration is sufficient, and no problems are caused by the lack of this configuration. You can directly delete it during migration. |

The Envoy streaming architecture does not require this concept. Data is forwarded as soon as it arrives and can be deleted directly during migration. |

This annotation controls the maximum size of the temporary file. Envoy does not use disk buffering at all. Therefore, this issue does not occur. You can directly delete Envoy during migration. |

#### 7.13.7 Migrate NGINX to Higress

This topic describes how to migrate a Higress from NGINX and how to configure it.

**Migration Priority**

**P0 (must deal with)-blocking problem**

1. **Snippet replacement**: All scenarios that use `*-snippet` must be refactored.
Evaluate specific logic. Develop the corresponding WASM plug-in. Or use the Higress built-in plug-in combination to achieve.
2. **Basic Auth Migration**: `auth-type` / `auth-secret` We recommend that you migrate to `basic-auth`
WASM plug-in (Higress v2.0.0 + recommended method). The plug-in supports multi-user credential management and has more complete functions. User credentials must be migrated from the Kubernetes Secret to the plug-in configuration. If you want Digest authentication, you must develop a custom WASM plug-in.
3. **Timeout configuration adjustment**: The three NGINX timeout annotations correspond to different
levels of configuration in Envoy.
**proxy-connect-timeout** (TCP connection establishment timeout) → Envoy cluster level
`connect_timeout` (default 5S). You can use Envoy Filter to configure the `connect_timeout` fields of the cluster or use DestinationRule `trafficPolicy.connectionPool.tcp.connectTimeout` .
**proxy-read-timeout / proxy-send-timeout** (idle timeout between two Data Transmission Service) →
Envoy `stream_idle_timeout` . Global configuration: `higress-config` the `upstream.idleTimeout` in the ConfigMap. Unit: seconds. Default value: 10 seconds. Route granularity: You can use Envoy Filter to set the `idle_timeout` of the route to overwrite the global value by route.
**Total request timeout** → `higress.io/timeout` annotation (corresponding to Envoy route level
`timeout` , default 15s), which is the end-to-end total timeout and has different semantics from NGINX idle timeout.

> **Important:** NGINX differentiates idle timeout between read and write, and Envoy is merged into one
> `stream_idle_timeout` . If the original read and send timeout values are different, only the larger value can be used.

**P1 (Recommended)-Feature Optimization**

NGINX.
2. **Security protection**: Configure a `waf` plug-in to replace ModSecurity, `useCRS: true` enable the
OWASP rule set, and `secRules` add custom SecRule rules. The plug-in is based on the Coraza engine and does not require external dependencies.
