**Create an application and configure SLS**

When you create an application in ACK, you can configure SLS to collect logs from containers. You can use only YAML templates to configure SLS.
1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name. You can also click
**Details** in the **Actions** column to go to the cluster details page.
3. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster details page, choose **Workloads > Deployments**. On the
Deployments page, click **Create from Template** in the upper-right corner.
4. Set **Sample Template** to **Custom** and configure the template.
YAML templates follow the Kubernetes syntax. You can use environment variables to add **collection**
**configurations** and **custom tags**. You must also configure volumeMounts and volumes. The following
sample code provides an example of pod configurations:

```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 kind: Deployment metadata:
  labels:
    app: logtail-test
  name: logtail-test
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: logtail-test
      name: logtail-test
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: logtail
        image: registry.acs.env28.intranet.com/acs/busybox:latest
        args:
        - ping
        - 127.0.0.1
        env:
        - name: aliyun_logs_log-stdout
          value: stdout
        - name: aliyun_logs_log-varlog
          value: /log/*.log
        - name: aliyun_logs_log_tags
          value: tag1=v1
        volumeMounts:
        - name: volumn-sls
          mountPath: /log
      volumes:
      - name: volumn-sls
        emptyDir: {}
```

Specify the following configurations in order as required: Add **log collection configurations** and **custom tags** by using environment variables. All environment variables related to log collection must use `aliyun_logs_` as the prefix. Add log collection configurations in the following format:

```
- name: aliyun_logs_{Logstore name}
  value: {Log collection path}
```

In the preceding YAML template, two environment variables are added to the log collection configuration. The `aliyun_logs_log-stdout` environment variable indicates that a Logstore named logstdout is created to store the stdout files collected from containers.

> **Note:** The name of the Logstore cannot contain underscores (_). You can use hyphens (-) instead.

Add **custom tags** in the following format:

```
- name: aliyun_logs_{Tag name without underscores (_)}_tags
  value: {Tag key}={Tag value}
```

After a tag is added, the tag is automatically appended to the log data that is collected from the container. If you specify a log path to collect log files other than stdout, you must set the volumeMounts parameter. In the preceding YAML template, the mountPath field in volumeMounts is set to /var/log. This allows Logtail to collect log data from the /var/log/*.log file.
5. After you modify the YAML template, click **Create** to submit the configurations.

**Environment variables**

You can configure container environment variables to customize log collection. You can configure advanced settings to meet your log collection requirement.

| Variable | Description | Example | Remarks |
|---|---|---|---|
| aliyun logs {key} _ _ | Required. {key} can contain only lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens (-), and cannot contain underscores ( ). _ If the specified aliyun logs {key} logst _ _ _ ore variable does not exist, a Logstore named {key} is automatically created to store the collected logs. To collect the stdout of a container, set the value to stdout. You can also set the value to a path inside the container to collect the log files. | - name: aliyun logs catali _ _ na stdout - name: aliyun logs access _ _ -log /var/log/nginx/acc ess.log | By default, the SLS component collects log data in simple mode. In this case, the collected log data is not parsed. If you want to parse the log data, we recommend that you change the collection mode in the SLS console. The value of {key} must be unique in the cluster. |
| aliyun logs {key} tags _ _ _ | Optional. The variable is used to add tags to log data. The value must be in the following format: {tag- key}={tag-value}. | - name: aliyun logs catalina _ _ _ tags app=catalina | - |
| aliyun logs {key} project _ _ _ | Optional. The variable specifies a project in SLS. By default, the project that you specified when you created the cluster is used. | - name: aliyun logs catalina _ _ _ project my-k8s-project | The project must be deployed in the same region as Logtail. |
| aliyun logs {key} logstore _ _ _ | Optional. The variable specifies a Logstore in SLS. By default, the Logstore is named {key}. | - name: aliyun logs catalina _ _ _ tags my-logstore | - |
| aliyun logs {key} shard _ _ _ | Optional. The variable specifies the number of shards of the Logstore. Valid values: 1 to 10. Default value: 2. | - name: aliyun logs catalina _ _ _ shard 4 | - |

| aliyun logs {key} ttl _ _ _ | Optional. The variable specifies the number of days for which log data is retained. Valid values: 1 to 3650. If you set the value to 3650, logs are permanently stored. Default value: 90. | - name: aliyun logs catalina _ _ _ ttl 3650 | - |
|---|---|---|---|
| aliyun logs {key} machin _ _ _ egroup | Optional. The variable specifies the machine group in which the application is deployed. The default node group is the one in which Logtail is deployed. | - name: aliyun logs catalina _ _ _ machinegroup my-machine-group | - |

Scenario 1: Collect logs from multiple applications and store them in the same Logstore In this scenario, set the **aliyun_logs_{key}_logstore** variable. The following example shows how to collect stdout from two applications and store the output in stdout-logstore. Configure the following environment variables for Application 1:

```
######### Configure environment variables.###########
    - name: aliyun_logs_app1-stdout
      value: stdout
    - name: aliyun_logs_app1-stdout_logstore
      value: stdout-logstore
```

Configure the following environment variables for Application 2:

```
######### Configure environment variables.###########
    - name: aliyun_logs_app2-stdout
      value: stdout
    - name: aliyun_logs_app2-stdout_logstore
      value: stdout-logstore
```

Scenario 2: Collect logs from different applications and store them in different projects In this scenario, perform the following steps: i. Create a machine group in each project and set the machine group ID in the following format: k8sgroup-{cluster-id}, in which {cluster-id} is the ID of the cluster. You can customize the machine group name. ii. Specify the project, Logstore, and the created machine group in the environment variables for each application.

```
######### Configure environment variables.###########
    - name: aliyun_logs_app1-stdout
      value: stdout
    - name: aliyun_logs_app1-stdout_project
      value: app1-project
    - name: aliyun_logs_app1-stdout_logstore
      value: app1-logstore
    - name: aliyun_logs_app1-stdout_machinegroup
      value: app1-machine-group
```

**View logs**

You can view the logs of containers in the SLS console.
1. Log on to the SLS console. For more information, see the Activate SLS section of this topic.
2. Click the project that is associated with the ACK cluster. By default, the project name is in the format of
k8s-log-{ACK cluster ID}.
3. In the Logstore list, find the Logstore that is specified when you configure log collection. Move the pointer
over the Logstore name and click the icon. Then, click **Search & Analysis**.
4. In this example, you can view the stdout of the application and text log files of containers. You can also
find that custom tags are appended to the collected log data. After SLS is enabled for the application, you can view the logs of containers in the ACK console. To do this, perform the following steps:
1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name. You can also click
**Details** in the **Actions** column to go to the cluster details page.
3. In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Operations > Log Center**.
4. On the **Log Center** page, click the **Application Logs** tab and select the required Logstore to view the
logs of containers.

#### 7.15.2 Configure Log4jAppender for Kubernetes and Log Service

**Log Service**

This topic describes how to configure a YAML file to export the log of a Container Service cluster to Log Service, without the need to modify the application. An application that can be managed by calling API operations is deployed in the cluster to generate the log for testing purposes.

**Prerequisites**

A Container Service cluster is created. For more information, see Create a Kubernetes cluster. An AccessKey pair is created or Resource Access Management (RAM) is activated. Make sure that the required permissions are granted. In this example, an AccessKey pair is created.

**Background information**

Log4j is an open source project of Apache. Log4j consists of three components: log level, log output destination, and log output format. You can configure Log4jAppender to export log data to the console, a log file, a GUI component, a socket server, an NT event viewer, or a UNIX syslog daemon.

**Procedure**

1. Configure Log4jAppender in Log Service.
i. Create a project in Log Service. In this example, a Log Service project named k8s-log4j is created in the same region as your cluster. For more information, see the **Manage projects** chapter of **Log Service User Guide**.

> **Note:** We recommend that you create a Log Service project in the same region as your cluster. When a Log Service project and a cluster are deployed in the same region, the log is transmitted over the internal network. This enables the real-time collection and quick retrieval of log data. This also avoids cross-region transmission, which requires additional bandwidth and time costs.

ii. Create a Logstore for the k8s-log4j project. In this example, a Logstore named k8s-logstore is created. For more information, see the **Manage**
**Logstores** chapter of **Log Service User Guide**.
iii. After the k8s-logstore Logstore is created, a message appears, which prompts you to use the Data Import wizard. Click **Data Import Wizard**. iv. At the top of the **Import Data** dialog box, click the **Custom Code** tab. Then, click Log4j and configure the data import parameters based on the instructions. In this example, Log4jAppender is configured with the default settings. You can also customize the settings to meet your business requirements.
2. Configure Log4jAppender for the cluster.
In this example, the demo-deployment and demo-Service files are used. i. Connect to your cluster. For more information, see Connect to an ACK cluster by using kubectl. ii. Obtain the demo-deployment.yaml file and configure the `JAVA_OPTS` environment variable. The following code is a sample template of the demo-deployment.yaml file:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata:
  name: log4j-appender-demo-spring-boot
  labels:
    app: log4j-appender
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log4j-appender
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log4j-appender
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: log4j-appender-demo-spring-boot
        image: registry.cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/jaegertracing/log4j-appender-demo-spring-
boot:0.0.2
        env:
          - name: JAVA_OPTS                ## Take note of this environment variable.
            value: "-Dproject={your_project} -Dlogstore={your_logstore} -Dendpoint={your_endpoint}
-Daccess_key_id={your_access_key_id} -Daccess_key={your_access_key_secret}"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
```

> **Note:** The following information is displayed:
> `-Dproject` : the name of your Log Service project. In this example, the name of the project is k8s-log4j.
> `-DlogStore` : the name of your Logstore. In this example, the name of the Logstore is k8s- logstore.
> `-Dendpoint` : the endpoint of Log Service. You must configure the endpoint based on the region of your Log Service project. In this example, the endpoint is cn- hangzhou.log.aliyuncs.com.
> `-Daccess_key_id` : your AccessKey ID.
> `-Daccess_key` : your AccessKey secret.

iii. Run the following command to create a Deployment:

```bash
kubectl create -f demo-deployment.yaml
```

iv. Obtain the demo-Service.yaml file and run the following command to create a Service: You do not need to modify the configurations in the demo-Service.yaml file.

```bash
kubectl create -f demo-service.yaml
```

3. Generate the log of the Kubernetes cluster log.
You can run the `kubectl get` command to view the deployment status of the related resource objects. After the Deployment and Service are deployed, run the `kubectl get svc` command to check the external IP address of the Service, which is the value of EXTERNAL-IP. Run the following command:

```bash
kubectl get svc
```

Output:

```
NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE log4j-appender-demo-spring-boot-svc LoadBalancer 172.21.XX.XX 120.55.XXX.XXX 8080:30398/TCP
```

`1h` In this example, you can run the `login` command to generate the log of the Kubernetes cluster log. Replace `K8S_SERVICE_IP` in the command with the value of `EXTERNAL-IP` .

> **Note:** For a complete list of API operations, see GitHub log4j-appender-demo.

```bash
curl http://${K8S_SERVICE_IP}:8080/login?name=bruce
```

4. View the log in Log Service
i. In the **Projects** list, click your Log Service project. ii. Click the icon to the right side of the k8s-logstore Logstore and select **Search & Analysis** to view the log of the Kubernetes cluster.

### 7.16 Monitoring management

#### 7.16.1 Enable Managed Service for Prometheus

After you enable Managed Service for Prometheus, you can view dashboards and performance metrics that are preset for Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK). This topic describes how to enable Managed Service for Prometheus for ACK clusters, how to configure alert rules in Managed Service for Prometheus, and how to customize monitoring metrics and use Grafana to display monitoring metrics.

**Background information**

Managed Service for Prometheus can be used to monitor a wide variety of components and provide various out-of-the-box dashboards. Managed Service for Prometheus is integrated with the open source Prometheus ecosystem. Managed Service for Prometheus is a comprehensive, ready-to-use monitoring service. You do not need to be concerned about managing the underlying services, such as data storage, data presentation, and system O&M.

**Enable Managed Service for Prometheus when you create a cluster**

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. On the Clusters page, click **Create**
**Kubernetes Cluster** in the upper-right corner.
2. On the **Create Kubernetes Cluster** page, select **Enable Prometheus Monitoring** to the right of the
**Monitoring Agents** parameter. For more information about other parameters, see Create an ACK cluster.
3. On the right side of the **Create Kubernetes Cluster** page, click **Create Cluster**.
4. In the **Confirm** dialog box, verify that all check items are passed, read and select the terms of service and
disclaimer, and then click **OK** to deploy the cluster. After the cluster is created, you can find the cluster on the **Clusters** page in the ACK console.

**Enable Managed Service for Prometheus for an existing cluster**

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name. Alternatively, click
**Details** in the **Actions** column.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Add-ons**.
4. On the **Add-ons** page, click the **Logs and Monitoring** tab, find the **ack-arms-prometheus** component
card, and then click **Install**. In the message that appears, click **OK**.

**View Grafana dashboards provided by Managed Service for Prometheus**

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name. You can also click
**Details** in the **Actions** column to go to the cluster details page.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Prometheus Monitoring**.
4. On the **Prometheus Monitoring** page, click the name of a Grafana dashboard to view the monitoring
data.

> **Important:** If this is the first time you log on to the Managed Service for Prometheus console, you must authorize the cluster to access Managed Service for Prometheus before you can view the monitoring data. If the authorization page does not appear after you log on to the Managed Service for Prometheus console, the cluster has been authorized to access Managed Service for Prometheus.

**Configure alert rules in Managed Service for Prometheus**

Managed Service for Prometheus allows you to create alert rules for monitoring jobs. When alert rules are met, you can receive alerts by using emails, text messages, and DingTalk notifications in real time. This helps you detect errors in a proactive manner. When an alert rule is met, notifications are sent to the contact group that you specified. Before you can create a contact group, you must create a contact. When you create a contact, you can specify the mobile phone number and email address of the contact to receive notifications. You can also provide a DingTalk chatbot webhook URL that is used to automatically send alert notifications.

**ACK dedicated clusters**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top navigation bar, choose **Products** >
**Middleware** > **Cloud-native Observability** > **Prometheus V2.0**.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Alerts > Notification Settings**.
3. On the **Contact** tab, click **New Contact** in the upper-right corner. In the dialog box that appears,
configure the parameters and click **OK**.
4. Configure alert rules.
i. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Alerts > Alert Rules**. ii. On the **Alert Rules** page, click **Create Alert Rule**. On the Create Alert Rule page, configure the parameters and click **Submit**.

**ACK edge clusters**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top navigation bar, choose **Products** >
**Middleware** > **Cloud-native Observability** > **Application Real-Time Monitoring Service**.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Alerts > Contact Management**.
3. On the **Contact** tab, click **New contact** in the upper-right corner. In the New contact dialog box,
configure the parameters and click **OK**.
4. Configure alert rules.
i. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Alerts > Alert Policies**. ii. On the **Alarm Policies** page, choose **Create Alarm** > **Application Monitoring Alarm**. In the Create Alarm dialog box, configure the parameters and click **Save**.

**Create custom metrics and use Grafana to display the metrics**

**Method 1: Use annotations to create custom metrics**

You can add annotations to pod configuration templates to define custom monitoring metrics. The application monitoring component of Application Real-Time Monitoring Service (ARMS) uses Managed Service for Prometheus to automatically obtain these custom monitoring metrics.
1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. On the **Clusters** page, find the
cluster that you want to manage and click its name.
2. Create an application.
i. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Workloads > Deployments**. On the Deployments page, click
**Create from Image**.
ii. In the **Basic Information** step, configure the parameters and click **Next**. iii. In the **Container** step, configure the parameters and click **Next**. In this example, a web application is created and exposed by using port 5000. The following table describes some of the application parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Image Name | The name of the image that you want to use. In this example, yejianhonghong/pindex is used. |
| Image Version | The version of the image. In this example, latest is used. |
| Port | The container port. Click Add, set the Name parameter to web and the Container Port parameter to 5000 , and then select the TCP protocol. |

iv. In the **Advanced** step, add pod annotations related to ARMS. a. In the **Labels,Annotations** section, click **Add** to the right of the **Pod Annotations** parameters and add the following annotations.

| Annotation | Value | Description |
|---|---|---|
| prometheus.io/scrape | true | Specifies whether to scrape the application. |
| prometheus.io/port | 5000 | The endpoint port that Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes. |
| prometheus.io/path | /access | The endpoint path that Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes. |

b. After the application configurations are complete, click **Create**.
3. Create a Service.
i. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Network > Services**. In the upper-right corner of the **Services** page, click **Create**. ii. In the **Create Service** dialog box, configure the parameters and click **Create**. The following table describes some of the parameters. For more information, see Create a Service.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Type | The Service type. In this example, Server Load Balancer and Public Access are selected. |
| Backend | The backend object that you want to associate with the Service. In this example the application that you created in Step 2 is used. |

4. Configure custom metrics.

**ACK dedicated clusters**

i. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Prometheus Monitoring**. You are redirected to the console of Managed Service for Prometheus. ii. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Integration Management**. iii. On the Integration Management page, find the environment that you want to manage and click **Metric**
**Scraping** in the **Actions** column.
iv. On the **Self-Monitoring** tab, view custom metrics in the Targets section.

**ACK edge clusters**

i. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Prometheus Monitoring**. On the page that appears, click **Settings** in the left-side navigation pane. ii. On the **Settings** page, click the **Targets (beta)** tab to view existing custom metrics. The custom metrics are configured.
5. Access the public IP address of the Service that you created in Step 3. This operation increases the value of
the following custom metric. For more information about metrics, see DATA MODEL.
6. Go to the Dashboards page of the ARMS console and click a dashboard to go to the Grafana page. Click
**Add panel** in the upper-right corner, select the **Graph** type, and then enter

```
current_person_counts for
```

**Metrics**.
Save the configurations to view the Grafana chart of the custom metric.

**Method 2: Use ServiceMonitors to create custom metrics**

To use ServiceMonitors to create custom metrics, you need to add labels to your Services. You do not need to add annotations.
1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to the cluster
details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Workloads > Deployments**.
3. Create an application.
i. On the Deployments page, click **Create from Image**. ii. In the **Basic Information** step, configure the parameters and click **Next**. iii. In the **Container** step, configure the parameters and click **Next**. In this example, a web application is created and exposed by using port 5000. The following table describes some of the application parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Image Name | The name of the image that you want to use. In this example, yejianhonghong/pindex is used. |
| Image Version | The version of the image. In this example, latest is used. |
| Port | The container port. Click Add, set the Name parameter to web and the Container Port parameter to 5000 , and then select the TCP protocol. |

iv. In the **Advanced** step, click **Create**.
4. Create a Service.
i. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Network > Services**. In the upper-right corner of the **Services** page, click **Create**. ii. In the **Create Service** dialog box, configure the parameters and click **Create**. The following table describes some of the parameters. For more information, see Create a Service.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Type | The Service type. In this example, Server Load Balancer and Public Access are selected. |
| Backend | The backend object that you want to associate with the Service. In this example the application that you created in Step 3 is used. |
| Labels | Click Add. Set the Name parameter to app and the Value parameter to custom-metrics-pindex . |

5. Specify the endpoint that Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes.

**ACK dedicated clusters**

i. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Prometheus Monitoring** ii. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Integration Management**. iii. On the Integration Management page, find the environment that you want to manage and click **Metric**
**Scraping** in the **Actions** column.
iv. On the Metric Scraping tab, click **Service Monitor** in the left-side pane, and then click **Create**. v. In the Add ServiceMonitor Configuration panel, click the **YAML** tab. On the YAML tab, enter the following YAML template in the editor and click **Create**:

```bash
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1 kind: ServiceMonitor metadata:
  # Enter a unique name.
  name: custom-metrics-pindex
  # Specify a namespace.
  namespace: default
spec:
  endpoints:
  - interval: 30s
    # Enter the name of the port that is opened for the Service that you created.
    port: web
    # Enter the path of the Service.
    path: /access
  namespaceSelector:
    any: true
    # The namespace of the NGINX demo application.
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      # Enter the label that you added to the Service.
      app: custom-metrics-pindex
```

**ACK edge clusters**

i. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Prometheus Monitoring**. On the page that appears, click **Settings** in the left-side navigation pane. ii. On the **Settings** page, click the **Service Discovery** tab. iii. On the right of the **ServiceMonitor** section, click **Add ServiceMonitor**. iv. In the **Add ServiceMonitor** dialog box, enter the following YAML template and click **OK**:

```bash
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1 kind: ServiceMonitor metadata:
  # Enter a unique name.
  name: custom-metrics-pindex
  # Specify a namespace.
  namespace: default
spec:
  endpoints:
  - interval: 30s
    # Enter the name of the port that is opened for the Service that you created.
    port: web
    # Enter the path of the Service.
    path: /access
  namespaceSelector:
    any: true
    # The namespace of the NGINX demo application.
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      # Enter the label that you added to the Service.
      app: custom-metrics-pindex
```

v. Click the **Targets (beta)** tab. Check the endpoints that Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes. You can find that the endpoints scraped by Managed Service for Prometheus are displayed.

> **Note:** The definition of a ServiceMonitor provides more information than an annotation, which includes the namespace and name of the Service.

the following custom metric. For more information about metrics, see DATA MODEL.

current_person_counts for

**FAQ**

**How do I check the version of the ack-arms-prometheus component?**

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to the cluster
details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Add-ons**.
3. On the **Add-ons** page, find **ack-arms-prometheus** and check the component version.
If the component is updatable, you can go to the Helm page, find the component, and then click **Update** in the **Actions** column to update the component.

> **Note:** You can update a component only if the component is not updated to the latest version.

**Why Managed Service for Prometheus cannot be used to monitor GPU-**

**accelerated nodes?**

Managed Service for Prometheus may not be able to monitor GPU-accelerated nodes that are configured with taints. You can perform the following steps to view the taints of a GPU-accelerated node.
1. Run the following command to view the taints of a GPU-accelerated node:
If you added custom taints to the GPU-accelerated node, you can view information about the custom taints. In this example, a taint whose `key` is set to `test-key` , `value` is set to `test-value` , and `effect` is set to `NoSchedule` is added to the node.

```bash
kubectl describe node cn-beijing.47.100.XXX.XXX
```

Expected output:

```
Taints:test-key=test-value:NoSchedule
```

2. Use one of the following methods to handle the taint:
Run the following command to remove the taint from the GPU-accelerated node:

```bash
kubectl taint node cn-beijing.47.100.XXX.XXX test-key=test-value:NoSchedule-
```

Add a toleration rule that allows pods to be scheduled to the GPU-accelerated node with the taint.

```bash
# 1 Run the following command to modify ack-prometheus-gpu-exporter:
kubectl edit daemonset -n arms-prom ack-prometheus-gpu-exporter
# 2. Add the following fields to the YAML file to tolerate the taint:
# Irrelevant fields are omitted.
# The tolerations field must be added above the containers field and both fields must be of the s
ame level. tolerations:
- key: "test-key"
  operator: "Equal"
  value: "test-value"
  effect: "NoSchedule"
containers:
 # Irrelevant fields are omitted.
```

**What do I do if I fail to enable Managed Service for Prometheus after I**

**delete the arms-prom namespace?**

If you delete only the arms-prom namespace, resource configurations may be retained. In this case, you may fail to enable Managed Service for Prometheus. You can perform the following operations to delete the residual resource configurations: Run the following commands to delete the related ClusterRoles:

```bash
kubectl delete ClusterRole arms-kube-state-metrics kubectl delete ClusterRole arms-node-exporter kubectl delete ClusterRole arms-prom-ack-arms-prometheus-role kubectl delete ClusterRole arms-prometheus-oper3 kubectl delete ClusterRole arms-prometheus-ack-arms-prometheus-role kubectl delete ClusterRole arms-pilot-prom-k8s
```

Run the following commands to delete the related ClusterRoleBindings:

```bash
kubectl delete ClusterRoleBinding arms-node-exporter kubectl delete ClusterRoleBinding arms-prom-ack-arms-prometheus-role-binding kubectl delete ClusterRoleBinding arms-prometheus-oper-bind2 kubectl delete ClusterRoleBinding kube-state-metrics kubectl delete ClusterRoleBinding arms-pilot-prom-k8s kubectl delete ClusterRoleBinding arms-prometheus-ack-arms-prometheus-role-binding
```

Run the following commands to delete the related Roles and RoleBindings:

```bash
kubectl delete Role arms-pilot-prom-spec-ns-k8s kubectl delete Role arms-pilot-prom-spec-ns-k8s -n kube-system kubectl delete RoleBinding arms-pilot-prom-spec-ns-k8s kubectl delete RoleBinding arms-pilot-prom-spec-ns-k8s -n kube-system
```

### 7.17 Alert configurations

The alert center provides alert notifications for anomalies and abnormal metrics in ACK clusters.

**Enable the alert management feature**

You can enable alert configurations for an existing or new cluster. After the alert management feature is enabled, you can set metric-based alerts for specific resources in the cluster to automatically receive alert notifications for any anomalies. This helps you efficiently manage and maintain your cluster and ensures service stability. For more information about resource alerts, see Default alert rule templates.

**Enable the feature for an existing cluster**

1. Log on to the ACK console, and in the navigation pane on the left, choose **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the target cluster. In the navigation pane on the left, choose
**Operations Management > Alert Configurations**.
3. On the **Alert Configurations** page, follow the on-screen instructions to install or upgrade the
components.
4. After the installation or upgrade is complete, go to the **Alert Configurations** page to configure alert
settings.

| Tab | Description |
|---|---|
| Alert Rule Management | Enabling Status: Turn on or off the target alert rule set. Important To ensure you receive cluster resource alerts, click Advanced Settings in the Alert Rule Management column to go to the Prometheus Monitoring console. Then, setN otification Rule information in the corresponding alert rule. |
| Alert History | You can view the 100 most recent history records sent within the last 24 hours. Click the link in the Alert Rule column to go to the corresponding monitoring system and view the detailed rule configuration. Click Troubleshoot to quickly locate the resource page where the anomaly occurred (resources with anomalous activities or abnormal metrics). |

**Enable the feature when creating a cluster**

On the cluster creation page, select **Use Default Alert Template To Configure Alerts** next to **Alert**
**Configurations**. For more information, see Create a Kubernetes cluster.
After you enable alert configurations during cluster creation, the system enables the default alert rules. To ensure that you receive alert notifications for cluster resources, click **Advanced Settings** in the **Alert Rule**
**Management** column to go to the Prometheus console. Then, configure the **Notification Rule** for the
corresponding alert rule.

**Configure alert rules**

After you enable the alert configuration feature, a CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) resource of the AckAlertRule type is created by default in the kube-system namespace. This resource includes the default alert rule template. You can modify this CRD resource to change the default alert rules and configure custom ACK alert rules.

**Console**

1. Log on to the ACK console, and in the navigation pane on the left, choose **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the target cluster. In the navigation pane on the left, choose
**Operations Management > Alert Configurations**.
3. On the **Alert Rule Management** tab, click **Edit Alert Configuration** in the upper-right corner. Then, in
the **Actions** column of the target rule, click **YAML** to view the configuration of the AckAlertRule resource.
4. Modify the content of the YAML file as needed. For more information, see Default alert rule templates.
The following is an example of a YAML file for an alert rule configuration:

**YAML file for an alert rule configuration**

```bash
apiVersion: alert.alibabacloud.com/v1beta1 kind: AckAlertRule metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  groups:
    # The following is a sample configuration for a cluster event alert rule.
    - name: pod-exceptions                             # The name of the alert rule group. This corre
sponds to the Group_Name field in the alert template.
      rules:
        - name: pod-oom                                # The name of the alert rule.
          type: event                                  # The type of the alert rule (Rule_Type). Enum
eration values: event (event type) and metric-cms (CloudMonitor metric type).
          expression: sls.app.ack.pod.oom              # The expression of the alert rule. If the ru
le type is event, the value of the expression is the Rule_Expression_Id value in the default alert rule template in this topic.
          enable: enable                               # The enabling status of the alert rule. Enume
ration values: enable and disable.
        - name: pod-failed
          type: event
          expression: sls.app.ack.pod.failed
          enable: enable
    # The following is a sample configuration for a basic cluster resource alert rule.
    - name: res-exceptions                              # The name of the alert rule group. This corr
esponds to the Group_Name field in the alert template.
      rules:
        - name: node_cpu_util_high                      # The name of the alert rule.
          type: metric-cms                              # The type of the alert rule (Rule_Type). Enu
meration values: event (event type), metric-cms (CloudMonitor metric), and metric-prometheus (Prometheus metric).
          expression: cms.host.cpu.utilization          # The expression of the alert rule. If the r
ule type is metric-cms, the value of the expression is the Rule_Expression_Id value in the default alert rule template in this topic.
          contactGroups:                                # The contact group configuration mapped to t
he alert rule. This is generated by the ACK console. Contacts are the same for the same account and can be reused across multiple clusters.
          enable: enable                                # The enabling status of the alert rule. Enum
eration values: enable and disable.
          thresholds:                                   # The alert rule threshold.
            - key: CMS_ESCALATIONS_CRITICAL_Threshold
              unit: percent
              value: '85'                                # The CPU utilization threshold. Default: 85
```

%.

```
            - key: CMS_ESCALATIONS_CRITICAL_Times
              value: '3'                                # An alert is triggered if the threshold is e
xceeded three consecutive times.
            - key: CMS_RULE_SILENCE_SEC                 # The cool-down period after the first alert
is reported.
              value: '900'
```

You can use `rules.thresholds` to customize alert thresholds. The parameters are described in the following table. For example, in the preceding configuration, an alert notification is triggered if the CPU utilization of a cluster node exceeds 85% three consecutive times and the cool-down period of 900 seconds has elapsed since the last alert.

| Parameter | Required | Description | Default value |
|---|---|---|---|

|---|---|---|---|---|

| CMS RULE SILENCE SEC _ _ _ |   | Optional | When CloudMonitor continuously sends exceptions that trigger the rule, this parameter specifies the cool-down period in seconds after the first alert is reported. This prevents overly frequent alerts. If this parameter is not configured, the default value is used. | 900 |

|---|---|---|

### 7.18 Resource profiling

#### 7.18.1 Enable resource profiling

The resource profiling feature intelligently analyzes the CPU and memory usage of workloads to provide precise resource configuration recommendations. It helps reduce cluster costs and improve efficiency while ensuring business stability. It can be flexibly enabled for all workloads or a custom-defined scope.
1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. In the left-side navigation pane, click
**Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the desired cluster. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster
details page, choose **Operations > Resource Profiling**.
3. On the **Resource Profiling** page, follow the on-screen instructions to install or update component.
i. **Install the component**: Click **Install**. ii. **Profiling Configuration**: You can select Default Configuration based on your business requirements. a. By default, resource profiling is enabled for all workloads except workloads in the arms-prom and kube-system namespaces. b. After resource profiling is enabled, you can click Profiling Configuration on the Resource Profiling page to modify the applicable scope of resource profiling. c. If your cluster has more than 1,000 nodes or you want to enable resource profiling only for specific workloads, you can clear the check box and customize the applicable scope of resource profiling on the Resource Profiling page. iii. **Enable Resource Profiling**.
4. On the **Resource Profiling** page, click **Profiling Configuration**, select a configuration method,
configure the following parameters, and then click **OK**.

**Global Configuration**

| Parameter | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Excluded Namespace | Select the namespaces to be excluded from enabling resource profiling. | None |
| Workload Type | Select a workload type | None |
| CPU Redundancy Rate | If the deviation between the recommended CPU specification and the original CPU request exceeds the specified redundancy rate, the system suggests a downgrade for the CPU configuration. Unit: %. | 30 |
| Memory Redundancy Rate | If the deviation between the recommended memory specification and the original memory request exceeds the specified redundancy rate, the system suggests a downgrade for the memory configuration. Unit: %. | 30 |

> **Note:** In global configuration mode, resource profiling is enabled for all workloads except workloads in the arms-prom and kube-system namespaces.
> If your cluster has more than 1,000 nodes or you want to enable resource profiling only for specific workloads, you can select the custom configuration mode to specify the applicable scope of resource profiling.

**Custom Configuration**

| Parameter | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Namespace | Select the namespaces for which you want to enable resource profiling. | None |
| Workload Type | Select the types of workloads for which you want to enable resource profiling. | None |
| CPU Redundancy Rate | If the deviation between the recommended CPU specification and the original CPU request exceeds the specified redundancy rate, the system suggests a downgrade for the CPU configuration. Unit: %. | 30 |
| Memory Redundancy Rate | If the deviation between the recommended memory specification and the original memory request exceeds the specified redundancy rate, the system suggests a downgrade for the memory configuration. Unit: %. | 30 |

#### 7.18.2 View resource profiles

The resource profile feature analyzes historical usage data to provide clear recommendations for scaling up, scaling down, or maintaining the CPU and memory configurations for your workloads. You can query, filter, and view detailed profiles and YAML information to fine-tune resource utilization.
1. Log on to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. In the left-side navigation pane, choose
**clusters**.
2. On the **clusters** page, click the name of your target cluster. Then, in the left-side navigation pane, choose
**O&M > resource profile**.
3. On the **resource profile** page, you can view the **Hotspot nodes**, **Resource profile data status**
**overview**, **CPU profile results**, and **Memory profile results** sections.
**Hotspot nodes**: Lists nodes where the CPU or memory load exceeds the configured threshold, helping
you identify resource bottlenecks. Click **Threshold Configuration** to set the **CPU Threshold** and **Memory Threshold**.

**Resource profile data status overview**

**Data Accumulating**: The resource profile component is collecting historical data to generate profile
results. Please check back later.
**Normal**: The resource profile results have been generated and are ready to use.
**Workload Deleted**: The corresponding workload has been deleted. The profile results will be
automatically removed after a retention period.

**CPU profile results**

**Scale-up recommended**: This workload should be scaled up.
**Scale-down recommended**: This workload should be scaled down.
**Maintain**: The current resource allocation for this workload should be maintained.

**Memory profile results**

**Scale-up recommended**: This workload should be scaled up.
**Scale-down recommended**: This workload should be scaled down.
**Maintain**: The current resource allocation for this workload should be maintained.
4. On the **resource profile** page, search for workloads by **workload name**.
In the resource profile list, you can view information such as **workload name**, **namespace**, **Workload**
**type**, **CPU requests**, **memory requests**, **Profile data status**, **Recommended CPU change**,
**Recommended memory change**, and **Creation time**.
In the resource profile list, click the icon to the right of **namespace**, **Workload type**, **Recommended**
**CPU change**, and **Recommended memory change** to filter the results.
5. In the resource profile list, click the target **workload name** or **Resource Modification** in the Actions
column. On the resource profile details page, you can view information such as **Basic Workload**
**Information**, **Profile Details**, and P**od total resources**.
In the **Basic workload information** section, you can view details such as **workload name**, **Profile data**
**status**, **Workload type**, **resizing suggestion**, **Current requests**, and **Profile creation time**.
In the Profile details section, you can view information such as **Resource curves** and **resource**
**modification**.
On the resource profile details page, click **YAML** in the upper-right corner to view the YAML file.

#### 7.18.3 Change resource configurations

Based on intelligent recommendations from resource profiling, the resource configuration change feature enables one-click autofill or manual adjustment of CPU and memory requests and limits for workloads, achieving precise and efficient resource optimization while ensuring business stability.

**Modify resource quotas**

1. Log in to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. In the left-side navigation pane, click
**Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the desired cluster. In the left-side navigation pane of the cluster
details page, choose **Operations > Resource Profiling**.
3. In the resource profiling list, click a workload name or **Change Resource Configuration** in the Actions
column. In the **Change Resource Configuration** section of the resource details page, change the resource configuration. Autofill Click **Auto Fill**.

> **Note:** The system automatically sets Target Required Resources and Target Limit Resources. The ratio of Target Required Resources to Target Limit Resources is fixed. Target Required Resources = Portrait Value + Portrait Value × Safety Margin. Target Limit Resources = Target Required Resources × (Current Limit Resources/Current Required Resources). If Current Required Resources is left empty, the value of Target Required Resources is the same as the value of Current Limit Resources.

Manual adjustment Set **Target Required Resources** and **Target Limit Resources** and click **Apply**.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Current Required Resources | The resources currently requested by the workload. |
| Current Limit Resources | The maximum number of resources that are currently available for the workload. |

| Portrait Value | The profile value provided by the system based on historical resource usage. You can specify Target Required Resources based on the profile value. |
|---|---|
| Safety Margin | The redundancy rate that is specified in the resource profiling policy. If the difference between the profile value and the original resource request exceeds the specified redundancy rate, the system recommends that you downgrade the resource configuration. You can specify Target Required Resources based on the following formula: Target Required Resources = Portrait Value + Portrait Value × Safety Margin. |
| Target Required Resources | You can change the CPU request and memory request based on the recommendations provided by ACK. |
| Target Limit Resources | You can change the CPU limit and memory limit based on the recommendations provided by ACK. |

### 7.19 GPU

#### 7.19.1 Create an ACK dedicated cluster with GPU-accelerated nodes

**accelerated nodes**

This topic describes how to create a dedicated GPU cluster.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Clusters**. On the Clusters page, click **Create Kubernetes**
**Cluster** in the upper-right corner.
3. On the **ACK Dedicated** tab of the **Create Kubernetes Cluster** page, configure the parameters that are
described in the following table.

| Configuration | Description |
|---|---|

| Cluster Name | Enter a name for the cluster. The name must be 1 to 63 characters in length, and can contain digits, letters, and hyphens (-). Note The cluster name must be unique among clusters that belong to the same Apsara Stack tenant account. |
|---|---|
| Resource Set | Select a resource set. A resource set is a container used to store resources. Each resource must belong to a resource set. After you select a resource set, virtual private clouds (VPCs) and vSwitches are filtered based on the selected resource set. |
| Region | Select the region where you want to deploy the cluster. |
| IPv4/IPv6 Dual- stack | Specifies whether to enable IPv4/IPv6 dual stack. Note You can enable IPv4/IPv6 dual stack only for clusters that run Kubernetes 1.20 or later. Master nodes and worker nodes still use IPv4 addresses to communicate with each other in a cluster. You must select Terway as the network plug-in. You must use a VPC and Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instances that support IPv4/IPv6 dual stack. |
| VPC | Select the VPC in which you want to deploy the cluster from the drop-down list. |
| vSwitch | You can configure the virtual switch. You can select up to three vSwitches that are deployed in differentz ones. |
| Kubernetes Version | Select a Kubernetes version. |
| Container Runtime | Only containerd is supported. You must deploy ECS bare metal instances. We recommend that you select the latest version available in the ACK console. |
| Master Node Quantity | The number of master nodes that you want to use. You can create three or five master nodes. Note You can create a single master node. By default, this feature is unavailable. To use this feature, contact the technical support of Apsara Stack. |
| Instance Type | The instance type of master nodes. You can select multiple instance types. You can also select a dedicated host group for the master nodes. For more information, see Instance types in the ECS documentation. |

| System Disk | The system disk category. Valid values: Ultra Disk, Premium Performance Disk, SSD Disk, and Standard Performance Disk. Note You can select Encrypt Disk to encrypt disks. To encrypt disks, you need to configure the following parameters: Encryption method: You can select AES256 or SM4. Encryption key: You can select a key that is created in Key Management Service (KMS). Encryption is supported only when you select Premium Performance Disk or Standard Performance Disk as the system disk category. |
|---|---|
| Attach Data Disk | The data disk category. Valid values: Ultra Disk, Premium Performance Disk, SSD Disk, and Standard Performance Disk. Note You can select Encrypt Disk to encrypt data disks. To encrypt data disks, you need to configure the following parameters: Encryption method: You can select AES256 or SM4. Encryption key: You can select a key that is created in Key Management Service (KMS). For ACK clusters that run Kubernetes of a version earlier than 1.32, ACK automatically formats the last data disk if you add two or more data disks, mounts the data disk to /var/lib/container , and mounts /var/lib/kubelet and /var/lib/containerd to /var/lib/container . For ACK clusters that run Kubernetes 1.32 or later, you can customize the data disk formatting setting. You can choose one of the following data disk formatting options: Not Formatted: does not format the data disk and retains the original data in the disk. Format and use as container runtime directory: formats the data disk and uses it as the container runtime directory. Format and configure custom mount directory: formats the data disk and mounts it to the user-defined path. For more information, see the How do I specify a mount directory for data disks in a node pool? section of this topic. Important If two or more disks are formatted, you must specify only one disk as the container runtime directory. Each node must have a disk used as the container runtime directory. If no disk is specified, ACK automatically uses the last data disk. In this case, ACK will automatically format the disk, mount the disk to /var/lib/container , and mount /var/lib/kubelet and /var/lib/containerd to /var/lib/container . |

#### 7.19.2 Upgrade the NVIDIA driver on a GPU node

This topic describes how to upgrade the NVIDIA driver on a GPU node when workloads are deployed on the node and when no workload is deployed on the node.

**Upgrade the NVIDIA driver on a GPU node where workloads are deployed**

1. Connect to an ACK cluster by using kubectl.
2. Run the following command to set the target node to unschedulable.

```bash
kubectl cordon node-name
```

> **Note:** Currently, you can only upgrade the NVIDIA driver on worker nodes.
> node-name must be in the format of your-region-name.node-id.
> your-region-name represents the region where your cluster is deployed.
> node-id represents the ID of the ECS instance where the target node is deployed.
> You can run the following command to query node-name.

```bash
kubectl get node
```

3. Run the following command to migrate pods from the target node to other nodes:

```bash
kubectl drain node-name --grace-period=120 --ignore-daemonsets=true
```

4. Run the following command to log on to the target node:

```
ssh root@xxx.xxx.x.xx
```

5. Run the following command to check the current NVIDIA driver version:

```
nvidia-smi
```

6. Run the following commands to uninstall the existing driver:

> **Note:** If your driver version is 384.111, perform the following steps.
> If your driver version is not 384.111, download the corresponding driver from the official NVIDIA website first.

```bash
cd /tmp curl -O https://cn.download.nvidia.cn/tesla/384.111/NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-384.111.run chmod u+x NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-384.111.run . /NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-384.111.run --uninstall -a -s -q
```

7. Run the following command to restart the target node:

```
reboot
```

8. Download the driver that you want to use from the official NVIDIA website. In this example, version 410.79
is used.
9. Run the following command to install the downloaded driver under the directory where it was saved:

```
sh . /NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-410.79.run -a -s -q
```

0. Run the following commands to configure the driver:

```
nvidia-smi -pm 1 || true nvidia-smi -acp 0 || true
```

1. Run the following commands to update device-plugin:

```
mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/nvidia-device-plugin.yml / mv /nvidia-device-plugin.yml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
```

2. Log on to a master node and run the following command to set the target node to schedulable:

```bash
kubectl uncordon node-name
```

Result Run the following command on a master node to check the NVIDIA driver version on the target node. The driver version is now 410.79.

> **Note:** Replace node-name with the target node name.

```bash
kubectl exec -n kube-system -t nvidia-device-plugin-node-name nvidia-smi
```

**Upgrade the NVIDIA driver on a GPU node where no workload is deployed**

1. Run the following command to log on to the target node:

```
ssh root@xxx.xxx.x.xx
```

2. Run the following command to check the current NVIDIA driver version:

```
nvidia-smi
```

3. Run the following commands to uninstall the existing driver:

> **Note:** If your driver version is 384.111, perform the following steps.
> If your driver version is not 384.111, download the corresponding driver from the official NVIDIA website first.

```bash
cd /tmp curl -O https://cn.download.nvidia.cn/tesla/384.111/NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-384.111.run chmod u+x NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-384.111.run
```

```
. /NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-384.111.run --uninstall -a -s -q
```

4. Run the following command to restart the target node.

```
reboot
```

5. Download the driver that you want to use from the official NVIDIA website. In this example, version 410.79
is used.
6. Run the following command to install the downloaded driver under the directory where it was saved:

```
sh . /NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-410.79.run -a -s -q
```

7. Run the following commands to configure the driver:

```
nvidia-smi -pm 1 || true nvidia-smi -acp 0 || true
```

Result Run the following command on a master node to check the NVIDIA driver version on the target node. The driver version is now 410.79.

> **Note:** Replace node-name with the target node name.

```bash
kubectl exec -n kube-system -t nvidia-device-plugin-node-name nvidia-smi
```

#### 7.19.3 Enable GPU sharing

This topic describes how to enable GPU sharing.

**Prerequisites**

A Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) dedicated cluster that runs Kubernetes 1.18 or later is created. For more information, see Create an ACK cluster.

> **Note:** If your cluster runs Kubernetes 1.28.3 or earlier, you need to configure the scheduler. If your cluster runs Kubernetes 1.28.9 or later, you do not need to configure the scheduler.

An ACK dedicated cluster that contains GPU-accelerated nodes is created. For more information, see Create an ACK dedicated cluster with GPU-accelerated nodes. A kubectl client is connected to the ACK cluster. For more information, see Connect to an ACK cluster by using kubectl.

**Step 1: Configure a RAM role**

For more information, see Configure RAM role authorization for ack-ai-installer.

**Step 2: (Optional) Configure the scheduler**

> **Note:** If your cluster runs Kubernetes 1.28.3 or earlier, you need to configure the scheduler. If your cluster runs Kubernetes 1.28.9 or later, you do not need to configure the scheduler.

1. Run the following command to query the number of master nodes:

```bash
kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/master
```

> **Note:** Perform the preceding operation to confirm the number of master nodes to be modified. If the cluster has five master nodes, you need to modify the scheduler configurations on the five master nodes.

Add scheduler configurations on each master node.

> **Important:** Add scheduler configurations on each master node.

1. Create a file named scheduler-framework-config.yaml in the /etc/kubernetes/ directory and copy the
following content to the file: In this example, the cluster runs Kubernetes 1.24.

```
apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1beta2 kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration clientConnection:
  kubeconfig: /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf
leaderElection:
  leaderElect: true
profiles:
- schedulerName: default-scheduler
  plugins:
    preFilter:
      enabled:
      - name: gpushare
    filter:
      enabled:
      - name: gpushare
    score:
      enabled:
      - name: gpushare
        weight: 20000
    reserve:
      enabled:
      - name: gpushare
  pluginConfig:
  - name: gpushare
    args:
      policy:
       - algorithm: binpack
       - algorithm: spread
         nodeSelectors:
           ack.node.gpu.placement: "spread"
```

2. Enable GPU sharing for the scheduler. For more information, see Configure the ACK scheduler.

**Step 3: Install ack-ai-installer**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Applications > Helm**.

```
ack-ai-installer.
```

4. On the **Helm** page, click **Deploy**. In the Deploy panel, search for
5. Click the ack-ai-installer component to go to the component details page.
6. On the Deploy page, click **Next** to view the configuration details. Click **OK** to complete the installation.

> **Important:** You can install ack-ai-installer only in ACK clusters that run Kubernetes version 1.18 and later. If the Kubernetes version of your cluster is earlier than 1.18, you can click **Upgrade Cluster** on the Clusters page to update the cluster.

**Step 4: Create a node pool**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click Clusters.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster in which the ack-ai-installer component is installed and click **Node**
**Pools** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the upper-right corner of the **Node Pools** page, click **Create Node Pool**.
5. In the **Create Node Pool** dialog box, configure the parameters and click **Confirm**.
For more information about the parameters, see Create a node pool.

**Step 5: Add GPU-accelerated nodes**

After the node pool is created, you can add GPU-accelerated nodes to the node pool. When you add GPUaccelerated nodes, you must select instances that belong to the **heterogeneous computing** instance family, such as GPU-accelerated, FPGA-accelerated, and NPU-accelerated instances. For more information, see Add an existing node or Scale out a node pool.

**Step 6: Label the GPU-accelerated nodes**

Run the following command to label a GPU-accelerated nodes:

```bash
kubectl label node <GPU-accelerated node name> ack.node.gpu.schedule=cgpu
```

After you label the GPU-accelerated node, gpu-device-plugin on the node automatically restarts.

**Step 7: Query GPU resources**

1. Log on to a master node.
2. Run the following command to find the image address that you want to use:
Run the following command to query the `image prefix` :

```bash
kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy-worker -o yaml | grep image:
```

The field before the `/acs/` keyword specifies the image prefix. Replace `<IMAGE_PREFIX>` with the image prefix that you obtained.

```
cat > /tmp/kubectl-inspect-gpushare.yaml <<-EOF apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata:
 name: kubectl-inspect-gpushare
spec:
 containers:
 - name: gpushare
 image: <IMAGE_PREFIX>/acs/kubectl-inspect-gpushare:v1.0
 command:
 - sleep
 - '5000'
EOF
```

3. Run the following command to create a pod:

```bash
 kubectl apply -f /tmp/kubectl-inspect-gpushare.yaml
```

4. Run the following command to copy kubectl-inspect-gpushare to the `/usr/local/bin` directory of the
master node.

```bash
# Perform the copy operation.
kubectl cp kubectl-inspect-gpushare:/usr/local/bin/kubectl-inspect-gpushare /usr/local/bin/kubectlinspect-gpushare
# Add execute permissions.
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/kubectl-inspect-gpushare
```

5. Run the following command on the master node to query the GPU usage of the cluster:

```bash
kubectl inspect gpushare
```

Expected output:

```
NAME IPADDRESS GPU0(Allocated/Total) GPU Memory(GiB) cn-wulan-env230-d01.192.168.3.XXXX 192.168.3.XXXX 0/8 0/8 ---------------------------------------------------------------------- Allocated/Total GPU Memory In Cluster: 0/8 (0%)
```

#### 7.19.4 Work with GPU sharing

This topic describes how to use the GPU sharing feature to request GPU memory for an application.

**Prerequisites**

The GPU sharing component is installed. For more information, see Enable GPU sharing.

**Procedure**

In this topic, a TensorFlow job is used as an example.
1. Run the following command to log on to a master node:

```bash
kubectl get nodes
```

2. Run the following command to query the GPU resource usage of the cluster:

```bash
kubectl inspect gpushare
```

Expected output:

```
NAME IPADDRESS GPU0(Allocated/Total) GPU Memory(GiB) cn-wulan-env230-d01.192.168.3.XXX 192.168.3.XXX 0/7 0/7 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Allocated/Total GPU Memory In Cluster: 0/7 (0%)
```

The output indicates that the cluster contains one GPU-accelerated node. The node can provide 7 GiB of GPU memory.
3. Deploy a job.
i. Run the following command to search for the prefix of the image used in this example:

```bash
kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy-worker -o yaml | grep image:
```

The content before /acs/ is the prefix of the image. Replace <IMAGE_PREFIX> with the prefix that you obtained. ii. Run the following command to create a job:

```
cat > /tmp/gpushare-test.yaml <<-EOF apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: Job metadata:
  name: tensorflow-mnist
spec:
  parallelism: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: tensorflow-mnist
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: tensorflow-mnist
        image: $IMAGE_PREFIX/acs/gpushare-sample:tensorflow-1.5
        command:
        - python
        - tensorflow-sample-code/tfjob/docker/mnist/main.py
        - --max_steps=100000
        - --data_dir=tensorflow-sample-code/data
        resources:
          limits:
            aliyun.com/gpu-mem: 3  # Request 3 GiB of GPU memory.
        workingDir: /root
      restartPolicy: Never
EOF
```

iii. Run the following command to submit the job:

```bash
kubectl apply -f /tmp/gpushare-test.yaml
```

4. Run the following command to query the status of the job:

```bash
kubectl get po
```

The following result is returned:

```
NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE tensorflow-mnist-l5k9v 1/1 Running 0 2s
```

The output indicates that the job is in the Running state.
5. Run the following command to query the GPU resource usage of the cluster:

```bash
kubectl inspect gpushare
```

The following result is returned:

```
NAME IPADDRESS GPU0(Allocated/Total) GPU Memory(GiB) cn-wulan-env230-d01.192.168.3.XXX 192.168.3.XXX 3/7 3/7 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Allocated/Total GPU Memory In Cluster: 3/7 (42%)
```

cn-wulan-env230-d01.192.168.3.XXX is allocated 3 GiB of GPU memory.
6. Run the following command to query the maximum amount of GPU memory available for the pod of the
job:

```bash
kubectl exec -ti tensorflow-mnist-l5k9v -- nvidia-smi
```

The following result is returned. The output indicates that the pod can use at most 3,261 MiB (about 3 GiB) of GPU memory.
7. Run the following command to request 4 GiB of GPU memory for the job:

```bash
kubectl exec -ti tensorflow-mnist-l5k9v -- cuda_malloc -size=4096
```

The output in Step 5 indicates that node cn-wulan-env230-d01.192.168.3.XXX is equipped with a GPU. The GPU can provide 7 GiB of memory. Only 3 GiB of memory is allocated to the job. The following result is returned. The output indicates that the application fails because the requested amount of memory exceeds the amount of memory allocated to the pod, which is 3 GiB.

#### 7.19.5 GPU scheduling for Kubernetes clusters with GPU-accelerated nodes

**GPU-accelerated nodes**

This topic describes how to enable GPU scheduling for Kubernetes clusters that contain GPU-accelerated nodes.

**Prerequisites**

Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) and Resource Orchestration Service (ROS) are activated.

> **Note:** ACK clusters use ROS to deploy applications. Before you create an ACK cluster, you must activate ROS.

**Background Information**

Starting from V1.8, Kubernetes adds support for the following hardware acceleration devices using device plug-ins: NVIDIA GPUs, InfiniBand devices, and field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). GPU solutions provided by the Kubernetes community will be deprecated in V1.10 and removed from the master code in V1.11. ACK lets you deploy GPU-accelerated nodes in Kubernetes clusters to run compute-intensive tasks such as machine learning tasks and image processing tasks. You can deploy applications and enable auto scaling for applications without the need to install NVIDIA drivers or Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA). When ACK creates a cluster, ACK performs the following operations: Creates Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instances, configures a public key to enable SSH logon from master nodes to other nodes, and configures the cluster using CloudInit. Creates a security group to allow access to the virtual private cloud (VPC) where the cluster resides over Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP). If you do not specify an existing VPC for the cluster, ACK creates a VPC and a vSwitch for the cluster and creates SNAT entries for the vSwitch. Adds route entries to the route table of the VPC. Creates a NAT gateway and an elastic IP address (EIP). Creates an internal-facing Server Load Balancer (SLB) instance and opens port 6443. Creates an Internet-facing SLB instance and opens ports 6443, 8443, and 22. If you enable SSH logon over the Internet, ACK opens port 22. If you do not enable SSH logon over the Internet, ACK does not open port 22. ACK clusters support only VPCs. By default, each Alibaba Cloud account has specific quotas on cloud resources that can be created. You cannot create clusters if the quota is reached. Check the quota of your account before you create a cluster. If you want to increase the quota, contact the ACK technical support team. By default, you can create at most five clusters across all regions with each account. Each cluster can contain at most 40 nodes. If you want to create more clusters or nodes, contact the ACK technical support team.

> **Note:** By default, you can add at most 48 route entries to the VPC where an ACK cluster is deployed. This means that you can create at most 48 nodes in an ACK cluster deployed in a VPC. If you want to create more nodes in a cluster, contact the VPC technical support team to increase the maximum number of route entries supported by the VPC where the cluster resides. After the quota of route entries is increased, contact the ACK technical support team to increase the node quota of the cluster.

By default, you can create at most 100 security groups with each account. By default, you can create at most 60 pay-as-you-go SLB instances with each account. By default, you can create at most 20 EIPs with each account. Limits on ECS instances: You can select operating systems such as Alibaba Cloud Linux 3, Anolis OS, UOS, Kylin V10, Alibaba Cloud Linux 3 64-bit (MLPS 2.0 Level 3), and Alibaba Cloud Linux 4.

**Create a GN5 Kubernetes cluster**

> **Note:** GN5 Kubernetes clusters are built on GPU-accelerated ECS instances from instance families that start with `ecs.gn5`. For more information, see **Instance Family & Instance Types > Intel Instance** **Families > Heterogeneous Computing & Bare Metal** in the Elastic Computing Service documentation.

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the navigation pane on the left, click Clusters.
2. In the upper-right corner of the **Clusters** page, click **Create Kubernetes Cluster**.
The Dedicated Kubernetes tab appears. Select GPU-accelerated ECS instance types for worker nodes. For more information about the parameters, see Create an ACK cluster.
3. Configure worker nodes. In this example, worker nodes are used to run GPU computing tasks and the gn5i-
c4gi1 instance type is selected. i. If you choose to create worker nodes, you must set Instance Type and Quantity. In this example, three GPU-accelerated worker nodes are created.

> **Note:** We recommend that you select standard SSDs for the **System Disk** and **Mount Data Disk** parameters.

ii. To add existing instances, you must first create GPU-accelerated instances in the region where you want to create the cluster.
4. Specify other parameters and click **Create Cluster** to start the deployment.
5. Check the GPUs that are provided by the nodes.
i. On the **Cluster** page, find the cluster whose details you want to view and click the name of the cluster. ii. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Nodes > Nodes**. iii. On the **Nodes** page, select a worker node and choose **More > Details** in the **Actions** column. On the node details page, you can view the GPUs provided by the node.

**Create a GPU experimental environment to run TensorFlow**

In most cases, data scientists use Jupyter to set up an environment for TensorFlow. The following example shows how to deploy a Jupyter application.
1. Log on to the ACK console. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of a cluster that you want to manage. In the navigation pane on the
left, choose **Workloads > Deployments**.
3. In the upper-right corner of the **Stateless** page, click **Create From Template**.
4. On the **Create** page, set the **Namespace** and **Sample Template** parameters, modify the YAML content
in the **Template** section as needed, and then click **Create**. The following YAML template creates a Jupyter application. The template specifies the configurations of a Deployment and a Service.

```bash
---
# Define the tensorflow deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata:
  name: tf-notebook
  labels:
    app: tf-notebook
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: # define how the deployment finds the pods it manages
    matchLabels:
      app: tf-notebook
  template: # define the pods specifications
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: tf-notebook
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: tf-notebook
        image: tensorflow/tensorflow:1.4.1-gpu-py3
        resources:
          limits:
            nvidia.com/gpu: 1                      # The number of NVIDIA GPUs that are requested by
the application.
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8888
          hostPort: 8888
        env:
          - name: PASSWORD                         # The password that is used to access the Jupyter
service. You can change the password as needed.
            value: mypassw0rd
# Define the tensorflow service
--apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata:
  name: tf-notebook
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8888
    name: jupyter
  selector:
    app: tf-notebook
  type: LoadBalancer                           #Creates an SLB service to ensure that the Jupyter
instance is accessible over the Internet.
```

5. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Network > Services**. Select the **namespace** where the **tf-**
**notebook** Service is created. In the **External Endpoint** column, view the external endpoint of the
Service.
6. Enter
`http://EXTERNAL-IP` into the address bar of your browser to access the Jupyter instance. Use the password that is specified in Step 4 to access the Jupyter instance.
7. Check whether the Jupyter instance can use GPUs.
Run the following command to query the GPUs that can be used by TensorFlow:

```python
from tensorflow.python.client import device_lib def get_available_devices():
    local_device_protos = device_lib.list_local_devices()
    return [x.name for x in local_device_protos]
print(get_available_devices())
```

#### 7.19.6 Enable Auto Scaling based on GPU metrics

Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) provides the Auto Scaling feature based on custom metrics. ACK can work with Managed Service for Prometheus to implement Auto Scaling based on GPU metrics. This topic describes how to deploy Managed Service for Prometheus to monitor applications. This topic also provides examples on how to view GPU metrics that are collected by Managed Service for Prometheus and enable Auto Scaling of pods based on GPU metrics.

**Prerequisites**

An ACK dedicated cluster that contains GPU-accelerated nodes is created.

**Feature overview**

GPU-accelerated computing is widely used in high-performance computing scenarios, such as the training of deep learning models and inference. To reduce resource costs, you can enable Auto Scaling for your cluster based on GPU metrics, such as GPU utilization and GPU memory usage. By default, a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) implements Auto Scaling based on CPU and memory metrics. If you have higher requirements in complex scenarios, you can use the Prometheus adapter to support the GPU metrics that are collected by Managed Service for Prometheus and use the custom metrics API to define custom metrics. This way, Auto Scaling is implemented by using the HPA based on GPU utilization and GPU memory usage. The following figure shows how Auto Scaling based on GPU metrics works.

| custom/metrics.k8s.io HPA Custom Metrics API Deployment Prometheus Adaptor ReplicaSet /metrics Pod Pod Pod Prometheus /metrics /metrics | HPA | custom/metrics.k8s.i |   |   | o Custom Metrics API |   |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|   |   |   | custom/metrics.k8s | .i | o |   |
|   |   |   |   |   | Prometheus Adaptor |   |
| Pod |   |   |   |   | Prometheus |   |

**Step 1: Deploy Managed Service for Prometheus and ack-alibaba-cloud-**

**metrics-adapter**

1. Enable Managed Service for Prometheus.
2. Install and configure ack-alibaba-cloud-metrics-adapter.
1. . Obtain the HTTP API endpoint**
i. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top navigation bar, choose **Products** > Middleware > **Cloud-native Observability** > **Prometheus V2.0**. ii. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Prometheus Instances > Instances**. iii. On the page that appears, find the instance that you want to manage and click its name to go to the instance details page. In the **HTTP API Endpoint** section, copy the internal endpoint.
2. . Configure the Prometheus URL**
i. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. ii. On the **Clusters** page, find the ACK dedicated cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to the cluster details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Operations > Add-ons**. iii. On the **Add-ons** page, find the **ack-alibaba-cloud-metrics-adapter** component card and click **Install**. In the dialog box that appears, set the `url` parameter to the HTTP API endpoint that you obtained and click OK.

**Step 2: Configure rules for ack-alibaba-cloud-metrics-adapter**

1. Collect GPU metrics.
2. Configure rules for ack-alibaba-cloud-metrics-adapter.
i. On the **Clusters** page, find the ACK dedicated cluster that you want to manage and click its name to go to the cluster details page. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Applications > Helm**. ii. On the Helm page, find ack-alibaba-cloud-metrics-adapter and click **Update** in the **Actions** column. In the Update Release panel, add the following `rules` to the `custom` field:

```
- metricsQuery: avg(<<.Series>>{<<.LabelMatchers>>}) by (<<.GroupBy>>)
  resources:
    overrides:
      NodeName:
        resource: node
  seriesQuery: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL{} # This metric indicates the GPU utilization.
- metricsQuery: avg(<<.Series>>{<<.LabelMatchers>>}) by (<<.GroupBy>>)
  resources:
    overrides:
      NamespaceName:
        resource: namespace
      NodeName:
        resource: node
      PodName:
        resource: pod
  seriesQuery: DCGM_CUSTOM_PROCESS_SM_UTIL{} # This metric indicates the GPU utilization of pods.
- metricsQuery: sum(<<.Series>>{<<.LabelMatchers>>}) by (<<.GroupBy>>)
  resources:
    overrides:
      NodeName:
        resource: node
  seriesQuery: DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED{} # This metric indicates the amount of GPU memory that is use
```

`d.`

```
- metricsQuery: sum(<<.Series>>{<<.LabelMatchers>>}) by (<<.GroupBy>>)
  resources:
    overrides:
      NamespaceName:
        resource: namespace
      NodeName:
        resource: node
      PodName:
        resource: pod
  seriesQuery: DCGM_CUSTOM_PROCESS_MEM_USED{} # This metric indicates the GPU memory usage of pod
```

`s.`

```
- metricsQuery: sum(<<.Series>>{<<.LabelMatchers>>}) by (<<.GroupBy>>) /
sum(DCGM_CUSTOM_CONTAINER_MEM_ALLOCATED{}) by (<<.GroupBy>>)

        resource: pod

indicates the GPU memory utilization.
```
