**Step 3: Enable Auto Scaling based on GPU metrics**

The following example shows how to deploy a model inference service on a GPU-accelerated node and perform stress tests on the node to check whether Auto Scaling can be performed based on GPU metrics.
1. . Deploy an inference service.**
1. Run the following command to deploy the inference service:

```
cat <<EOF | kubectl create -f apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata:
  name: bert-intent-detection
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: bert-intent-detection
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: bert-intent-detection
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: bert-container
        image: registry.cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/ai-samples/bert-intent-detection:1.0.1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        resources:
          limits:
            nvidia.com/gpu: 1
--apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata:
  name: bert-intent-detection-svc
  labels:
    app: bert-intent-detection
spec:
  selector:
    app: bert-intent-detection
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 80
  type: LoadBalancer
EOF
```

2. Query the status of the pod and Service.
Run the following command to query the status of the pod:

```bash
kubectl get pods -o wide
```

Expected output:

```
NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE IP NODE NOMINATED NODE READINESS GATES bert-intent-detection-7b486f6bf-f**** 1/1 Running 0 3m24s 10.15.1.17 cn-beiji ng.192.168.94.107 <none> <none>
```

The output indicates that only one pod is deployed on the GPU-accelerated node 192.168.94.107. Run the following command to query the status of the Service:

```bash
kubectl get svc bert-intent-detection-svc
```

Expected output:

```
NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE bert-intent-detection-svc LoadBalancer 172.16.186.159 47.95.XX.XX 80:30118/TCP 5m1s
```

If the output displays the name of the Service, the Service is deployed.
3. Log on to the node 192.168.94.107 by using SSH and run the following command to query GPU utilization:

```
nvidia-smi
```

Expected output:

```
Wed Feb 16 11:48:07 2022 +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| NVIDIA-SMI 450.102.04   Driver Version: 450.102.04   CUDA Version: 11.0     |
|-------------------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| GPU  Name        Persistence-M| Bus-Id        Disp.A | Volatile Uncorr. ECC |
| Fan  Temp  Perf  Pwr:Usage/Cap|         Memory-Usage | GPU-Util  Compute M. |
|                               |                      |               MIG M. |
|===============================+======================+======================|
|   0  Tesla V100-SXM2...  On   | 00000000:00:07.0 Off |                    0 |
| N/A   32C    P0    55W / 300W |  15345MiB / 16160MiB |      0%      Default |
|                               |                      |                  N/A |
+-------------------------------+----------------------+----------------------+ +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Processes:                                                                  |
|  GPU   GI   CI        PID   Type   Process name                  GPU Memory |
|        ID   ID                                                   Usage      |
|=============================================================================|
|    0   N/A  N/A   2305118      C   python                          15343MiB |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The output indicates that the inference service is running on the GPU-accelerated node. The GPU utilization is 0 because no request is sent to the service.
4. Run the following command to send requests to the inference service and check whether the service is
deployed:

```bash
curl -v "http://47.95.XX.XX/predict?query=Music"
```

Expected output:

```
*   Trying 47.95.XX.XX...
* TCP_NODELAY set
* Connected to 47.95.XX.XX (47.95.XX.XX) port 80 (#0)
> GET /predict?query=Music HTTP/1.1
> Host: 47.95.XX.XX
> User-Agent: curl/7.64.1
> Accept: */*
```

`>`

```
* HTTP 1.0, assume close after body
< HTTP/1.0 200 OK < Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < Content-Length: 9 < Server: Werkzeug/1.0.1 Python/3.6.9 < Date: Wed, 16 Feb 2022 03:52:11 GMT
```

`<`

```
* Closing connection 0
PlayMusic # The query result.
```

If the HTTP status code 200 and the query result are returned, the inference service is deployed.
2. . Configure the HPA**
The following example describes how to trigger Auto Scaling when the GPU utilization of a pod exceeds 20%. The following table describes the metrics that are supported by the HPA.

| Metric | Description | Unit |
|---|---|---|

| DCGM FI DEV GPU UTIL _ _ _ _ | The GPU utilization. This metric is available only for GPUs that are scheduled in exclusive mode. Important If a GPU is shared among multiple pods, only the utilization of the GPU is returned after you run the nvidia-smi command in one of the pods. This is because NVIDIA does not provide information about the GPU utilization of pods. |   | % |   |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DCGM FI DEV FB USED _ _ _ _ | The amount of GPU memory that is used. This metric is available only for GPUs that are scheduled in exclusive mode. |   | MiB |   |
| DCGM CUSTOM PROCESS SM UTIL _ _ _ _ | The GPU utilization of pods. |   | % |   |
| DCGM CUSTOM PROCESS MEM USE _ _ _ _ D | The amount of GPU memory that is used by pods. |   | MiB |   |
| DCGM CUSTOM PROCESS GPU MEM | The GPU memory utilization of pods. GPU memory utilization of a pod = Current GPU memory |   |   |   |
|   |   | GPU memory utilization of a pod = Current GPU memory | % |   |
| _ _ _ _ USED RATIO _ _ | used by the pod (Used)/Current GPU memory allocated to |   |   |   |
|   | the pod (Allocated) |   |   |   |

1. Run the following command to deploy the HPA based on the Kubernetes version of your cluster.

**Clusters that run Kubernetes 1.23 or later**

```
cat <<EOF | kubectl create -f apiVersion: autoscaling/v2 # Use the HPA configuration for API version autoscaling/v2. kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata:
  name: gpu-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: bert-intent-detection
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Pods
    pods:
      metric:
        name: DCGM_CUSTOM_PROCESS_SM_UTIL
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageValue: 20 # If the GPU utilization exceeds 20%, pods are scaled out.
EOF
```

**Clusters that run a Kubernetes version earlier than 1.23**

```
cat <<EOF | kubectl create -f apiVersion: autoscaling/v2beta1 # Use the HPA configuration for API version autoscaling/v2beta1. kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata:
  name: gpu-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: bert-intent-detection
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Pods
    pods:
      metricName: DCGM_CUSTOM_PROCESS_SM_UTIL # The GPU utilization of pods.
      targetAverageValue: 20 # If the GPU utilization exceeds 20%, pods are scaled out.
EOF
```

2. Run the following command to query the status of the HPA:

```bash
kubectl get hpa
```

Expected output:

```
NAME REFERENCE TARGETS MINPODS MAXPODS REPLICAS AGE gpu-hpa Deployment/bert-intent-detection 0/20 1 10 1 74s
```

The output shows that the value in the `TARGETS` column is `0/20` . This indicates that the current GPU utilization is 0. When the GPU utilization exceeds 20%, pods are scaled out.
3. . Test Auto Scaling on the inference service**

**Test the scale-out effect**

1. Run the following command to perform the stress test:

```
hey -n 10000 -c 200 "http://47.95.XX.XX/predict?query=music"
```

|   | Note The following formula is used to calculate the expected number of pods after Auto Scaling: Expected |   |
|---|---|---|
|   |   | Expected |
|   | number of pods = ceil [Current number of pods × (Current GPU utilization/Expected GPU |   |
|   | utilization)] |   |

> expected GPU utilization is 20, the expected number of pods after Auto Scaling is 2.

2. During the stress test, run the following command to query the status of the HPA and the pods:
i. Run the following command to query the status of the HPA:

```bash
kubectl get hpa
```

Expected output:

```
NAME REFERENCE TARGETS MINPODS MAXPODS REPLICAS AGE gpu-hpa Deployment/bert-intent-detection 23/20 1 10 2 7m56s
```

The output shows that the value in the `TARGETS` column is `23/20` . This indicates the current GPU utilization exceeds the threshold 20%. In this case, Auto Scaling is triggered and the ACK cluster starts to scale out pods. ii. Run the following command to query the status of the pods:

```bash
kubectl get pods
```

Expected output:

```
NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE bert-intent-detection-7b486f6bf-f**** 1/1 Running 0 44m bert-intent-detection-7b486f6bf-m**** 1/1 Running 0 14s
```

The output indicates that two pods are running. This value is the same as the expected number of pods calculated based on the preceding formula. The output returned by the HPA and the pods indicates that the pods are scaled out.

**Test the scale-in effect**

When the stress test stops and the GPU utilization drops below 20%, the ACK cluster starts to scale in pods.
1. Run the following command to query the status of the HPA:

```bash
kubectl get hpa
```

Expected output:

```
NAME REFERENCE TARGETS MINPODS MAXPODS REPLICAS AGE gpu-hpa Deployment/bert-intent-detection 0/20 1 10 1 15m
```

The output shows that the value in the `TARGETS` column is `0/20` . This indicates that the current GPU utilization drops to 0. The ACK cluster starts to scale in pods after about 5 minutes.
2. Run the following command to query the status of the pods:

```bash
kubectl get pods
```

Expected output:

```
NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE bert-intent-detection-7b486f6bf-f**** 1/1 Running 0 52m
```

The output shows that the number of pods is 1. This indicates that the pods are scaled in.

#### 7.19.7 Use labels to schedule pods to GPU-accelerated nodes

**accelerated nodes**

To use Kubernetes clusters for GPU computing, you must schedule pods to GPU-accelerated nodes. Container Service allows you to schedule pods to specific GPU-accelerated nodes by adding labels to the GPU-accelerated nodes.

**Background information**

When Kubernetes deploys nodes with NVIDIA GPUs, the attributes of these GPUs are discovered and exposed as node labels. These labels have the following benefits: You can use the labels to filter GPU-accelerated nodes. The labels can be used as conditions to schedule pods.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
3. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click **Details** in the **Actions** column.
4. In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Nodes > Nodes**.

> **Note:** In this example, the Kubernetes cluster contains three master nodes, among which two are equipped with GPUs. Record the node IP addresses.

5. On the **Nodes** page, select the node that is equipped with GPUs and choose **More > Details** in the
Actions column to view the labels that are added to the node. You can also log on to a master node and run the following command to view the labels of GPUaccelerated nodes:

```bash
# kubectl get nodes
NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION cn-beijing.i-2ze2dy2h9w97v65u**** Ready master 2d v1.12.6-aliyun.1 cn-beijing.i-2ze8o1a45qdv5q8a**** Ready <none> 2d v1.12.6-aliyun.1 # Compare these nodes with the nodes displayed in the console to identify GPU-accelerated nodes. cn-beijing.i-2ze8o1a45qdv5q8a**** Ready <none> 2d v1.12.6-aliyun.1 cn-beijing.i-2ze9xylyn11vop7g**** Ready master 2d v1.12.6-aliyun.1 cn-beijing.i-2zed5sw8snjniq6m**** Ready master 2d v1.12.6-aliyun.1 cn-beijing.i-2zej9s0zijykp9pw**** Ready <none> 2d v1.12.6-aliyun.1
```

Select a GPU-accelerated node and run the following command to query the labels of the node:

```bash
# kubectl describe node cn-beijing.i-2ze8o1a45qdv5q8a****
Name: cn-beijing.i-2ze8o1a45qdv5q8a7luz Roles: <none> Labels: aliyun.accelerator/nvidia_count=1 #Note
                    aliyun.accelerator/nvidia_mem=12209MiB
                    aliyun.accelerator/nvidia_name=Tesla-M40
                    beta.kubernetes.io/arch=amd64
                    beta.kubernetes.io/instance-type=ecs.gn4-c4g1.xlarge
                    beta.kubernetes.io/os=linux
                    failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/region=cn-beijing
                    failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone=cn-beijing-a
                    kubernetes.io/hostname=cn-beijing.i-2ze8o1a45qdv5q8a****
 ......
```

In this example, the following labels are added to the GPU-accelerated node.

| key | value |
|---|---|
| aliyun.accelerator/nvidia count _ | The number of GPU cores. |
| aliyun.accelerator/nvidia mem _ | The size of the GPU memory. Unit: MiB. |

| aliyun.accelerator/nvidia name _ | The name of the NVIDIA GPU. |
|---|---|

GPU-accelerated nodes of the same type have the same GPU name. You can use this label to locate GPUaccelerated nodes.

```bash
# kubectl get no -l aliyun.accelerator/nvidia_name=Tesla-M40
NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION cn-beijing.i-2ze8o1a45qdv5q8a**** Ready <none> 2d v1.12.6-aliyun.1 cn-beijing.i-2ze8o1a45qdv5q8a**** Ready <none> 2d v1.12.6-aliyun.1
```

6. In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Workloads > Deployments**.
7. On the **Deployments** page, select the namespace and click **Create from Template** in the upper-right
corner.
8. Create a Deployment for a TensorFlow job. The Deployment is used to schedule pods to a GPU-
accelerated node.
9. You can also exclude an application from GPU-accelerated nodes. The following example shows how to
schedule a pod based on node affinity for an NGINX application. For more information, see the section that describes node affinity in Create an application from an image. The following YAML template is used as an example:

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata:
  name: not-in-gpu-node
spec:
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
        - matchExpressions:
          - key: aliyun.accelerator/nvidia_name
            operator: DoesNotExist
  containers:
  - name: not-in-gpu-node
    image: nginx
```

**Result**

In the left-side navigation pane of the details page, choose **Workloads > Pods**. On the Pods page, select the namespace to view pods created in the namespace. On the Pods page, you can find that the pods in the preceding examples are scheduled to the desired nodes. This means that labels can be used to schedule pods to GPU-accelerated nodes.

#### 7.19.8 Manually upgrade the kernel of a GPU node in a cluster

**in a cluster**

This topic describes how to manually upgrade the kernel of a GPU node in a cluster.

**Background information**

The current kernel version is earlier than `3.10.0-957.21.3` .

**Procedure**

1. Connect to an ACK cluster by using kubectl.
2. Run the following command to set the target GPU node to unschedulable. This example uses node cn-
beijing.i-2ze19qyi8votgjz12345 as the target node.

```bash
kubectl cordon cn-beijing.i-2ze19qyi8votgjz12345 node/cn-beijing.i-2ze19qyi8votgjz12345 already cordoned
```

3. Run the following command to drain the target GPU node:

```bash
# kubectl drain cn-beijing.i-2ze19qyi8votgjz12345 --grace-period=120 --ignore-daemonsets=true
node/cn-beijing.i-2ze19qyi8votgjz12345 cordoned WARNING: Ignoring DaemonSet-managed pods: flexvolume-9scb4, kube-flannel-ds-r2qmh, kube-proxyworker-l62sf, logtail-ds-f9vbg pod/nginx-ingress-controller-78d847fb96-5fkkw evicted
```

4. Uninstall the existing nvidia-driver.

> **Note:** This step uninstalls the version 384.111 driver. If your driver version is not 384.111, you need to download a driver from the official NVIDIA website and replace `384.111` with your actual version number.

| Log on to the target GPU node and run the | nvidia-smi | command to query the driver version. |
|---|---|---|
| # nvidia-smi -a \| grep 'Driver Version' Driver Version : 384.111 |   |   |

ii. Run the following commands to download the driver installation package:

```bash
cd /tmp/ curl -O https://cn.download.nvidia.cn/tesla/384.111/NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-384.111.run
```

> **Note:** The installation package is required to uninstall the driver.

iii. Run the following commands to uninstall the existing nvidia-driver:

```
chmod u+x NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-384.111.run . /NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-384.111.run --uninstall -a -s -q
```

5. Run the following commands to upgrade kernel:

```bash
yum clean all && yum makecache yum update kernel -y
```

6. Run the following command to restart the GPU node:

```
reboot
```

7. Log on to the GPU node and run the following command to install the kernel-devel package.

```bash
yum install -y kernel-devel-$(uname -r)
```

8. Run the following commands to download the required driver and install it on the target node. In this
example, version 410.79 is used.

```bash
cd /tmp/ curl -O https://cn.download.nvidia.cn/tesla/410.79/NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-410.79.run chmod u+x NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-410.79.run sh . /NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-410.79.run -a -s -q
# warm up GPU
nvidia-smi -pm 1 || true nvidia-smi -acp 0 || true nvidia-smi --auto-boost-default=0 || true nvidia-smi --auto-boost-permission=0 || true nvidia-modprobe -u -c=0 -m || true
```

9. Check the /etc/rc.d/rc.local file and check whether the following configurations are included. If not, add the
following content.

```
nvidia-smi -pm 1 || true nvidia-smi -acp 0 || true nvidia-smi --auto-boost-default=0 || true nvidia-smi --auto-boost-permission=0 || true nvidia-modprobe -u -c=0 -m || true
```

0. Run the following commands to restart kubelet and Docker.

```
service kubelet stop service docker restart service kubelet start
```

1. Run the following command to set the GPU node to schedulable:

```bash
# kubectl uncordon cn-beijing.i-2ze19qyi8votgjz12345
node/cn-beijing.i-2ze19qyi8votgjz12345 already uncordoned
```

2. Run the following command on the nvidia-device-plugin container to check the driver version:

#### 7.19.9 Configure RAM role authorization for ack-ai-installer

**installer**

After you deploy the ack-ai-installer component in your Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster, ackai-installer may need to make API calls. To allow ack-ai-installer to make API calls, you must grant the required permissions to the worker Resource Access Management (RAM) role of your cluster. This topic describes how to configure RAM role authorization for ack-ai-installer in Apsara Stack V3.18.2.

**Step 1: Obtain the worker RAM role of a cluster**

1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, find the cluster that you want to manage and click its name. You can also click
**Details** in the **Actions** column to go to the cluster details page.
3. On the **Cluster Information** page, click the **Cluster Resources** tab and obtain the **worker RAM role**.

**Step 2: Obtain the ******************************************

**organization to which the cluster belongs**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top navigation bar, click **Enterprise**.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Resources > Organizations**.
3. On the **Organizations** page, select the organization to which the cluster belongs and click **Manage**
**AccessKey Pairs** on the right side of the page.
4. In the **Manage ***************** dialog box, obtain the **************** and ********************.

**Step 3: Create a RAM policy**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top menu bar, choose **Products >**
**Developer Tools > Developer Portal**.
2. At the top of the **Developer Portal** page, choose **API Integration** > **Unified Cloud Management**
**Platform** > **API Debugging**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, select **2015-05-01** from the **Version** drop-down list, enter **CreatePolicy**
in the search box, and then find and click CreatePolicy.
4. On the **CreatePolicy** page, configure the parameters on the **Parameter** tab.
The following table describes some of the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| AccessKeyId | The AccessKey ID that you obtained in Step 2. |
| AccessKeySecret |   |
| PolicyName | The name of the policy. Enter a name based on your business requirements. |
| PolicyDocument | The required permissions in the Action field. The following sample code shows an example: { "Version": "1", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "cs:DescribeUserQuota*", "cs:SyncClusterNodePool*" ], "Resource": "*" } ] } |

5. After you complete the configuration, click **Initiate Call** in the lower part of the **Parameter** tab.
If **200** is displayed on the **Call Result** tab, the API call is successful and the policy is created.

**Step 4: Attach the policy to the RAM role**

1. Log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console. In the top menu bar, choose **Products >**
**Developer Tools > Developer Portal**.
2. At the top of the **Developer Portal** page, choose **API Integration** > **Unified Cloud Management**
**Platform** > **API Debugging**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, select **2015-05-01** from the **Version** drop-down list, enter
**AttachPolicyToRole** in the search box, and then find and click AttachPolicyToRole.
4. On the **AttachPolicyToRole** page, configure the parameters on the **Parameter** tab.
The following table describes some of the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|

| AccessKeyId | The AccessKey ID that you obtained in Step 2. |
|---|---|
| AccessKeySecret |   |
| PolicyType | The type of the policy. In this example, Custom is used. |
| PolicyName | The name that you specified for PolicyName in Substep 5 of Step 3. |
| RoleName | The worker RAM role that is obtained in Step 1. |

5. After you complete the configuration, click **Initiate Call** in the lower-part of the **Parameter** tab.
If **200** is displayed on the **Call Result** tab, the call is successful. The permissions are granted to the worker RAM role of the cluster.

#### 7.19.10 Specify an NVIDIA driver version

This topic describes how to specify an NVIDIA driver version for GPU-accelerated nodes.

**Prerequisites**

A Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) dedicated cluster whose Kubernetes version is 3.16.2 or later is created. For more information, see Create an ACK cluster.

**Usage notes**

ACK does not guarantee the compatibility of NVIDIA drivers with the CUDA toolkit. You need to verify their compatibility. If you use a custom NVIDIA driver, the NVIDIA driver may be incompatible with the operating system version, Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instance type, or container runtime. As a result, GPU-accelerated nodes fail to be added. ACK does not guarantee that all nodes can be successfully added to a cluster. If you add a label to a node pool to specify an NVIDIA driver version for GPU-accelerated nodes, the specified NVIDIA driver is installed only when a node is added to the node pool. The NVIDIA driver is not installed on the existing nodes in the node pool. If you want to install the NVIDIA driver on the existing nodes, you need to remove these nodes from the node pool and re-add them to the node pool.

**Procedure**

**Upload the driver files**

1. Find the service role component Cert in Apsara Infrastructure Management and upload the following files
to the virtual machines (VMs) where the Cert component is deployed. The following table describes the drive files.

| Driver version | Download link | MD5 |
|---|---|---|
| 470.161.03 | nvidia-driver-470.161.03.tar.gz | 4bed9ef157aaef4fda4f4ecd74501ad8 |
| 525.105.17 | nvidia-driver-525.105.17.tar.gz | 69e7fbb699a59f069545c98775ae22bb |

2. Upload the files to the `/opt/static/static/k8s/private/pkg/nvidia-driver` directory of the Cert
component.

> **Note:** Run the following command on the two VMs where the Cert component is deployed:

```bash
# In this example, the installation package of NVIDIA driver 470.161.03 is uploaded. To upload othe
r packages, modify the package name. export NVIDIA_DRIVER=nvidia-driver-470.161.03.tar.gz container_id=`docker ps | grep Cert_ | awk '{print $1}'` docker cp $NVIDIA_DRIVER $container_id:/opt/static/static/k8s/private/pkg/nvidia-driver/
```

**Create a node pool and specify the NVIDIA driver version**

In the following example, the driver version 470.161.03 is used.
1. Log on to the ACK console. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**.
2. On the **Clusters** page, click the name of the cluster that you want to manage and choose **Nodes > Node**
**Pools** in the left-side navigation pane.
3. In the upper-right corner of the Node Pools page, click **Create Node Pool**. In the **Create Node Pool**
dialog box, configure the basic information and click **Show Advanced Options**. In the **Node Label** section, click the icon, set **Key** to `ack.aliyun.com/nvidia-driver-version` , set **Value** to `470.161.03` , and then click **Confirm Order**. For more information about the parameters, see Create a node pool.
4. In the **Create Node Pool** dialog box, make sure that the **configurations** are valid and the **dependency**
**check** is passed, and then click **Submit**.

**Verify the result**

### 7.20 Scheduling

#### 7.20.1 CPU scheduling

##### 7.20.1.1 CPU Burst

CPU Burst is a service level objective (SLO)-aware resource scheduling feature provided by Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK). You can use CPU Burst to improve the performance of latency-sensitive applications. CPU scheduling for a container may be throttled by the kernel due to the CPU limit, which downgrades the performance of the application. The ack-koordinator component automatically detects CPU throttling events and adjusts the CPU limit to a proper value. This greatly improves the performance of latency-sensitive applications. This topic introduces CPU Burst. This topic also describes how to use CPU Burst and how to verify the performance improvement.

**Prerequisites**

An ACK dedicated cluster is created. For more information, see Create an ACK cluster. ack-koordinator is installed. For more information, see ack-koordinator. The following table describes the versions of the system components that are required for enabling CPU Burst.

| Component | Required version |
|---|---|
| Kubernetes | ≥ 1.18 |
| ack-koordinator | ≥ 0.8.0 |

**Use scenarios**

CPU Burst is suitable in the following scenarios:
1. CPU throttling is triggered for an application though the CPU usage of the application is less than the CPU
limit of the application. As a result, the performance of the application is degraded. You can enable CPU Burst to resolve this issue and improve the performance of the application.
2. The CPU usage during an application startup is higher than the CPU usage after the application is started.
You can enable CPU Burst to meet the CPU requirements during an application startup. This way, you do not need to specify an excessively high CPU request for the application, which reduces resource waste.

**How CPU Burst works**

CPU resources can be reused based on time-sharing. Kubernetes allows you to specify a CPU limit for a container. If you specify a CPU limit for a container, the OS limits the amount of CPU resources that can be used by the container within a specific time period. For example, you set the CPU limit of a container to 2. The OS kernel limits the CPU time slices that the container can use to 200 milliseconds within each 100millisecond period. CPU utilization is a key metric that is used to evaluate the performance of a container. In most cases, the CPU limit is specified based on CPU utilization. CPU utilization on a per-millisecond basis shows more spikes than that on a per-second basis. If the CPU utilization of a container reaches the limit within a 100millisecond period, CPU throttling is enforced by the OS kernel and threads in the container are suspended for the rest of the time period, as shown in the following figure. The following figure shows the thread allocation of a web application container that runs on a node with four CPU cores. The CPU limit of the container is set to 2. The overall CPU utilization within the last second is low. However, Thread 2 cannot be resumed until the beginning of the third 100-millisecond period, because CPU throttling occurs at a specific point during the second 100-millisecond period. This increases the response time (RT) and causes long-tail latency problems in containers. Alibaba Cloud Linux 2 provides the CPU Burst feature in kernel version 4.19.91-22.al7. CPU Burst allows a container to accumulate CPU time slices when the container is idle. The container can use the accumulated CPU time slices to burst above the CPU limit when CPU utilization spikes. This improves performance and reduces the RT of the container. For kernel versions that do not support CPU Burst, ack-koordinator detects CPU throttling events and dynamically adjusts the CPU limit to achieve the same effect as CPU Burst.

> **Note:** ack-koordinator achieves this by modifying the value of the `Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) quota` in the cgroup parameters instead of modifying the value of the CPU limit in the pod specifications.

The preceding CFS quota adjustment policy can be used to handle CPU usage spikes For example, when traffic spikes occur, ack-koordinator can eliminate CPU bottlenecks within a few seconds, while ensuring a proper number of workloads on the node. The CPU Burst feature supported by the kernel of Alibaba Cloud Linux handles CPU usage spikes at a faster rate. We recommend that you enable the CPU Burst feature provided by the kernel of Alibaba Cloud Linux for latency-sensitive applications. For more information about CPU Burst, see the Alibaba Cloud presentation at KubeCon 2021: CPU Burst: Getting Rid of Unnecessary Throttling, Achieving High CPU Utilization and Application Performance at the Same Time.

**How to use CPU Burst**

**Use an annotation to enable CPU Burst**

> **Important:** To enable CPU Burst for a pod, configure the `annotations` parameter in the `metadata` section of the pod configuration.
> To enable CPU Burst for a Deployment, configure the `annotations` parameter in the
> `template.metadata` section of the Deployment configuration.

```bash
annotations:
  # Set the value to auto to enable CPU Burst for the pod.
  koordinator.sh/cpuBurst: '{"policy": "auto"}'
  # Set the value to none to disable CPU Burst for the pod.
  #koordinator.sh/cpuBurst: '{"policy": "none"}'
```

**Use a ConfigMap to enable CPU Burst for all pods in a cluster**

Modify the ack-slo-config ConfigMap based on the following content to enable CPU Burst for all pods in a cluster:

```
apiVersion: v1 data:
  cpu-burst-config: '{"clusterStrategy": {"policy": "auto"}}'
  #cpu-burst-config: '{"clusterStrategy": {"policy": "cpuBurstOnly"}}'
  #cpu-burst-config: '{"clusterStrategy": {"policy": "none"}}'
kind: ConfigMap metadata:
  name: ack-slo-config
  namespace: kube-system
```

To avoid modifying other configurations in the ConfigMap, we recommend that you update the ConfigMap by using a patch. To do this, run the following command:

```bash
kubectl patch cm -n kube-system ack-slo-config --patch "$(cat configmap.yaml)
```

**Enable CPU Burst for pods in specified namespaces**

```bash
apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata:
  name: ack-slo-pod-config
  namespace: koordinator-system # If this is the first time you use CPU Burst, you must first creat
e a namespace named koordinator-system. data:
  # Enable or disable CPU Burst for pods in specified namespaces.
  cpu-burst: |
```

`{`

```json
      "enabledNamespaces": ["white-ns"],
      "disabledNamespaces": ["black-ns"]
```

`}`

**Advanced configurations**

You can specify advanced configurations in the ConfigMap or the `annotations` parameter in the `metadata` section of the pod configuration.

```bash
# Example of the ack-slo-config ConfigMap.
data:
  cpu-burst-config: |
```

`{`

```json
      "clusterStrategy": {
        "policy": "auto",
        "cpuBurstPercent": 1000,
        "cfsQuotaBurstPercent": 300,
        "sharePoolThresholdPercent": 50,
        "cfsQuotaBurstPeriodSeconds": -1
```

`}` `}`

```bash
# Example of pod annotations.
  koordinator.sh/cpuBurst: '{"policy": "auto", "cpuBurstPercent": 1000, "cfsQuotaBurstPercent":
300, "cfsQuotaBurstPeriodSeconds": -1}'
```

The following table describes the advanced parameters of CPU Burst.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| policy | string | none: disables CPU Burst. If you set the value to none, the related fields are reset to their original values. This is the default value. cpuBurstOnly: enables the CPU Burst feature only for the kernel of Alibaba Cloud Linux 2. cfsQuotaBurstOnly: enables automatic adjustment of CFS quotas of general kernel versions. auto: enables CPU Burst and all the related features, including CPU Burst for the kernel of Alibaba Cloud Linux and automatic adjustment of CFS quotas of general kernel versions. |
| cpuBurstPercent | int | Default value: 1000 . Unit: %. This field is used to configure the CPU Burst feature for the kernel of Alibaba Cloud Linux 2. This field specifies the percentage to which the CPU limit can be increased by CPU Burst. If the CPU limit is set to 1 , CPU Burst can increase the limit to 10 by default. For more information, see Enable the CPU Burst feature for cgroup v1. |

| cfsQuotaBurstPerce nt | int | Default value: 300 . Unit: %. This field specifies the maximum percentage to which the value of cfs quota _ in the cgroup parameters can be increased. By default, the value of cfs quota _ can be increased to at most three times. |
|---|---|---|
| cfsQuotaBurstPeriod Seconds | int | Default value: -1 . Unit: seconds. This indicates that the time period in which the container can run with an increased CFS quota is unlimited. This field specifies the time period in which the container can run with an increased CFS quota, which cannot exceed the upper limit specified by cfsQuotaBurstPercent . |
| sharePoolThreshold Percent | int | Default value: 50 . Unit: %. This field specifies the CPU utilization threshold of the node. If the CPU utilization of the node exceeds the threshold, the value of cfs quota in _ cgroup parameters is reset to the original value. |

> **Important:** After you set `policy` to `cfsQuotaBurstOnly` or `auto` , the `CFS quota` assigned by the node OS is automatically adjusted based on whether CPU throttling is triggered.
> When you perform stress tests on a container, we recommend that you record the CPU utilization of the container throughout the test period or set `policy` to `cpuBurstOnly` or
> `none` . This ensures higher resource elasticity for your production environment.

**Verify the effect of CPU Burst**

1. Use the following YAML template to create an apache-demo.yaml file:
To enable CPU Burst for a pod, specify an annotation in the `annotations` parameter in the `metadata` section of the pod configuration.

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata:
  name: apache-demo
  annotations:
    koordinator.sh/cpuBurst: '{"policy": "auto"}'   # The annotation is used to enable or disable C
PU Burst. spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - httpd
    - -D
    - FOREGROUND
    image: registry.cn-zhangjiakou.aliyuncs.com/acs/apache-2-4-51-for-slo-test:v0.1
    imagePullPolicy: Always
    name: apache
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "4"
        memory: 10Gi
      requests:
        cpu: "4"
        memory: 10Gi
  nodeName: $nodeName # Replace nodeName with the actual node name.
  hostNetwork: False
  restartPolicy: Never
  schedulerName: default-scheduler
```

2. Run the following command to create an application by using Apache HTTP Server:

```bash
kubectl apply -f apache-demo.yaml
```

3. Use the wrk2 tool to perform stress tests.

```bash
# Download, decompress, and then install the wrk2 package. For more information, visit
https://github.com/giltene/wrk2.
# Gzip compression is enabled in the Apache image to simulate the request processing logic of the s
erver.
# Run the following command to send requests. Replace the IP address in the command with the IP add
ress of the application. ./wrk -H "Accept-Encoding: deflate, gzip" -t 2 -c 12 -d 120 --latency --timeout 2s -R 24 http://$target_ip_address:8010/static/file.1m.test
```

> **Note:** Replace the IP address in the command with the pod IP address of the Apache application.
> You can modify the -R field to change the number of queries per unit time from the sender.

**Analyze the result**

The following tables show metrics before and after CPU Burst is enabled for Alibaba Cloud Linux 2 and CentOS 7. The Disabled column shows the metrics when the CPU Burst policy is set to `none` . The Enabled column shows the metrics when the CPU Burst policy is set to `auto` .

| Alibaba Cloud Linux 2 | Disabled | Enabled |
|---|---|---|
| apache RT-p99 | 107.37 ms | 67.18 ms (-37.4%) |
| CPU Throttled Ratio | 33.3% | 0% |
| Average pod CPU utilization | 31.8% | 32.6% |

| CentOS 7 | Disabled | Enabled |
|---|---|---|
| apache RT-p99 | 111.69 ms | 71.30 ms (-36.2%) |
| CPU Throttled Ratio | 33% | 0% |
| Average pod CPU utilization | 32.5% | 33.8% |

The preceding metrics indicate the following information: After CPU Burst is enabled, the P99 latency is greatly reduced. After CPU Burst is enabled, CPU throttling is stopped and the average pod CPU utilization remains approximately at the same value.

#### 7.20.2 Fine grained scheduling

##### 7.20.2.1 CPU Suppress

The ack-koordinator component provides the CPU Suppress feature. You can use this feature to limit the CPU usage of BestEffort (BE) pods on a node. This topic describes how to use the CPU Suppress feature provided by ack-koordinator.

**Background information**

To ensure sufficient CPU resources for latency-sensitive (LS) pods on a node, you can use ack-koordinator to limit the CPU usage of the BE pods on the node. The CPU Suppress feature can maintain the resource utilization of a node below the specified threshold and limit the amount of CPU resources that can be used by BE pods. This ensures the stability of the containers on the node. The CPU Suppress feature can limit the amount of CPU resources that can be used by BE pods when the overall resource usage of the node is below the threshold. This ensures that the containers on the node have sufficient resources to run stably. In the following figure, CPU Threshold indicates the CPU usage threshold of a node. Pod (LS).Usage indicates the CPU usage of LS pods. CPU Restriction for BE indicates the CPU usage of BE pods. The amount of CPU resources that can be used by BE pods is adjusted based on the fluctuation of the CPU usage of LS pods. We recommend that you use the same value for CPU Threshold and the reserved CPU watermark in the dynamic resource overcommitment model. This ensures a consistent level of CPU resource utilization.

**Prerequisites**

ack-koordinator 0.4.0 or later is installed. For more information about how to install ack-koordinator, see ack-koordinator.

**Procedure**

1. Create a file named configmap.yaml based on the following ConfigMap content:

```bash
apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata:
  name: ack-slo-config
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  # Enable CPU Suppress.
  resource-threshold-config: |
```

`{`

```json
      "clusterStrategy": {
        "enable": true
```

`}` `}`

| hether the | ack-slo-config |
|---|---|
| ack-slo-config ConfigMap |   |

2. Check whether the `ack-slo-config` ConfigMap exists in the `kube-system` namespace.
If the `ack-slo-config` ConfigMap exists, we recommend that you run the kubectl patch command to update the ConfigMap. This avoids changing other settings in the ConfigMap.

```bash
kubectl patch cm -n kube-system ack-slo-config --patch "$(cat configmap.yaml)"
```

If the `ack-slo-config` ConfigMap does not exist, run the following command to create a ConfigMap named ack-slo-config:

```bash
kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml
```

3. Run the following command to query the CPU cores that are allocated to the BE pods on the node:

```
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset/kubepods.slice/kubepods-besteffort.slice/cpuset.cpus
```

Expected output:

```
10-25,35-51,62-77,87-103
```

The output shows that the following CPU cores are allocated to the BE pods on the node: `10-25, 35-51,`

```
62-77, and 87-103 .
```

4. **Optional:** Configure advanced parameters based on the following ConfigMap content.
CPU Suppress allows you to configure the CPU utilization threshold in a fine-grained manner.

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata:
  name: ack-slo-config
  namespace: kube-system
data:
```

```json
        "enable": true,
        "cpuSuppressThresholdPercent": 65
```

| cpuSuppressThresholdPerce nt | Int | 0~100 | The CPU utilization threshold of the node. Unit: %. Default value: 65 . |

##### 7.20.2.2 CPU QoS

Kubernetes lets you deploy multiple types of containerized applications on the same host. This causes applications with different priorities to compete for CPU resources. As a result, the performance of the applications with high priorities cannot be guaranteed. The ack-koordinator component lets you use quality of service (QoS) classes to guarantee CPU resources for applications with high priorities. This topic describes how to configure the CPU QoS feature for pods.

**Background Information**

To make full use of computing resources, workloads of different priorities are usually deployed on the same node. For example, a latency-sensitive (LS) workload (with a high priority) and a best-effort (BE) workload (with a low priority) can be deployed on the same node. However, this may cause these workloads to compete for computing resources. In Kubernetes, CPU requests and CPU limits are used to control the amount of CPU resources that pods can use. However, pods may still compete for CPU resources. For example, BE pods and LS pods can share CPU cores or vCPU cores. When the loads of the BE pods increase, the performance of the LS pods is compromised. As a result, the response latency of the application that uses the LS pods increases. To improve the stability of CPU resource usage for LS applications and reduce interference from BE applications, ack-koordinator provides the container CPU QoS feature based on Alibaba Cloud Linux. ackkoordinator uses Linux scheduling priorities provided by Group Identity to differentiate CPU scheduling for applications with different priorities. It identifies LS applications as high-priority and BE applications as lowpriority. This effectively improves the service quality of LS applications in co-located scenarios. You can gain the following benefits after you enable the CPU QoS feature: The wake-up latency of tasks for LS workloads is minimized. Waking up tasks for BE workloads does not adversely affect the performance of LS pods. Tasks for BE workloads cannot use the simultaneous multithreading (SMT) scheduler to share CPU cores. This further reduces the impact on the performance of LS pods.

**Prerequisites**

A Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) dedicated cluster is created. For more information, see Create an ACK cluster. ack-koordinator is installed. For more information, see ack-koordinator. The following table describes the version requirements for the system components.

| Component | Required version |
|---|---|
| Kubernetes | 1.18 or later |
| ack-koordinator | 0.8.0 or later |
| Helm | 3.0 or later |
| OS | Alibaba Cloud Linux |

> **Note:** If you do not use Alibaba Cloud Linux, you can use the elastic resource limit feature provided by ack- koordinator to ensure container CPU service quality. For more information, see Elastic resource limits.

**Procedure**

1. Create a file named configmap.yaml based on the following ConfigMap content:

```bash
# Example of the ack-slo-config ConfigMap.
apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata:
  name: ack-slo-config
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  # Enable the CPU QoS feature.
  resource-qos-config: |
```

`{`

```json
      "clusterStrategy": {
        "lsClass": {
          "cpuQOS": {
            "enable": true,
            "groupIdentity": 2
```

`}` `},`

```json
        "beClass": {
          "cpuQOS": {
            "enable": true,
            "groupIdentity": -1
```

`}` `}` `}` `}` `lsClass` and `beClass` are used to configure pods with the LS and BE QoS classes, respectively. `cpuQOS` is used to configure the container CPU QoS feature. The key parameters are described as follows:

|   | Parameter |   | Type | Value range | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|   | enable |   | Boolean | true false | true: enables the CPU QoS feature for all containers in the cluster. false: disables the CPU QoS feature for all containers in the cluster. |
|   | groupIdentit y |   | Int | -1~2 | Specify group identities for CPU scheduling. By default, the group identity of LS pods is 2 and the group identity of BE pods is -1. A value of 0 indicates that no group identity is assigned. A larger groupIdentity value indicates a higher kernel scheduling priority for the container. For example, with the default configurations, the Group Identity interface for a container with the LS QoS class is set to cpu.bvt warp ns=2 , and for a BE container, it is set _ _ to cpu.bvt warp ns=-1 . _ _ |
|   |   | groupIdentit |   |   |   |
|   | y |   |   |   |   |

> **Note:** For pods that do not have `koordinator.sh/qosClass` specified, ack-koordinator sets parameters based on the native QoS class of the pod. Pods of the BestEffort class use the BE configuration from the ConfigMap. Pods with other QoS classes use the LS configuration from the ConfigMap.

| hether the | ack-slo-config |
|---|---|
| ack-slo-config ConfigMap |   |

2. Check whether the `ack-slo-config` ConfigMap exists in the `kube-system` namespace.
If the `ack-slo-config` ConfigMap exists, run the patch command to update it. This prevents interference with other configuration items in the ConfigMap.

```bash
kubectl patch cm -n kube-system ack-slo-config --patch "$(cat configmap.yaml)"
```

If the `ack-slo-config` ConfigMap does not exist, run the following command to create it.

```bash
kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml
```

3. Create a file named ls-pod-demo.yaml and copy the following content to the file:

```
    koordinator.sh/qosClass: 'LS' # Set the QoS class of the pod to LS.

    - FOREGROUND
    image: registry.cn-zhangjiakou.aliyuncs.com/acs/apache-2-4-51-for-slo-test:v0.1
    imagePullPolicy: Always

    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "4"

  restartPolicy: Never
```

4. Run the following command to deploy the ls-pod-demo pod in the cluster:

5. Run the following command to check whether the CPU group identity of the LS pod in the control group

6. Create a file named be-pod-demo.yaml and copy the following content to the file:

```
  labels:
```

##### 7.20.2.3 Memory QoS for containers

ack-koordinator provides memory Quality of Service (QoS) for containers. This feature improves the runtime memory performance of applications and ensures the fair allocation of memory resources. This topic describes how to use the container memory QoS feature.

**Background information**

Containers have two main constraints when using memory: Container memory limit: When a container's memory usage, including the page cache, approaches its limit, the kernel's memory reclamation subsystem is triggered. This process affects the performance of memory requests and releases within the container. Node memory limit: If container memory is overcommitted (Memory Limit > Request) and causes the node to have insufficient memory, the kernel triggers global memory reclamation. This process has a significant performance impact and, in extreme cases, can cause the node to become abnormal. To improve application runtime performance and node stability, ACK introduces the container memory QoS feature. ack-koordinator works with Alibaba Cloud Linux to enhance memory performance for applications. When this feature is enabled, ack-koordinator automatically configures the memory subsystem (Memcg) based on container parameters. This optimizes the performance of memory-sensitive applications while ensuring the fair allocation of node memory resources.

**Prerequisites**

An ACK dedicated cluster is created. For more information, see Create an ACK cluster. ack-koordinator is installed. For more information, see ack-koordinator. The following table lists the required component versions.

| Component | Version requirement |
|---|---|
| Kubernetes | 1.18 or later |
| ack-koordinator | 0.8.0 or later |
| Helm version | v3.0 or later |
| Operating system | Alibaba Cloud Linux |

**Function introduction**

Applications deployed in a Kubernetes cluster follow the standard Kubernetes Request/Limit model for resource usage. As shown in the following figure, a pod's memory request serves only as a reference for scheduling capacity. The memory limit is the actual constraint on a single node. In the figure, memory.limit_in_bytes represents the memory usage limit. When a pod's memory usage, including the page cache, approaches its declared limit, it triggers direct memory reclamation at the memory subsystem (Memcg) level, which blocks process execution. If the memory request rate exceeds the reclamation rate, the container triggers an OOMKilled event and releases its memory. An administrator might increase the application's memory limit to reduce the risk of a pod OOM. However, this can lead to memory overcommitment, where the sum of memory limits on a node exceeds its physical capacity. In an overcommitted state, a pod requesting a large amount of memory can cause the entire node to run out of memory. This can trigger node-level memory reclamation or OOM events for other pods that request memory, because Kubernetes does not enable Swap by default. In both scenarios, a single pod can impact the memory access performance of other pods, which significantly affects their performance even if they have not exceeded their declared memory requests. ack-koordinator, combined with Alibaba Cloud Linux, provides container memory QoS. It automatically configures the memory subsystem (Memcg) based on pod parameters. It enables Memcg QoS, background memory reclamation, and global minimum watermark classification for containers. This ensures both QoS and fairness for container memory resources. Enabling container memory QoS provides the following features: When a pod's memory usage approaches its limit, a portion of its memory is asynchronously reclaimed in the background. This mitigates the performance impact of direct memory reclamation. Memory reclamation among pods is fairer. When a node has insufficient memory resources, memory is first reclaimed from pods that are overusing memory (Memory Usage > Request). This prevents individual pods from degrading the quality of the node's memory resources. In memory overcommitment scenarios with BestEffort pods, the memory quality for Guaranteed and Burstable pods is prioritized. When differentiated Service Level Objective (SLO) co-location is enabled for a cluster, the system prioritizes the memory QoS of Latency-Sensitive (LS) pods. This delays the triggering of node-level memory reclamation for LS pods. In the following figure, memory.limit_in_bytes is the memory usage limit, memory.high is the memory throttling threshold, memory.wmark_high is the background memory reclamation threshold, and memory.min is the locked memory usage threshold.

> **Note:** Kubernetes 1.22 introduced the MemoryQoS feature. You can enable it on the Kubelet to support container memory locking and proactive throttling, which improves the fairness of memory resource allocation. This feature is currently in the Alpha stage. It supports only Linux cgroups v2, which requires a kernel version of 4.15 or later and is incompatible with cgroups v1. Enabling it affects all containers on the node. The ACK container memory QoS feature supports this capability on cgroups v1. It also provides additional performance optimizations and differentiated SLO capabilities, such as background memory reclamation and minimum watermark classification.

**Procedure**

When you enable container memory QoS for a pod, the memory subsystem (Memcg) automatically adjusts based on coefficient configurations and pod parameters. Follow these steps to enable the feature.
1. Add the following annotation to the pod's YAML file to enable the container memory QoS feature for an
individual pod.

```bash
annotations:
  # Set the value to auto to enable the container memory QoS feature for this pod.
  koordinator.sh/memoryQOS: '{"policy": "auto"}'
  # Set the value to none to disable the container memory QoS feature for this pod.
  #koordinator.sh/memoryQOS: '{"policy": "none"}'
```

2. Use a ConfigMap to enable container memory QoS globally.
i. Use the following sample ConfigMap to enable the container memory QoS feature for the entire cluster.

```
apiVersion: v1 data:
  resource-qos-config: |-
```

`{`

```json
      "clusterStrategy": {
        "lsClass": {
           "memoryQOS": {
             "enable": true
```

`}` `},`

```json
        "beClass": {
           "memoryQOS": {
             "enable": true
```

`}` `}` `}` `}`

```
kind: ConfigMap metadata:
  name: ack-slo-config
  namespace: kube-system
```

ii. In the pod's YAML file, specify the QoS class to use the cluster configuration.

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata:
  name: pod-demo
  labels:
    koordinator.sh/qosClass: 'LS' # Specify the QoS class of the pod as LS.
```

`LS` and `BE` represent two typical application types that correspond to the cluster-wide settings in the preceding ConfigMap. After the cluster-wide setting is enabled, you only need to add the `koordinator.sh/qosClass` annotation to a pod for the parameters to take effect. You do not need to repeat the configuration in the pod's annotations. For pods that do not have the

| koordinator.sh/qosClass |   |   |
|---|---|---|
| QoSClass. | Guaranteed | po |

`koordinator.sh/qosClass` annotation, ack-koordinator sets the parameters based on the pod's native QoSClass. `Guaranteed` pods use the system's internal default values. Burstable and BestEffort pods use the default configurations for `LS` and `BE` from the ConfigMap, respectively. For more information about the default configurations, see Parameter descriptions. You can use `koordinator.sh/qosClass` to centrally manage memory QoS parameters. iii. Check whether the ConfigMap `ack-slo-config` exists in the `kube-system` namespace. If the `ack-slo-config` ConfigMap exists, use the PATCH method to update it. This prevents interference with other configuration items in the ConfigMap.

```bash
kubectl patch cm -n kube-system ack-slo-config --patch "$(cat configmap.yaml)"
```

If the `ack-slo-config` ConfigMap does not exist, run the following command to create it.

```bash

```

3. Use a ConfigMap to enable container memory QoS for pods in a specific namespace.
To enable or disable parameter settings for `LS` and `BE` pods in specific namespaces, you can use the following sample ConfigMap. This lets you enable or disable the container memory QoS feature for pods within a specified namespace. i. Create a file named ack-slo-pod-config.yaml with the following ConfigMap content. This example enables or disables the container memory QoS feature for pods in the kube-system namespace.

```bash

  name: ack-slo-pod-config
  namespace: koordinator-system # You must manually create this namespace before the first use.
data:
  # Enable or disable the feature for pods in specific namespaces.

```

`{`

```json

```

`}` ii. Run the following command to update the ConfigMap.


4. (Optional) Configure advanced parameters.
Container memory QoS supports fine-grained configuration at the pod and cluster levels. The following table describes the relevant parameters. For other requirements, you can contact technical support.

| Parameter | Type | Value range | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| enable | Boolean | true false | true : Enables the container memory QoS feature globally for the cluster. Containers of the corresponding QoS class use the recommended memory subsystem configuration. false : Disables the container memory QoS feature globally for the cluster. The memory subsystem configuration for containers of the corresponding QoS class is reset to its initial value at creation. |
| policy | String | auto default none | auto : Enables the container memory QoS feature for the pod and uses the recommended parameters. This setting takes precedence over the cluster ConfigMap configuration. default : The pod inherits the cluster ConfigMap configuration. none : Disables the container memory QoS feature for the pod. The relevant memory subsystem configuration is reset to its initial value at creation. This setting takes precedence over the cluster ConfigMap configuration. |

|   | minLimitPercen t |   | Int |   | 0 to 100 | Unit: Percent. The default value is 0 , which means the feature is disabled. This parameter specifies the percentage of the memory request that is absolutely locked for the container and cannot be reclaimed globally. The calculation is memory.min = request * minLimitPercent / 100 . This is suitable for scenarios sensitive to the page cache. It reserves a portion of the file cache to improve read and write performance. For example, if a container has Memory Request=100 MiB and minLimitPercent=100 , then memory.min=104857600 . |   |   |   |

The calculation is memory.low = request * lowLimitPercent / 100 . For example, if a container has Memory Request=100 MiB and lowLimitPercent=100 , then memory.low=104857600 . |   |   |   |

**Usage example**

The evaluation environment for this example is as follows: A dedicated cluster of version 1.20. The cluster contains two nodes: a stress testing node (8 cores, 32 GB) and a test node (8 cores, 32 GB).
1. Create a file named redis-demo.yaml with the following YAML content.

```
--apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata:
  name: redis-demo-config
data:
  redis-config: |
    appendonly yes
    appendfsync no
--apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata:
  name: redis-demo
  labels:
    koordinator.sh/qosClass: 'LS' # Specify the QoS class of the Redis instance as LS.
  annotations:
    koordinator.sh/memoryQOS: '{"policy": "auto"}' # Add the container memory QoS configuration.
spec:
  containers:
  - name: redis
    image: redis:5.0.4
command:
```

```
    command:
      - redis-server
      - "/redis-master/redis.conf"
    env:
    - name: MASTER
      value: "true"
    ports:
    - containerPort: 6379
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: "6Gi"
      requests:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: "2Gi"
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /redis-master-data
      name: data
    - mountPath: /redis-master
      name: config
  volumes:
    - name: data
      emptyDir: {}
    - name: config
      configMap:
        name: redis-demo-config
        items:
        - key: redis-config
          path: redis.conf
  nodeName: # Change nodeName to the name of your test node.
--apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata:
  name: redis-demo
spec:
  ports:
  - name: redis-port
    port: 6379
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 6379
  selector:
    name: redis-demo
  type: ClusterIP
```

2. Run the following command to deploy Redis Server as the target evaluation application.
You can access the application from within the cluster through the redis-demo Service.

```bash
kubectl apply -f redis-demo.yaml
```

3. Simulate a memory overcommitment scenario.
Use the Stress tool to create high memory pressure on the node and trigger system memory reclamation. The sum of the memory limits of the pods allocated on the node exceeds the node's total memory. i. Create a file named stress-demo.yaml with the following pod YAML content.

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata:
  name: stress-demo
  labels:
    koordinator.sh/qosClass: 'BE' # Specify the QoS class of the Stress instance as BE.
  annotations:
    koordinator.sh/memoryQOS: '{"policy": "auto"}' # Add the memory QoS configuration.
spec:
  containers:
    - args:
        - '--vm'
        - '2'
        - '--vm-bytes'
        - 11G
        - '-c'
        - '2'
        - '--vm-hang'
        - '2'
      command:
        - stress
      image: polinux/stress
      imagePullPolicy: Always
      name: stress
  restartPolicy: Always
  nodeName: # Change nodeName to the name of your test node. This should be the same node as the
Redis node.
```

ii. Run the following command to deploy stress-demo.

```bash
kubectl apply -f stress-demo.yaml
```

4. Run the following command to view the system's global minimum watermark.

> **Note:** Because the system's global minimum watermark is low, memory might not be reclaimed in time to prevent a node-level OOM in a memory overcommitment scenario. Therefore, this feature is typically used with a higher global minimum watermark. For example, for a test machine with 32 GiB of memory, you can set the minimum watermark to 4,000,000 KB.

```
cat /proc/sys/vm/min_free_kbytes
```

Expected output:

```
4000000
```

5. Create and run a pod that uses the memtier-benchmark stress testing tool to send requests.

```
apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata:
  labels:
    name: memtier-demo
  name: memtier-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - command:
        - memtier_benchmark
        - '-s'
        - 'redis-demo'
        - '--data-size'
        - '200000'
        - "--ratio"
        - "1:4"
```
